column121: Taxiing on inner line to spot XX at CLT west ramp our clearance was spot XX to join the line to 5W. Approaching the spot I looked left and didn't see anything. We were slowing to make a right turn and the FO said clear right. I looked left to say clear left and saw Aircraft Y approaching which appeared close and I applied brakes. Firm at first then eased off. We sat at the spot for a minute and the Aircraft Y pilot asked ramp controller what going on. Who was giving way and why weren't they notified. Ramp controller said that she didn't think Aircraft Y was going to turn the corner that fast and it wasn't going to be an issue. Well it was. The ramp controller told Aircraft Y to give way to us and we proceeded to take off. I didn't call the cabin to see if everyone was ok. I thought they would call us if something was wrong. We flew to ZZZ without incident and had normal communications with the cabin. After shut down and leaving the flight deck a couple of F/A's asked what happened taxiing in CLT. When we got to the top of the bridge by the gate we told them what happened. The number 1 said she bumped her arm in the galley and the number 3 bumped her head. The number 2 said her back hit the galley wall. I asked why they didn't call us in CLT. They were preparing for takeoff was the answer I got. I asked if anyone needed medical attention and was told not yet. I called dispatch per the FOM for a follow up since everyone was able to preform their duties.Cause: Ramp control to give specific instructions as to who is following who. Communication from the cabin telling us they were injured before we depart. Not after completing the flight.
column123: When departing the west ramp from the gate in Charlotte we received instructions to taxi to spot XX; then join the line to 5W and contact ground. As we approached spot XX I looked out the right windows to make sure we were clear for the turn on to the line. After I said clear right" the captain applied the brakes as there was Aircraft Y coming from our left. The braking was firm but did not seem like it was an aggressive or instantaneous stop; especially as it appeared we were at an appropriate speed to begin the turn on to the line. There was confusion as to which aircraft was to proceed. Aircraft Y was first to ask; and ramp told the jet to let us go first; and ramp admitted that they didn't expect Aircraft Y to have caught up to us so quickly. We continued our taxi and the flight resumed as normal. Only after landing did the flight attendants ask about the firm braking in CLT; and then explained that the 1; 2; and 3 FAs had potential injuries. The captain asked if anyone needed medical attention; and none of the FAs said they did at that time. The FAs did not mention any issues or injuries during the flight; even during cruise communications to discuss en-route turbulence. Cause: If ramp had given instruction to either us or Aircraft Y to clarify which aircraft would be first then we could have avoided any confusion. The braking did not feel hard enough that I would have thought any injuries would have occurred; otherwise we would have called back to check if everyone was ok. It would have also been helpful to have had a call from the flight attendants if there were any concerns until waiting after landing."

column121: Flight was dispatched with MEL 24-XXX (inoperative IDG (Integrated Drive Generator)) configuration requiring use of APU during flight as a secondary electrical power source. Approx 120 West of ZZZ APU failed in flight. QRH requires land ASAP with one power source; several attempts to restart APU were unsuccessful. While discussing our diversion a ACARS was sent to our dispatcher to coordinate/discuss our intentions. After receiving an additional ECAM (ECAM IDG 1 OIL OVERHEAT) and noted IDG#1 temperature increasing; IDG#1 was disconnected per the second ECAM and we requested priority handling with the decision that we would be diverting to ZZZ. During the descent dispatch acknowledged our status and suggested a diversion to ZZZ but in the interest of safety (after the overheat msg) we decided to not fly further than required. A normal precautionary landing was made with a taxi to the gate. FO was the flying pilot and did an excellent job having the diversion airport/approach and a few ATC calls handled during time period I briefed the Flight Attendants and advised the passengers about our diversion; his efficiency was very much appreciated and he completely reduced my workload during a very short time frame from cruise at altitude to landing.
column123: We were dispatched that day with MEL 24-XXX which was an imperative #1 IDG (Integrated Drive Generator). Per the MEL we were able to depart with the APU continuously running to provide backup electrical power and generator. While in cruise flight at FL330 (max altitude per the MEL) and approx 120 miles west of ZZZ the APU  performed an auto shutdown. The FO announced my aircraft and took over radio communication with ATC while the CA ran the ECAM and subsequent QRH. The QRH led him to attempt a restart of the APU which was momentarily successful (less than a minute). The FO then began to look for nearest suitable airport to divert to per the QRH. At that time ZZZ was directly in front of the flight path and less than 200nm away. The FO asked for a decent to FL270 and was granted this by ATC whom was then notified by the FO that the flight was requesting priority handling and likely diverting to ZZZ. The CA agreed that was the nearest suitable airport and related this information to dispatch via ACARS message. At FL270 the CA attempted another APU restart which was unsuccessful. While descending out of FL240 a third and final APU restart attempt was made but unsuccessful. The FO continued to fly to ZZZ via new ATC clearance of direct and set up the MCDU (Multi-purpose Control Display Unit) for an ILS to runway XXR and entered the performance information for arriving at ZZZ. The CA made a call the inform the FAs of the diversion and made an announcement to the pax regarding the diversion. At this time the FO noticed IDG temperature of the #1 IDG began rising continuously until an ECAM message alerted the crew of IDG #1 OILOVRHEAT. The FO checked the reference sheet to ensure this was not a quick action item and not an ECAM exception. After verifying the ECAM was nether; he ran the ECAM procedures while conferring with the CA on each item. This led to a disconnection of IDG #1. After ECAM actions were complete a decent checklist was initiated by the CA and a normal precautionary landing was made at ZZZ runway XXR. We were able to taxi on our own power to the gate where we parked; shutdown; and all pax got off the aircraft for rebooking.Cause: APU failure caused our aircraft to be reduced to sickle stage electrical system. Increasing IDG temp on the #1 IDG resulted in ECAM that directed us to disconnect the #1 IDG. Mitigation suggestion would have been to shut down the APU whole on the ground in ZZZ1 to reduce its workload.

column123: We were flying the ZZZZZ2 arrival from ZZZ. We subsequently received vectors to intercept the ILS for runway XXL.While descending through 8;000 FT; ATC instructed us to reduce speed to 200 knots. I had already requested Flaps 1 in anticipation of slowing below 220 knots. At that point; I observed significant airspeed fluctuations caused by a tailwind component in excess of 45 knots that continued to increase. I was required to make multiple vertical speed (V/S) interventions because the speed brakes alone were insufficient to achieve and maintain the assigned speed.ATC was delayed several times in issuing further descent clearances due to multiple aircraft ahead executing go-arounds; resulting in us being slightly high on the approach. When ATC subsequently directed a reduction to 180 knots; the airspeed oscillations remained pronounced; and the stick shaker activated for approximately one second. Flaps 5 were promptly selected; and the remainder of the approach was flown in accordance with standard operating procedures.The aircraft was landed safely on runway XXL despite the challenging weather conditions. No further anomalies were noted.I am submitting this report to document the event and support any safety review or analysis.

After correcting the issue and running a few verification test we were able to depart a few hours later.Cause: The aircraft did not pressurize during the climb out.Suggestion: Maintenance could have verified the pressurization prior to signing off.
column123: On Day 0 at approximately XA00 we were operating flight ABCD ZZZ to ZZZ1. Maintenance had signed off the aircraft for an intermittent pax (Passenger) door indication written up by the previous crew. On the climb out we started to feel pressure that didn't seem normal and I asked my FO who was the pilot flying to reduce her climb. We were cleared to I believe 18;000 but at 10;000 we got the cabin alt" caution message. I advised ATC we needed to level off and we did at 10;000 feet. I took control of the aircraft and we ran the QRH for the "cabin alt". We advised ATC that we would be returning to ZZZ but we needed a few minutes to get ready. We entered a hold and ran all of our checks and briefings. Since we caught the issue early and didn't continue climbing; which would have created a bigger problem; we did not declare an emergency. Then we advised ATC we were ready to return to ZZZ where we landed without further incident. ATC did a great job handling us and my FO and FAs did terrific dealing with the situation. After maintenance corrected the issue several hours later we were able to board back up and complete the flight.Cause: The aircraft did not pressurize as it should have during climb out.Suggestion: After we returned to the gate the maintenance crew did a pressurization check. They saw the aircraft was not pressurizing. They corrected the issue after several hours."

column121: A routine instructional flight was being conducted to practice airwork and maneuvers in a multi-engine training aircraft. While maneuvering in an area of moderate turbulence; we experienced erratic RPM indications on the left engine. The tachometer rapidly fluctuated; momentarily indicating approximately 4000 RPM (overspeed) before dropping to zero RPM and then returning to a normal reading. The indications continued to fluctuate unpredictably. Simultaneously; the manifold pressure indication decreased to approximately 3 inches and fuel flow reduced significantly. At the time the anomaly first occurred; my student had the controls and the aircraft was in a bank while exiting moderate turbulence. Due to the turbulence and aircraft attitude; it was initially difficult to determine whether the aircraft itself was responding abnormally. Aurally; the engine did not sound significantly different from normal operation. I took control of the aircraft and began running the appropriate checklist procedures with the student. We verified each step and monitored engine indications. Due to the continued erratic indications and the possibility of an engine malfunction; I made the decision to secure the left engine. After completing the engine shutdown procedure; I contacted ZZZ Approach and advised them that we had secured the left engine and would be returning to ZZZ. An emergency was not declared. The aircraft was configured for single-engine operation and we conducted a precautionary return to the airport.The remainder of the flight was uneventful and we landed safely at ZZZ.

column123: Landed Runway 18; Tallahassee International Airport; at XA:21 on Day 0 in VFR conditions with slight mist forming in calm winds. Tower was closed as was Runway 9/27 per NOTAMs. Noted numerous vehicular warning lights at the approach end of Runway 09. Called the approach and exiting the runway on CTAF (118.7). Taxied to ramp; refueled and filed IFR flight plan utilizing Foreflight. Originally filed: ZZZZZ VXX ZZZ VXY ZZZZZ1. Foreflight notified that the flight plan had been alter to: ZZZZZ2 ZZZZZ3 TXXX ZZZZZ4 which I acknowledge and received notification that the later routing had been filed with an ETD of XB:30 and altitude of 11;000 MSL. Started aircraft and typed in my expected flight plan in my Garmin 430W and autopilot. Announced on CTAF that I was taxing from the ramp to Runway 18 and activated runway/taxiway lighting. Taxied via taxiway A11 then A to A1 - holding short of the runway in such a manner that I could clear taxiway A. Still calm winds and increasing mist - but could see the lit taxiway and runway lights to end. Accomplished engine runup and tried to contact clearance on 126.65 - was unsuccessful as tower was closed. Then attempted to contact Tallahassee Approach via phone as per the Chart Supplement at XA:23. This too was unsuccessful; Then tried to reach Jacksonville ARTCC - but failed as I had misdialed the number. I the dialed the FSS Clearance Delivery at - directed me to contact Jacksonville Center on 128.625. I attempted contact; but received no answer nor did I hear any radio traffic on that frequency. I again contacted FSS Clearance Delivery who instructed me to try again and then was able to hear radio traffic but had considerable trouble contacting the controller. The net result was that I was off the Tallahassee CTAF from XA:23 until XA:52 until I got my clearance. The clearance received was not that which Foreflight had said was filed. More scrambling to enter the data to this revision of my flight plan. I finally received clearance to take off at XA:56; called on CTAF that I was taking Runway 18 for takeoff; lined up and started rolling. After some 2500 plus feet of takeoff roll I noted white lights on the east side of the runway which I determined to be another aircraft back taxiing on Runway 18. These lights blended in with the runway lights and the lights at the approach end of Runway 09. There was insufficient time/space to do anything except maneuver to the west side to the runway - thereby avoiding a collision. I never heard any call from that aircraft - either before or after we passed each other.Being off the CTAF for some 30 minutes contributed to this almost mishap. During this time I probably missed the call from the other aircraft that he was taxiing - as he probably turned his radios on during that 30 minute period and; not hearing any conversation from me on the CTAF was not aware there was another aircraft moving on the airdrome. Possibly we both assumed we were the only aircraft active at TLH.I am not aware to the RCO situation at TLH; but it appeared that initially; no one was monitoring/transmitting through the local RCO until a second phone call from my cockpit got Jacksonville Center to start transmitting through whatever RCO was being used at THL. This might be an equipment or manning issue - and I am definitely not blameless in obtaining my clearance (though I have done it successfully many times before).Pilot controlled situations (like tower closed and with only CTAF to control aircraft actions with reduce visibility at night) demand the participating pilots adhere to set procedures. Back taxiing on a runway when a well lit taxiway is available to move to the number one position incurs additional; unnecessary risks. If the other aircraft had used taxiway A the entire conflict could have been avoided. If one is in a back taxi situation under pilot controlled conditions; one must monitor the CTAF for any unexpectedincursion or use of the runway. I never heard a call fromthe other aircraft when I announced my departure on Runway 18 nor when I passed close by the other aircraft. If the crew was using the back taxi to coordinate their departure - it was the wrong time.

At this time; the aircraft automatically began a rapid climb to begin the sequence. Knowing I was relatively close to the 100' approval ceiling; I manually overrode the sequence; which I had to accomplish twice within an approximately 15 second window. For approximately 2 seconds; the aircraft traveled up to approximately 112' before I could manually lower it; then again; for approximately 3 seconds; it traveled up to approximately 119' before I could manually lower it. It was at these maximum altitudes for approximately 1 second each prior to being manually flown lower; below the 100' approval ceiling. I landed the aircraft without further issue. No injuries or aircraft damage resulted from this incident. In the future; I will consider landing the aircraft prior to the initiation of the 'return to home' sequence; and will maintain increased situation awareness regarding the return to home sequence/ altitude and the aircraft's remaining battery power.

column121: Day 0 I was to perform a confined are landing in a field near the ZZZ airport and prior to the landing I did a site survey; walked off the the area from the tree line for rotor clearance on the left side and the front of the helicopter to ensure that I had rotor clearance on my blind side before doing the first landing. The tail section was clear of any obstacles and was not blocked. The tree line on my left side was my primary concern. I made a reference mark on the ground to place my right wheel. The video shot was to hover over the confined landing area and hold in a hover at approximately 100ft (AGL) and then descend vertically slowly to the target area mark for the right wheel. The winds were typical winds variable from the northeast at about 15kts with occasional gust to 25kts. Sky was clear and visibility was unlimited and no other aircraft was flying during this time. At approximately XA:15 I did the first landing without any problems; but from the inside the cockpit the pilots view from the right side looked closer than I was comfortable with; and decided to place my wheel chocks further to my right to provide more rotor clearance on my left blind side. The plan was still the same; lift straight up to 100ft(AGL)and hold for several minutes then descend vertically slowly to the wheel chock marker that we had moved to the right about 15 more feet. During the second second landing as I was slowly descending is when I heard heard the sound of the rotor blade tip caps hitting the tree branches; I immediately raised collective and moved farther away to my right before landing.Contributing factors:(1) Strong left Gusty Cross winds; and pilot not accounting for the leaning angle of the helicopter that changed the pilots visual reference to the landing marker; and in order for the pilot to see it he drifted to the left and had the rotor over the tree tops as he slowly descended; causing damaged to the tip caps. (2) Not having a safety ground crew person on the landing aera that would have better outside visual observations and a hand held radio to communicate with the pilot on rotor clearance; and to make corrections as needed. (3) Customer pressure pushing to get the job done in one shot. (4) Customer changed plan at the last minute from original location discussed a week prior to this new location causing the scope of work to change and making the crew become complacent in just trying to get the job done before dark.Action taken: what seemed to be a simple Photo / Video shoot became very complex with all of the last minute changes; and the should have been stopped; regroup with better weather conditions and a very clear plan for all involved with distances actually measured and verified by another person with an actual measuring device and not just walked off by the pilot. My stride was most likely shorter than usual from being distracted by the camera person and putting me closer to the tree line than expected. Preventative measures: A written plane of action and Tail board meeting will be conducted for all persons involved with more clearer directions besides the standard safety briefing; and other concerns such as the effects of weather; visibility; winds; rain; dust; obstacles will be addressed; discussed and documented with a collection of signatures. The physical distance from the tree line and gusty winds was the contributing factor on this incident.

column121: Just after takeoff; in light rime icing and IMC; I noticed we weren't climbing. We were at 2400 or so MSL and flaps/gear up; shortly after the after takeoff checklist was completed. The CA disengaged the auto throttles and we manually set the appropriate climb N1. At this point; the aircraft resumed climbing and the bug jumped to 250 knots at the appropriate altitude. However; upon acceleration; the FD (Flight Director) began commanding an erroneous pitch attitude. While still hand flying; the captain followed the FD momentarily until quickly realizing following it would cause us to exceed the FMS speed of 250 knots. Because of this; we momentarily accelerated to around 270 knots (around 7-8000 MSL) until catching that the VNAV function was commanding an incorrect airspeed. The CA quickly returned to 250 knots then disregarded the FD vertical guidance until we got well above 10;000 MSL. When we got higher and above the bad weather; we tried to reengage the Auto throttle; but it started retarding the throttles again like it did earlier. Ultimately; we reset both flight directors and the auto throttle; which restored normal function to both systems. At that time; we engaged autopilot and the rest of the flight proceeded normally. ATC did not contact us about our momentary speed exceedance. During this entire event; LNAV guidance worked normally; so whatever the issue was ended up being isolated to the VNAV vertical guidance and the auto throttles.

column121: Aircraft X was a ferry flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  It was the second ferry flight of the day.  CA and FO were only crew onboard.  From preflight; we had issues getting the actual fuel load on the jet updated by dispatch onto Performance Data and flight plan.  Taxiing out we exceeded our EDCT (Estimated Departure Clearance Time); because of delays in receiving a load close out.  Once we were ready; we were cleared for takeoff on runway XX and advised of arrival traffic.  Halfway through turn from taxiway to centerline of XX; tower advised traffic was short final.  As CA lined up on centerline; he called TOGA.  Aircraft then veered hard right as engines spooled up.  Between 30 and 40 knots; CA initiated a rejected TO: throttles idle; manual braking to a stop.  After full stop; we exited at 1 to the south of runway XX to evaluate.  On taxiway 2; we discussed the parameters of the reject; including no 'Thrust Set' call or RTO (Rejected Takeoff) braking; and brake temperatures.  We determined that asymmetric thrust during right turn onto runway led to asymmetric thrust during engine advancement to TO.  We decided to attempted a second static takeoff.  Second TO from runway XYL was normal and uneventful.  Flight concluded safely at ZZZ1.Cause: Minor coordination delays and then traffic calls from tower added to feeling of 'hurry up'.  While we did discuss mental status; ie 'being in the green';  this is a reminder at each break point in taxi/flight to take a deep breath and focus on the next event.Closer evaluation of throttle advancement to approximately 40 percent N1 and prioritize static takeoff; especially from maintenance base.Avoid using asymmetric thrust entering runway for takeoff.
column123: ZZZ - ZZZ1 Ferry flight to pick up a 787-8 being put back into service.  CA and FO only souls on aircraft.   During the first takeoff attempt on Rwy XX with a direct left crosswind; we were rushed to takeoff by tower because of an aircraft on short final.  Per SOP:  Rolling takeoff; lined up on runway; advanced throttles; checked EPR's; engaged TOGA.  Aircraft veered right as the left engine spooled up faster that the right.  At approximately 30 knots:  Idle; hard braking to an immediate stop.  Exited at 1 which is less than 500' into the takeoff roll.    Status at reject:  TOGA was selected; thrust set" did not occur; no RTO (Rejected Takeoff) braking.   Evaluated the aircraft: brake temperature and tire pressures remained normal.  Engines appeared normal.   I determined that it was either and engine issue or asymmetric thrust before the selection of TOGA; noting that I had been using differential power to turn on the smaller taxiways at ZZZ.  I may have had the left engine spooled up higher than the right; even though I remember checking the EPR's (Engine Pressure Ratio) before TOGA.  We decided to attempt another takeoff with a thorough run up before TOGA.  This second takeoff attempt was accomplished uneventfully and normally.  Proceeded to ZZZ1 uneventfully.Cause: Became rushed to get the takeoff completed before aircraft on final; with a clearance limit within 1 minute.  Using differential power to turn on smaller taxiways.  This technique may have carried over to my first rolling takeoff event.  Low time Captain on reserve with low experience in left seat."

column121: On Day 0; I was the First Officer for ZZZ- ZZZ1. I arrived at the airplane at about XA:20am; having taken the XA:00 am van from the hotel. After arriving at the airplane and putting my bags in the flight deck; I accomplished an origination flow; with the exception of first flight of the day items and went outside to do an exterior inspection. I completed the inspection; following the recommended inspection route; and I did not notice any damage. I returned to the flight deck; and completed first flight of the day items; having ensured that wheel chocks were in place. The Captain arrived shortly thereafter; and the flight proceeded normally without incident or any abnormal indications. On  Day 2; I received a voice mail from Person A asking me to call him back. When I did; he let me know that there was damage found on the #2 engine nacelle by the crew who was working the outbound leg after our arrival in ZZZ1. He also shared that he or someone reporting to him had looked back at the camera data in ZZZ; and found evidence that the damage was present on the ramp at ZZZ. He shared pictures of the damage with me by text.Cause: Causal factors include my failure to recognize the damage to the #2 Engine Nacelle. My recency of flight may have played a role; as this was my third day back on the line after 3 months of schoolhouse work as an IP (Flight Instructor). During the whole trip I was mindful to arrive early to each flight and give myself plenty of time to complete my duties as I knew it had been more than 3 months since I had flown the line. I went into this trip being especially mindful that I had not been around an airplane for a while; and tried especially hard to take my time and make sure that I wasn't missing anything. During the exterior inspections; I must not have looked closely enough at the aft part of the nacelle before I walked the right wing leading edge. I must have only been looking up as I inspected the leading edge and trailing edge; before walking behind the engine to inspect the right side landing gear and fuselage. I imagine that I walked right by the damage without ever seeing it on the aft portion of the nacelle while I was looking up to inspect the right wing trailing edge. My recommendation would be simply to be even more deliberate and observant during exterior inspections; and to carefully inspect the entirety of the engine nacelle and fuselage skin for damage on all sides.

column121: FO leg; at cruise; FL230; somewhere abeam ZZZ we received three simultaneous cautions:  HYD 2 LOW PRESS; ADS 1 FAIL; and AP FAIL.  My FO is now hand flying; and I'm grabbing the QRH for the hydraulic issue (top message).  By the time I'm at the hydraulic section; the HYD 2 message has disappeared; so I move to the ADS 1 fail message.  It basically says to make sure the ADS has reverted; which it did.  Next; AP (AutoPilot) FAIL... we tried unsuccessfully to re-engage the AP so no CAT II approaches.  ZZZ1  is VFR.  Now; out of curiosity; I circle back and check the HYD page to see what's going on there.  That's when I see amber dashes for the HYD SYS 2 pressure (see attached ).  After a discussion with my FO; we decide it would be best to treat this as if SYS 2 has no pressure.  First; we don't know if there is any pressure (we have a QTY indication) the flow lines are showing green.  It could be a faulty pressure sensor; but we can't rule out a faulty warning system because we initially got the warning; and then it disappeared.  We didn't want to assume everything was fine and find out on the ground that we were wrong; so we went with the HYD SYS 2 LOW PRESS procedure anyway.  Then we got a HYD 2 ELEC PUMP FAIL message (see attached).  Then we were led to the LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2 procedure and advising ATC.  I gave the FAs the information but I forgot to make the announcement to the passengers as we were on the arrival; and pretty busy with the QRH.  Somewhere on the approach; after we got through the Loss of Hydraulic System 2 Descent Checklist; I took the controls.  The gear extended normally; normal landing on XXR with what felt like normal braking; but as we slowed on the roll out I found that I had no steering.  I exited the high speed and came to stop on the taxiway.  I gave the passengers a brief explanation of what was going on; that we were going to be towed to the gate; and it could take some time for the tug to get out to us.  Our EICAS was now full of more messages and REMOTE CB TRIP that; I guess; had been inhibited in flight (see attached). We had multiple conversations with CFR (Crash Fire Rescue); Ground; and ops and eventually got towed to the gate.

Maintenance said they 'could not locate the source of the urine leak' and that the same a/c had a leak a couple months earler but; the carpet was cleaned. Nonetheless; the a/c stil smelled like urine. Capt ASKED if we were 'comfortable taking this plane with the urine odor?' We said 'no.' She said she would advise 'her boss.' The agents were making comments such as 'I've been here since XA:00 and SOMEONE needs to take this plane out of here!'...'there is absolutely nothing compromising the integrity of this a/c!' As pax began to board; one by one; each started either making comments or asking questions about the 'bad smell on this plane.' One of the most difficult things that our crew encountered was the pure aloofness that was presented by the agents regarding the strong urine odor. It's as if; the fact that urine; which is considered a biohazard and unsanitary was completely disregarded. And when attempting to speak to the Lead Agent about it; she laughed as if it wasn't being taken seriously and I attempted to explain to her that 'this is not funny.' The entire incident was just heightened by the disconnect between our pilots; crew and ZZZ agents. Avoid overflying ZZZ in the future.  I just had one route that takes me over ZZZ so I will no longer use that one.2. When approaching airports with jumpers; make sure the primary radio frequency is tuned to that airport at least 10 miles away.

column121: -36 F initial engine startup manually due to a weak battery. Aircraft tires were chocked by pinching the tires with the hydraulically-operated snow skis. After manually starting the engine; and as the pilot entered the cabin door; the aircraft began to slowly move forward and caused the pilot to slip and fall next to the cabin door. The aircraft moving forward; the propeller contacted a snow berm. The engine continued to run after contacting the snow berm; and was shut down in the normal procedure. The problem arose from not using the aircraft parking brake. Contributing factors were the extremely cold temperature and un-willingness to use the normal parking brake and the extreme cold not allowing the pinching factor of the snow skis to deform the tires and provide braking action such as has been demonstrated in less-cold (warmer) temperatures. Additionally; the contributing factor of a weak battery due to extreme cold; and the necessity of manually starting the engine were significant.The pilot believes that manually starting an aircraft engine is not an abnormal operation; but understands that the perceptions of individuals who do not regularly perform this action will be significantly different. The ranking of contributing factors would be re-arranged by those individuals. Extreme cold; and a desire to perform a start-up; run-up; charging system check; and shutdown and engine blanket coverup in order to allow time for the engine compartment to 'heat soak' while the pilot enjoyed a warm mug of coffee are a very real human factor consideration. Thank You

column121: Whilst in the cruise at FL470 we encountered some fairly severe mountain wave activity.  This caused a loss of airspeed from M0.80 to M0.72 and with it a STALL WARNING; STICK SHAKER and Auto Pilot disconnect.The PF ( I ; as the PIC was on my crew rest); applied full power and reduced the pitch attitude of the aircraft and started a descent. The PM spoke to ZZZ ATC and requested an immediate descent. The stall warnings; almost immediately went to an over speed warning.  We eventually leveled at FL380 and away from the mountain wave activity settled down into the cruise once more.Whilst this was happening; I managed to get from crew rest and into a kneeled position between; the pilot's seats to observe what was happening. Immediately I was satisfied that we were not stalled; as it was the STALL WANRING and STICK SHAKER that had alerted me to the problem.  I could see that the pitch of the aircraft was at about 1 degree below the horizon with wings level and the power was at full.  The airspeed was showing above MMO (Maximum Mach Operating Speed)  and we were descend8ng at about 3;700ft per min.  I reassured the PF that his actions were correct and that we could now re-engage the autopilot and cruise at the lower level.  I returned to the galley and assured the Flight Attendant and when to talk to the passenger.  We landed at destination about two hours later; without incident.
column123: We were cruising at M.80 at FL450 in the vicinity of ZZZ VOR when we encountered some moderate turbulence. As this turbulence was forecasted at FL450 for the next hour; we asked the controller how the rides were at FL470. The controller asked the traffic passing by us in the opposite direction at FL470 and pilot reported the ride to be smooth. We chose to climb to FL470 hoping for a smoother ride. Once we reached FL470; it was smooth for about 5 minutes before we encountered the first mountain wave. It was relatively light with the usual gain/loss of airspeed ranging from M.76 to M.83 and very little turbulence associated with it. As we continued at FL470 at M.80 for a few more minutes in smooth air; we hit the second mountain wave which initially gave us an increase of about 100 feet in altitude; immediately followed by a sudden loss of airspeed from M.80 down to M.72 with a decreasing speed trend on the tape within a second or two. I immediately pushed the throttles full forward and grabbed the yoke. Realizing that a high altitude stall was imminent; I feel like I instinctively disconnected the autopilot and pushed forward on the yoke to initiate a stall recovery. I am not sure if my recovery or the 'stall' and shaker came first but we were immediately in a nose down attitude trying to recover from the high altitude stall.As we proceeded in the recovery procedure; the PNF reported the loss of altitude to ATC and he cleared us to a lower altitude; eventually clearing us all the way down FL300; noticing a rapid descent from our aircraft. During the recovery; I noticed that the speed tape was indicating red on both the high speed and low speed tape; indicating that we haven't recovered from the stall; even though we were most likely overspeeding the aircraft as well. Eventually; after a couple thousand feet of altitude loss; the red low speed tape cleared and we were able to gradually level the aircraft and gain positive control. By the time we fully recovered; we were at FL395. ATC informed us that FL380 would be a better altitude to continue the flight so we descended further down to FL380 and continued the last 2 hours of flight cruising at FL380 with no further incident.Due to the forecasted turbulence; about 10 minutes before the incident; we turned the seatbelt signs on and told the Flight Attendant to inform the passengers of possible turbulence and to stay seated and keep their seatbelts on; which they did. No injuries resulted from the rapid loss of altitude to either the crew or the passengers. One glass cup fell to the ground in the galley and broke but that was the only noticeable damage that resulted from the incident.Looking at PIREPs after the flight; it seems that several other aircraft encountered and reported similar or even worse Mountain Wave in the vicinity of the incident from FL400 up to FL470 with similar outcomes. Based on all the information; we believe that we used great CRM; excellent teamwork; and handled the situation the best we could with the best outcome possible.

column121: Chain of EventsHow the Problem Arose / Contributing FactorsI am a CFII and was conducting instrument training at M54 while flying a practice RNAV (GPS) RWY 19 approach with a student. The airport was using Runway 01 for traffic pattern operations at the time. Our intention was to fly the RNAV 19 approach to LNAV minimums and perform a low approach while yielding to all traffic operating in the pattern.Throughout the approach; I made multiple CTAF position and intention reports advising traffic that we were conducting the RNAV 19 approach for a low approach only and that we would give way to all traffic in the pattern. I recall specifically making calls at approximately 9 NM; 6 NM; 4 NM; 2 NM; and again at approximately 1.5 NM final.At the time of the incident; there was only one aircraft in the traffic pattern; which was turning left base for Runway 01.While descending on a 1.5-mile final toward LNAV minimums; an aircraft identifying as Aircraft Y announced on CTAF that he intended to depart Runway 01 from the A1 intersection. Immediately after hearing that transmission; I announced that we were on a 1.5-mile final for the RNAV Runway 19 approach.The departing aircraft replied that he was 'rolling' and began the takeoff roll on Runway 01. The aircraft departed directly toward our position on opposite headings while we were established on final.From our perspective on final; the aircraft initially appeared to be a small single-engine aircraft. I did not recognize the aircraft type until after passing. After liftoff; the aircraft accelerated rapidly and continued climbing toward us.How the Problem Was DiscoveredThe conflict became apparent when the departing aircraft announced he was rolling for departure while we were already established on a 1.5-mile final for the RNAV 19 approach.Corrective ActionsAs the aircraft climbed toward our flight path; I initiated a right turn to ensure separation before resuming the runway course. The departing aircraft then began a right turn away from our position.At the closest point of approach; the aircraft appeared to pass approximately 200 feet below our altitude with an estimated 300-400 feet of horizontal separation.After passing; the departing pilot asked over CTAF why we were flying an opposite-direction RNAV approach while Runway 01 was in use. He further indicated that he believed we were flying the RNAV (GPS) 01 approach and that I was making calls for Runway 01 instead of Runway 19. I responded that multiple CTAF calls had been made advising traffic that we were flying the RNAV 19 approach as a low approach only.There were no injuries and no damage to either aircraft.Human Performance ConsiderationsPerceptions; Judgements; and DecisionsBased on the limited traffic in the pattern and the multiple CTAF advisories made during the approach; I assessed that the practice RNAV 19 approach could be conducted safely while yielding to traffic in the pattern.When the departing aircraft announced his intention to depart; I immediately transmitted our position on a 1.5-mile final. When the aircraft began climbing toward our flight path after departure; I determined that initiating a right turn would provide additional separation.Factors Affecting the Quality of Human PerformanceThis event occurred at a non-towered airport where aircraft were operating both in the traffic pattern and conducting a straight-in instrument training approach opposite the runway in use.The departing aircraft was Aircraft Y; which has high acceleration and climb performance. This reduced the time available to resolve the situation once the aircraft began its takeoff roll.Actions or InactionsMultiple CTAF calls were made throughout the approach advising traffic that we were conducting the RNAV 19 low approach. An additional call was made when the departing aircraft announced his departure.When the departing aircraft climbed toward our position; a right turn was initiated to ensure separation while continuing to monitor the aircraft's climb and trajectory.Note: After completing the final approach segment and the MAP; my student maneuvered our aircraft to the right; then back to the left. This movement was not the evasive action taken earlier during the final approach to runway 19.

column121: I was the PIC and pilot flying a Learjet LR-60 departing RWY XX at ZZZ. We obtained our IFR clearance via telephone from ZZZ Departure and were released for departure with instructions to climb and maintain 5;000 MSL. Weather at the airport was MVFR with strong gusting winds (270/G40+); snow flurries; and very cold temperatures (later determined to be approximately ISA -18). Based on the conditions; I anticipated entering IMC and encountering turbulence shortly after departure. My SIC and I conducted a thorough briefing of the takeoff and climb profile. I executed a crosswind takeoff on RWY XX without incident. After takeoff I established a climb at 250 KIAS. The SIC completed the after-takeoff checklist. Moderate turbulence was encountered shortly after departure.At approximately 2;500 MSL; just prior to entering IMC; I engaged the autopilot in heading mode (laterally) and level change (vertically) to continue the climb at 250 KIAS to the assigned altitude of 5;000 MSL. We entered solid IMC and continued climbing in moderate turbulence. Approaching the assigned altitude; I observed that the aircraft climb rate had increased to approximately 3;000-4;000 FPM and was continuing to increase. The increase in climb rate occurred without a corresponding pitch increase or thrust change; suggesting the aircraft had encountered strong vertical air movement. It became apparent that the autopilot would not capture the assigned altitude. I reduced thrust and disconnected the autopilot to manually level the aircraft. Although airspeed decreased as expected; the aircraft continued climbing at a significant rate. I reduced thrust to flight idle and lowered the pitch attitude; however; the aircraft continued to climb while the speed decreased to about 170 KIAS. The aircraft was experiencing moderate turbulence and control responses seemed atypical. I suspected a strong updraft or unstable air mass. Due to concern about imposing excessive negative-G loads on the aircraft structure; I elected not to force an abrupt level-off and instead allowed the aircraft to 'ride it out;' and stabilize. We subsequently exceeded the assigned altitude. The ZZZ Departure controller queried our status and I advised that we were 'correcting.' ATC then issued a climb to 8;000 MSL. At approximately 7;000 MSL the rate of climb began to decrease and the aircraft stabilized. I re-established a normal climb profile. As we approached 8;000 MSL I re-engaged the autopilot; however; the autopilot again failed to capture the altitude.  In retrospect I suspect this occurred because I engaged the auto pilot too close to the level off; not allowing sufficient time to capture. I again disconnected the autopilot and manually leveled the aircraft as we exited IMC into VMC on top. The aircraft leveled at approximately 8;500 MSL. ATC again queried our status and I advised that we appeared to be experiencing an autopilot issue and were working the problem. We were instructed to climb to 10;000 MSL and proceed on course and were then handed off to ARTCC. The ARTCC controller asked if we required assistance or had an emergency. We advised that we were not declaring an emergency and that the aircraft was under control. We were subsequently cleared to climb to 17;000 MSL. I hand-flew the aircraft to that altitude and leveled off.After completing the cruise checklist and confirming that all systems appeared normal; I re-engaged the autopilot. The autopilot then appeared to function normally for the remainder of the flight. Lessons Learned:  This event caused me to give serious consideration to the fact that; in conditions involving strong winds; turbulence; and cold temperatures; significant vertical air movement may be present even outside of convective activity. This highlighted the importance of more closely monitoring climb performance and autopilot modes before; during; and after altitude capture. If the aircraft energy state becomes excessive or automation behavior is unexpected; transitioning more promptly to manual control and managing the aircraft more conservatively would help prevent future altitude deviations or structural loading concerns.  The SIC and I debriefed this incident at length after the flight and discussed strategies for prevention of such occurrences in the future.

column121: On Day 0; in Aircraft X; I was the PF on an empty leg from ZZZ to MYAM. The initial plan was a visual approach to Runway 09 using the RNAV as a backup; as Runway 09 tends to be more commonly used runway at this airport. This airport does not report the weather; and we were unable to pick up any other nearby weather stations. Upon arrival in the area; traffic in the pattern was operating for Runway 27; so I asked the FO what the correct downwind is. He looked it up and found the correct pattern is left traffic for Runway 27. So we joined the correct downwind for Runway 27 to integrate with existing traffic and planned to fly a visual approach to Runway 27. We did load the RNAV approach for 27 into the FMS; but with the last minute change; we did not have time to brief it. There was a small plane in the pattern and I believe two other jets making callouts further away. On the downwind on the near side of the final approach fix; I disconnected the autopilot to fly the remainder of the approach manually; as there were people lining up and back-taxiing; and the timing required that we have a short base before the FAF.While turning onto final for Runway 27; we observed what appeared to be an aircraft positioned on the taxiway that looked as though it was holding short of the runway; as we had heard on the frequency that someone announced they were holding short. It appeared that the aircraft was waiting for traffic to land.As the approach continued; the runway and taxiway surfaces were difficult to distinguish due to very faint runway markings and the runway surface appearing slightly wet. At approximately 200 - 300 feet; we initiated a go-around due to the lack of complete certainty about the runway markings. The aircraft remained airborne during the entire maneuver and did not touch down at any point. While our go-around was in progress; and while we were on crosswind; another pilot in the sequence directly behind us transmitted on the radio asking which surface was the runway; specifically asking whether the runway was the one on the right or the left. We believed him to be joking and responded with; That's why we went around." He then responded; "No; seriously; I can't tell; is it the right or the left?" We responded that it was the left one; and he proceeded to sidestep and land on Runway 27. Shortly afterward; the third aircraft in the landing sequence (two aircraft behind us and a jet) landed on the taxiway.During our approach it became apparent that the runway markings were very faint; and with the runway surface wet the contrast between the runway and taxiway was reduced. One of the cues that helped clarify the situation was the ability to begin seeing yellow taxiway markings through the water; which helped distinguish the taxiway from the runway.After parking; we went to the airport office. We spoke with airport personnel as they initially believed the aircraft may have touched down based on the amount of fuselage visible above the surrounding tree/shrub line. We clarified to the airport manager that the aircraft did not touch the ground on go-around and that the go-around had been initiated at approximately 200 - 300 feet AGL.During the go-around and pattern activity; the aircraft immediately behind sidestepped and also went around; while the jet behind that ultimately landed on the taxiway. The only reason we were able to perform a go-around is because my FO was vigilant; and spoke up.The runway markings at MYAM appeared very faint; and with a wet surface the distinction between the runway and taxiway was reduced. Also the jet we believed was holding short when we began our approach was actually a disabled aircraft that had turned clear of Runway 09 at the end; and was positioned to look like it was holding short. Given the radio transmissions questioning runway identification and the report of an aircraft landing on the taxiway; the condition of the markings may contribute to runway and taxiway misidentification; particularly during busy traffic periods.We are lucky we went around and are safe; but this is clearly a problem if three aircraft in a row; two of which were operated by professional pilots; had mistaken a taxiway for a runway at an uncontrolled airport. This could have ended completely differently and tragically."

column121: Below is a summary of the unforeseen malfunction with the Autopilot/Trim that caused the pilot deviation while transporting 6 passengers to include infant today. This event occurred after takeoff on the initial climb out of ZZZ VFR. As I proceeded to climb to 1000ft under the Bravo shelf; I received a blinking Trim Error notification on the autopilot display panel and the plane began gradually porpoising. I followed the standard operating procedure by disconnecting the autopilot to reset the system. It worked initially; however; after 10-15 seconds and activating autopilot again; the Trim gave an error indication; once more; and the plane began an abrupt nose up pitch. After disconnecting the Autopilot again; in an attempt to recover the aircraft; the Trim wheel was still rolling aft and the plane kept increasing the rate of climb. I ran the system reset flow and recovered the aircraft after approximately 2-4min. While regaining full control of the aircraft by hand flying; I attempted to make contact with ZZZ App on XXX.X to inform them of my flight deviation; however due to the high volume of radio calls they were handling at the time because of severe weather; I never got a reply from ATC. After receiving no response; I switched frequencies and contacted ZZZ App XXY.XX to explain what had just occurred. This can be verified by the squawk code that I received to get VFR flight following. By this time; I was able to resolve the issue with the trim and eventually land the plane safely . After deplaning the passengers; I immediately contacted our lead mechanic to inform him about the event that had just occurred while in flight. I explained that this was my first time experiencing something like this and he recommended additional measures to take in the event that this ever happens again. I; in no way; had any intention of this happening and sincerely apologize for the deviation or possible inconvenience this may have caused. I pray this type of malfunction or incident does not occur again. Thank you for your time.

I did observe a deployed chute from the X10; and the downed X10 appeared to be lying on the ground halfway between the dock and the light pole that was struck.

Aircraft X responded with we are having a pressurization issue and need lower. I said Aircraft X I have your request. He said how about the requested priority handling. I said roger I cannot issue lower for traffic within 5 NM of you. Aircraft X said that we are having a communication issue and I said I do not believe we are. Aircraft Y still has not checked on and I was unsure at this moment if I could turn Aircraft X more if he was having this issue as we typically turn other aircraft.Aircraft X immediately said you need to turn the other aircraft. I told Aircraft X I am not talking to the other aircraft yet and that I cannot issue lower due to separation requirements and that Aircraft X is the pilot in command of the aircraft and to take control of his aircraft as I am unable to issue lower. Aircraft X said that he was descending. I said roger. While this was happening the instructor was coordinating with Sector XY who was talking to Aircraft Y to see if they were there and if they could turn him. They did not have the aircraft. I heard all this with my other ear and then called in the blind to Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y was sitting on frequency and I had them turn XXR as by this point I had 4.8 NM and [Runway] XX would get them clear in 5 seconds and a bigger turn would not have accomplished it faster. There was never a loss of separation and all the rest of the coordination was done without land line as they knew we were busy. I issued FL290 as soon as they were clear and then Sector XZ gave me control to FL190 and I asked if they wanted me to turn the Aircraft X on course and they said they would take care of it and I gave control to Sector XZ and then shipped Aircraft X to Sector XZ.This is a tough one. Are we allowed to turn an aircraft that is an emergency hydraulic problem that is screaming for lower? The communication between the aircraft and controller needed to be better and more clear on what is going on as they checked on just requesting and were very short and not helpful for me to understand to gravity of his situation. The frequency tied up for this did make it to where Aircraft Y did not check on and had he I would have turned them sooner and did everything in a more timely manner to ensure the safe travel of Aircraft X.

column121: We were level at FL330 after descending from FL370 and the cabin altitude warning started sounding. Both pilots accomplished their memory items for the associated checklist. Communication was established quickly. When I looked at the cabin altitude indication; we were indicating 10;000 ft. cabin altitude. We initiated an emergency descent to 10;000 ft. MSL and requested priority handling with ZZZ Center. During the descent; I did notice at one point in the descent the PF had gone from LVL CHNG to VS and our IAS was increasing. I commanded the PF back to LVL CHNG and to reduce speed back to 280 kt. IAS as that is when the warning occurred and I knew the checklist would later say not to increase speed if structural damage is suspected. We had not reached that point in the checklist yet and had not made that determination. The cabin altitude warning checklist did not regain pressurization. According to the cabin altitude needle; we remained at 10;000 ft. cabin altitude. Later on when we were level at 10;000 ft.; the cabin altitude needle indicated as high as 50;000 ft. The cabin altitude needle changed multiple times during the rest of the flight making indications that didn't make logical sense and I suspected it was an indication problem. My theory was further reinforced that prior to the event; there were no physiological symptoms reported by any crew member. Regardless of this theory we still treated the problem as an actual depressurization. Physiological symptoms of ear and sinus pain did occur for some crew members as a result of directions for manual control of pressurization from the checklist. The cabin oxygen masks never deployed. An uneventful approach and landing occurred. Emergency personnel followed our aircraft to the gate.
column123: At cruise; as pilot flying; I briefed the Captain (CA) per the briefing card for our arrival into ZZZ. Weather was discussed as a possible threat that was northwest of ZZZ; as well as some gusty winds and possible choppy rides for descent. The ZZZZZ Arrival to the ILS XXL was briefed and descent checklist completed. The passengers were seated and seatbelt sign was turned on by the CA and flight attendants (FAs) were instructed to prepare the cabin prior to descent. We descended from our cruise altitude of FL370; with an intermediate level off at FL330. Shortly thereafter; the cabin altitude warning sounded and cabin altitude annunciator illuminated. Both the CA and I performed our associated memory items. We both saw a cabin altitude of 10;000 ft. The CA relayed the situation to ATC and we were given a clearance to descend to 10;000 ft. Priority handling was requested with ZZZ ATC and an urgent descent was initiated down to that assigned altitude. The CA ran the associated QRC and QRH checklists for the cabin altitude warning. The checklist never recovered a lower cabin altitude; from the 10;000 ft. cabin until below 10;000 ft. MSL. At one point while level at 10;000 ft. MSL the CA pointed out the gauge became erroneous and pegged out to the maximum cabin altitude of 50;000 ft. No passenger injuries were reported. FAs were briefed prior to arrival. Dispatch and Maintenance were notified as time allowed.A normal approach and landing ended the flight and emergency vehicles followed us to the gate; as a precaution. The CA and I debriefed at the gate.

column121: At approximately 90 minutes prior to touchdown; we completed the descent checklist and briefings. At about 40 minutes out; while maintaining FL360; I reached for the sun visor to detach and stow it. The visor fell inadvertently and landed on the aft section of the center console. While the visor struck the left start lever; neither pilot immediately realized the lever had been moved to the cutoff position.We noticed a discrepancy a few seconds later; a thrust lever split developed and the autothrottle disconnect light began flashing. Initial diagnosis suggested a mechanical issue with the left thrust lever; I attempted to prevent the lever from retarding and tried to re-engage the autothrottle; but the system would not engage and the lever would not maintain its position.The FO identified that the left start lever was in the cutoff position and verbalized the state while I observed the airspeed dropping. Recognizing the engine loss; I reiterated that I had control of the aircraft and radios; and commanded the FO to perform the appropriate checklist. We requested priority handling and initiated a descent. When the FO requested to return the start lever to idle; I concurred; however; upon observing an engine EGT over-temp; the FO correctly returned the lever to cutoff to protect the engine.While the FO was waiting for the APU to start; he contacted the flight attendants (FAs) to inform them of the engine shutdown; they were instructed to wait for further guidance; though no brief was conducted at that time. We both agreed to delay the passenger announcement until the results of the engine restart were known.In accordance with the checklist; once we descended below FL240 and accelerated toward 300 kt.; we initiated the engine restart. The engine restarted successfully at FL220 and 300 kt. Once the engine stabilized and checklists were complete; the FAs were updated and a passenger announcement was made stating that we had experienced abnormal engine indications which were successfully resolved.Dispatch was notified of the engine shutdown and subsequent restart. I transferred radio communications back to the FO and directed him to cancel the priority handling. We continued for an uneventful landing in ZZZ. Following the shutdown checklist; we conducted a crew debrief. Maintenance received a full briefing on the flight deck; and an entry was made in the Electronic Logbook (ELB). We then briefed the Chief Pilot and Dispatch. Although we initially felt fit to continue our deadhead to ZZZ1; the Chief Pilot later informed us of a schedule change for review; and we were released to go home.

column123: While at Gate XX in ZZZ rampers had us keep brakes on while they hooked up the tug. After we were secured to tug rampers gave us the all secure below; FOD check complete; steering disengaged ready for break release. We released brake and called for push. Ramp cleared us for push; rampers notified us that the tug was broken and they would need to get a new one. Ramper told us standby he will let us know when to set the brake. Both the FO and I agreed that we heard the ramper  say to hold on he will let us know when to set the brake. We heard rampers working below the aircraft. I continually over the headset asked ramp if they were ready for the brakes with no answer. We could hear them banging on something below the nose. We heard the interphone disconnect as the plane was lowed from the tug and felt the plane move back slightly. I had my feet on the brakes and applied slight pressure to come to a stop. We saw rampers below move the broken tug back. I kept giving hand signals to the ramper that came into view to set brakes. He gave me the set brake signal and I set the brakes. Another ramper came onto the headset and told us we had a rollback event. She also stated that she saw the green light illuminated after the rollback happened. Rampers said they did not see any damage and we did not roll back far. I called Maintenance Control and asked if we need to have anything checked out; we had no indications and ramp saw no damage; Maintenance Control said we were good to go. We elected to get hooked back up and push back to continue the flight with no issues.Cause: There was a miscommunication from ramp on setting the brakes. The FO and I agreed we heard the ramper say hold on I'll let you know when to set the brake. We could hear the rampers on the headset doing something below the nose but they did not respond to my repeated questioning if they needed brakes set.Suggestions: Need better communications with ramp to verify brakes were set when they needed to be.

column121: This event happened while on the ILS Runway XX approach at approximately the ZZZZZ intersection or right around 10;000 ft. We had just maneuvered around a heavy return on the radar for precipitation and we were cleared direct back to ZZZ [VOR] to resume the approach. At this time we were only in moderate turbulence and moderate rain. As we descended on the approach the turbulence started to increase in intensity to the point where the stability of the aircraft was in question and the turbulence became severe in intensity. We elected then to conduct the missed approach; we informed tower of the missed approach and they told us to contact center. As we switched to center frequency the severe turbulence that we encountered became a windshear escape procedure. We conducted the escape procedure with the thrust levers set to maximum thrust and we were still descending. Center was trying to contact us to get a pilot report but we had become task saturated in the recovery of the aircraft. The aircraft did eventually start to climb again but the severe turbulence existed through the missed approach altitude and through 16;000 ft.; making it difficult to determine if we were out of windshear. When we were able to resume communications again ATC finally cleared us to FL200 and asked of our intentions. We then informed ATC that we were diverting to ZZZ. We conducted the recovery exactly as trained. We flew the aircraft first; we navigated the aircraft in a tight mountainous area; and finally when the aircraft became stable did we resume communications. It took two of us to fly that aircraft; one on the controls and the other on the thrust levers making call outs.Cause: Extreme weather that wasn't accurately being conveyed by ATC or the pilots of the aircraft that conducted the approach in front of us. The pilots of the aircraft in front of us only reported that they were in moderate turbulence and were unstable.Suggestions: The only thing that could have possibly been done was a communication of the windshear escape procedure; but as I said in the narrative; our sole task was flying that aircraft. Communication came third.
column123: During descent to the initial approach fix we entered into IMC with moderate precipitation and continuous light with pockets of moderate turbulence. Requested right deviation to get around the middle of the cell ahead. Once clear; we turned direct IAF and advised ATC; as per instruction; that we did so. We were then cleared for the approach again.While on the approach; still in IMC; moderate precipitation; and now continuous moderate turbulence; we began picking up icing. We prepared icing speeds for landing ahead of time due to report of aircraft that went missed and diverted to another airport ahead of us. As we continued on approach; we were switched to tower and we were cleared to land. As we descended on the approach the moderate turbulence turned into severe turbulence. We decided to execute the missed approach around 10;000 MSL and let tower know. We were then switched back to ATC. At that point we also entered into wind shear. No wind shear warning populated on the Primary Flight Display (PFD) as we were above 1;500 ft. AGL. With excessive airspeed fluctuations; -3;000 fpm on the VSI; and 30-degree roll either direction; the captain (CA) elected to regain as much control of the aircraft as possible with two hands on the yoke and gave throttles to me. With the wind shear now a factor with the severe turbulence I pushed the thrust levers to max. We eventually climbed while focusing on maintaining control of the aircraft on the published missed track. As soon as we could we contacted ATC to report we had severe turbulence and we were going missed. As the turbulence started to turn back into moderate; we realized we still needed to put in an altitude. CA requested FL230; something that would be well above the turbulence; and to let ATC know. After I put in the altitude; ATC told us to climb and maintain FL200 before I was able to request 230. We accepted that altitude; as at that point we were now starting to feel the turbulence become more manageable. I then returned thrust levers back to normal and turned on appropriate automation. CA then gave me controls while he managed the situation with ATC; the flight attendants; the passengers; and company. Giving a report for the next aircraft; who subsequently diverted back to their departure airports immediately after the pilot report. As did another. CA then set us up for diverting to our alternate and I remained pilot flying for the remainder of the flight. Once to the gate; the CA wrote up the severe turbulence so maintenance could start their inspection.Cause: The weather moving through over the nearby terrain caused the severe turbulence and wind shear event. The sequence of events happening the way they did were a contributing factor.Suggestions: Advise ATC sooner while climbing up out of severe turbulence and wind shear that we needed a higher altitude.

column121: At ZZZ; we planned to conduct traffic pattern training in VMC conditions. The aircraft was a Cessna 172 being flown by a student pilot under my supervision as a flight instructor. The preflight inspection and engine run-up were completed with no abnormalities noted.After receiving takeoff clearance; we departed normally. During the initial climb; the student was making altitude callouts every 100 ft. as part of the training procedure. While monitoring the climb; I noticed that the aircraft was flying below Vy. I instructed the student to adjust pitch to maintain Vy; however; the student reported that despite pitch adjustments the aircraft was unable to achieve the expected climb speed.When the student called out passing 600 MSL; I checked the engine instruments and observed the oil pressure indicating approximately 1 PSI. I immediately took control of the aircraft. While still on the upwind leg; I initiated a 180-degree turn back toward the airport and requested priority handling to the control tower due to a possible engine failure.This was my first time requesting priority handling; and my initial transmission did not include complete information such as aircraft identification; position; and intentions.The tower initially cleared us to land on Runway XX; the departure runway. However; based on our position during the return; I determined that Runway XY provided a more direct approach path. The tower observed our alignment toward Runway XY and asked if we could land on that runway. I responded that I would attempt the landing; and the tower issued landing clearance for Runway XY.Due to the extremely low oil pressure indication and the potential for engine failure; my priority was to maximize glide capability and ensure reaching the runway. I elected not to use flaps in order to preserve glide distance and focused on maintaining a stable approach to the runway. The aircraft landed safely and came to a stop near the end of Runway XY.After landing; the engine continued to operate normally. No abnormal engine roughness or vibration was observed. We were able to taxi back to the parking area without further difficulty; and the tower provided progressive taxi instructions.After parking; airport management came to check on the situation and inspected the aircraft. During the inspection; an oil leak was discovered.This event highlighted the importance of early recognition of abnormal engine indications and continuous monitoring of engine instruments during the initial climb phase. It also reinforced the importance of providing a complete and structured priority handling radio call; including aircraft identification; position; nature of the priority handling; and intentions. In future operations; I will place greater emphasis on prompt recognition of abnormal indications and clear; complete communication during these situations.

column121: A private pilot student and I took off from Runway XXL at ZZZ. I observed all normal engine indications during the run-up and magneto checks. At the hold short line; we were told to turn direct to our destination and cleared for takeoff. Engine indications remained normal during the takeoff roll; and we climbed to 400 feet before turning to our destination. At just over 500 feet AGL; I heard the engine lose power. I glanced down at the throttle control; expecting to see it less than full; instead seeing that it was full forward. Upon seeing this and feeling more vibration than normal from the nose; I took controls from the student and called ZZZ Tower; reporting engine roughness and saying that we needed to return to the airport. The controller advised us to turn 180 degrees to the left and enter a left downwind for Runway XXL. I declined; explaining that the situation was too urgent; and said; I would like Runway XYL" - parallel to my departure runway. I began a right turn toward XYL as I said this. The controller cleared me to land on XYL. I read back the clearance; and set up for a landing on XYL; during which I worked through troubleshooting checklists and explained the situation to the student. My RPMs continued to drop and the vibration continued. I executed the landing on XYL; exited the runway onto Runway XZ as per ATC instructions; and shut down the airplane.According to a mechanic who examined the airplane after the incident; cylinder 4 lost compression during the climb. Examination of the flight data confirmed this. It also confirmed that all engine indications were normal through the run-up; takeoff roll; and early climb. The situation could not have been prevented by any normal pilot checklist.Because of the gravity of the situation (the low altitude and the engine power loss in a single-engine aircraft); I chose not to comply with the tower's initial instruction to enter a left downwind for Runway XXL; and I named the runway I wanted: 91.103 states that a pilot in command may; in a priority handling situation; deviate from a rule; and I judged that the situation warranted such a deviation. Hindsight has confirmed my decision.I had briefed this kind of situation perhaps hundreds of times; and when I recognized the failure; it felt natural to execute the brief: maintain positive control; request the parallel; conduct a low-power; low-altitude landing. I believe that my lack of delay in acting was a direct result of this habit of briefing and of thinking through possible scenarios."

column121: We were in cruise about 10-15 min from TOD (Top of Descent) at FL360. The sun was in our eyes so we both had our sun visors installed. CA's visor was over center pedestal. We continued to discuss and analyze the threat as we flew across the country from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. During our discussions; we looked at the proposed alternates by dispatch that reflected the same geographic region of the severe weather; so we both agreed that going to a 'sure thing' alternate was best and we changed it to ZZZ2/ZZZ3 with dispatches concurrence. As we descended on the STAR; the front that we had been monitoring hit ZZZ and we encountered continuous moderate turbulence with occasional severe turbulence. ATC was having intermittent comms that we had to mitigate concurrently. The airport was shut down for landing and due to the severe weather conditions we were in; we decided to divert to ZZZ2. During the STAR and the divert; we had very sporadic support from ATC. We were being held down in the turbulence despite multiple requests to climb and head towards our divert airport after we relayed that we needed to divert. I understand that ATC becomes very overwhelmed in these circumstances; but I personally felt our handling by ATC in the severe weather we were encountering wasn't as prioritized as it should have been. As we were able to divert to ZZZ2 and as we were descending through 7000 feet; we encountered severe turbulence again that was completely undetected by our radar; SkyPath; jepp fd; WSI (Weather App); or any tools we had. The severe turbulence was so bad that we had to focus the entirety of our mental aptitude on regaining control of the aircraft which was done around 5;500 feet. We experienced moderate turbulence after and light turbulence on final. We landed without incident; no passenger or crew injuries; and no aircraft exceedences. I truly believe that the Captain's tremendous situational awareness; commitment to excellence; and CRM skills yielded the safe outcome of this flight.
column123: During pre-flight; weather conditions at ZZZ were noted for our XA:46Z ETA  that would potentially not allow for a landing on runway XX due to vis below approach mins. Deteriorating conditions were forecast later in the evening. Phone call was made to dispatch discussing alternate options and it was agreed to add ZZZ1 as an additional alternate with ZZZ2.En route; the First Officer and I discussed various alternate options; radiating outward from ZZZ. Based on the severity of conditions at our ETA in ZZZ; we did not want an alternate listed that had TS (Thunderstorm) in the forecast for our ETA or conditions w +SN (Heavy Snow). ZZZ3/ZZZ4 was selected as the closest conservative options and dispatch was conferenced on this decision via ACARS and VHF. ZZZ4 was added to the Flight Plan. Prior to top of descent to ZZZ; ATIS reported gusty winds within aircraft limitations and landing XYR. Moderate turbulence was reported on SkyPath and the vertical profile of WSI (Weather App)  weather radar on. Passengers were briefed of the turbulence and flight attendants were in jumpseats prior to top of descent. We had to self initiate turns away from weather due to inability to get timely response from ATC on the arrival. At one point; there was no communication at all from ATC for a period of time; as if they had lost communications. We encountered continuous moderate turbulence on the descent and at approximately 11;000 feet entered occasional severe turbulence. During this time; the landing runways changed two times due to rapidly changing wind direction with  increasing gust and reports of severe windshear from other aircraft on approach. Due to these factors and approaching our bingo fuel; we notified ATC we were diverting to ZZZ4.ATC turned us to a westerly heading and did not allow for a climb up and out of the moderate to occasional severe turbulence for an unacceptable period of time. The First Officer made repeated request for a climb; which were not approved. A turn to the south towards ZZZ4 was delayed for an unacceptable period of time. Prior to top of descent into ZZZ4; all flight attendant and passenger announcements were made aware of the diversion. The seatbelt sign remained on and flight attendants remained in their jumpseats for the duration of the divert. WSI; SkyPath and weather radar were on/used to evaluate the descent portion of the flight prior to T/D (Touch Down).  There were some areas of moderate turbulence displayed; and no ATC reports or displays of severe turbulence. On the ZZZZZ arrival to ZZZ4 at approximately 7500 feet;  we encountered severe turbulence which disconnected the autopilot and required immediate manual flight intervention. ATC was notified and we were instructed there were smoother rides below 5000 feet with an ATC clearance to an altitude below 5000 feet. Both pilots were required to devote 100% attention to aircraft path with speed fluctuations of approximately +-30kts; large thrust addition inputs and uncommanded role/pitch events. Aircraft exited severe turbulence at approximately 5500 feet.The flight proceeded via vectors for the ILS XXR in continuous light turbulence for an uneventful landing. ELB write up for severe turbulence was made. FOM severe turbulence report guidance was followed along with diversion QRG (Quick Reference Guide) and all stakeholders contacted. No flight attendant or passenger injuries noted.

We also told the controller that we were looking for the traffic behind us. In less than 20 seconds the traffic was passing in front of us; which is where the near miss occurred. Shortly after we clarified with XXX.XY to make sure we were supposed to be on this frequency; which the controller confirmed. I believe the near miss was caused by a combination of factors but it is hard to say without more information from the pilot and controller for the other plane - Unfortunate timing of the controller switch; lack of traffic acknowledgement from the controller; and a lack of communication between pilot and controller on what course was to be flown could have all been factors. From my perspective; the controller switch did not give anyone enough time to react to the traffic conflict. I believe if we had stayed on XXX.XX for longer; we would have had some traffic resolution (I'm not sure what frequency the other plane was on at the time). Remaining on this frequency would have also allowed the controller to clarify directions of traffic for each plane; reducing the risk of the subsequent conflict.
