column121: On Day 0; ground personnel informed the crew that the following day's passengers were 'high-profile' aircraft owners who often travel with significant baggage and advised the crew to monitor weight and balance closely.On Day 1; the assigned crew arrived approximately one hour prior to departure to preflight Aircraft X for a Part 91 flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. The crew planned to reposition back to ZZZ as passengers on Aircraft Y following the flight. The crew completed a standard preflight briefing (weather; NOTAMs; route; fuel; weight and balance; and contingency planning) early in case passengers arrived ahead of schedule. Internal and external preflight inspections were completed without discrepancy.Passengers began arriving planeside with baggage. Ambient ramp temperature was approximately 85-90°F; resulting in elevated cabin temperatures. The SIC (Second in Command) requested an air cart from ground personnel but none were available. Passengers began boarding prior to the crew indicating boarding was ready. The crew had planned for seven passengers; however; nine passengers boarded the aircraft. This was the first time the crew became aware of the two additional passengers. All passengers were around 70 years old. With all nine passenger seats occupied and the cabin door closed; cabin temperatures exceeded 100°F.Upon returning to the cockpit; the SIC observed the PIC recalculating weight and balance due to the additional passengers. Final calculations indicated the aircraft remained within limits but required a revised seating arrangement. The PIC informed the aircraft owner of the situation. Passengers and the SIC deplaned and reboarded according to the revised seating plan. Engines were then started. PIC requested the SIC contact the company to obtain the names of the additional passengers for the manifest while the PIC completed first-flight-of-the-day after-start items. After the SIC completed the call; the crew completed the After Start Checklist together in accordance with SOP. Run-up and takeoff were completed without further issue.While climbing through approximately 6;000 feet MSL approaching the ZZZ VOR; the crew observed multiple annunciations; including L BLEED AIR FAIL; a left engine fire bottle discharge indication; torque differential; and yaw damper disengagement. The autopilot remained engaged. The crew performed the memory items for the L BLEED AIR FAIL procedure; re-engaged the yaw damper; adjusted power settings; and referenced the QRH. The fire bottle discharge indication extinguished after the left bleed air switch was placed to PNEU/ENVIR (Pneumatic/Environment) OFF.The crew confirmed remaining checklist items using the QRH and reviewed the MEL to determine operational limitations associated with a bleed air failure and if the plane would be grounded upon landing at ZZZ1. Guidance said as long as aircraft remained capable of maintaining pressurization; along with other related functions; operations below FL250 were permitted; therefore; the crew elected to continue toward ZZZ1.During the climb; the crew observed that cabin altitude was trending approximately 3;000 feet higher than the pressurization controller setting. For example; when the cabin altitude was set near 4;500 feet for a planned cruise altitude of FL240; the cabin altitude indication approached approximately 7;500 feet. The crew verified the pressurization rate knob was set to minimal and that the dump switch was not activated.The crew adjusted the cabin altitude setting to approximately 7;500 feet; consistent with the planned landing elevation at ZZZ1; to observe whether the system would stabilize. However; cabin altitude continued to increase during the climb and began to approach 10;000 feet while the aircraft was climbing through FL180-FL200.To provide additional margin below the FL250 limitation; the PIC directed the SIC to request a lower altitude. ATC cleared the aircraft to FL220 and subsequently FL200. The crew elected to remain at FL200 to monitor pressurization performance.The crew agreed that continuing over the mountains with a rising cabin altitude and known bleed air malfunction presented increased operational risk. Shortly thereafter; the white CABIN ALTITUDE annunciation activated; indicating cabin altitude had exceeded 10;000 feet and was continuing to climb.The PIC initiated an emergency descent and instructed the SIC to prepare oxygen masks. The SIC advised ATC of the emergency descent and the aircraft was cleared to 10;000 feet and subsequently 9;000 feet. During the descent through approximately 10;000 feet MSL; cabin altitude began decreasing toward the controller setting of approximately 7;500 feet and the CABIN ALTITUDE annunciation extinguished.The PIC then directed the SIC to request a diversion back to ZZZ. ATC approved the diversion with a top altitude of 9;000 feet. The crew referenced the QRH to confirm checklist completion and adjusted the pressurization controller for landing.One passenger briefly entered the cockpit and was informed the aircraft was returning to ZZZ due to an inability to maintain cabin pressure at higher altitudes. The remainder of the flight was uneventful and the aircraft landed at ZZZ without further incident.After landing; passengers deplaned and waited in the airport restaurant while the crew coordinated with company personnel. The PIC contacted Maintenance and the Chief Pilot while the SIC contacted Logistics. Maintenance personnel inspected the aircraft and identified a ruptured left-side bleed air line and determined the aircraft was not airworthy.The company advised the crew that they were expected to depart in approximately one hour in a replacement aircraft to complete the ZZZ1 trip and return to ZZZ. The crew advised the company they were uncertain of their fitness for flight due to physiological symptoms following the event. The PIC reported feeling the effects of fatigue following the high-workload event. The SIC reported symptoms including headache; nausea; fatigue; and difficulty concentrating.The crew contacted a senior representative to inquire about alternate crewing options. None were immediately available. The crew also contacted the Chief Pilot for guidance. The Chief Pilot stated that if the crew determined they were not fit to fly; they should not fly; but advised them to make a decision promptly.The crew conducted a self-assessment of their physiological condition. The SIC determined that they were not fit for continued flight duty under applicable aeromedical guidance. The crew also determined that adequate recovery time exceeded the available one-hour turnaround.The SIC notified Logistics and the Chief Pilot that the crew was not fit for flight and would be removing themselves from duty. The crew then informed the aircraft owner and passengers of the situation.On Day 2; the PIC met with the Director of Operations and the SIC met with the Chief Pilot to review the event. During these discussions; company management suggested the crew could have leveled at an intermediate altitude to attempt to continue to ZZZ1. The crew stated that; based on the known bleed air malfunction; rising cabin altitude; terrain considerations; forecast turbulence; and passenger factors; they believed returning to ZZZ was the safest course of action.The Chief Pilot verbally stated the crew had not violated any regulations or company procedures. When the SIC asked whether a report should be filed; the Chief Pilot advised against it because no regulatory violations had occurred. After further review; the crew determined the event met the criteria for voluntary safety reporting. In the 48 hours following the event; the SIC developed a symptomatic sinus infection/cold. This suggests that during the flight; the SIC was operating with an unknown yet underlying medical deficiency that; when combined with the prior heat exposure; likely accelerated the onset of hypoxia symptoms and exacerbated the physiological recovery time; further validating the decision to decline further flight duty under 14 CFR 61.53.

Not ideal conditions; but we still were optimistic and wanted to try. It was my leg. They asked us to run the engine with passengers on board; we declined due to safety reasons and potential damage to the engine with people on board. The mechanic told us upon further inspection the engine had ingested those particles into the core and would need to be pulled. While waiting for a swap; we assumed that even if we left at XC:00 best case scenario (roughly an hour from when we deplaned) we would be on another min rest layover.Already on a sleep deficit after a stressful redeye into stormy conditions and 9-hour day sleep layover; I did not feel safe operating into the same weather facing another min rest layover and almost guaranteed trip disruption in PIT. column121: On the date of the event; the flight departed ZZZ1 en route to ZZZ. During the initial climb; at approximately 1;300 feet AGL; the aircraft received a windshear warning. The windshear escape maneuver was executed in accordance with company procedures; including the application of maximum thrust. I assumed control of the aircraft from the First Officer during the maneuver. Once the aircraft was clear of the windshear condition and stabilized; ATC was notified of the event; and a PIREP was issued for traffic in the area. Control was then returned to the First Officer.During the enroute phase; weather conditions along the route and at the destination were continuously monitored. Given the reported gusty winds;  I elected to assume pilot flying duties for the landing.Transfer of control occurred during cruise flight. At that time; the autopilot was transferred to the Captain's flight director; and the transponder was switched from position 2 to position 1; allowing ADC 1 to provide the associated data.The approach to RWY XX at ZZZ was stabilized by 1;000 feet AGL. Surface winds were reported as approximately 160 degrees at 13 knots; gusting to 23 knots. The runway was wet; with braking action reported as good (5/5/5). The calculated gust crosswind component for RWY XX remained within the CRJ-200 published crosswind limitations of 27 knots throughout the approach and landing attempt.During the flare at approximately 10 feet AGL; with thrust at idle per normal procedure; the aircraft encountered a sudden and severe wind disturbance consistent with windshear or a strong localized microburst. This resulted in a rapid uncommand roll displacement; with the left wing rising and the right wing dropping. Control inputs were applied as trained to counteract the roll and maintain alignment with the runway. Within approximately less than 2 seconds; a second abrupt wind disturbance occurred during the same low-altitude flare regime.As a direct result of these sequential; uncommand wind disturbances in the flare; the left wingtip contacted the runway surface momentarily. The landing was completed without further incident; the aircraft was decelerated normally; and it taxied to the FBO at ZZZ under its own power.A post-flight walkaround inspection revealed damage to the left wingtip.This report is submitted solely to document the sequence of events; the prevailing environmental conditions (including low-level wind disturbances/gusts); and to support identification and mitigation of potential hazards associated with similar windshear/gust encounters during the critical flare phase on the CRJ-200 in gusty; wet runway conditions.
column123: We departed from runway XZ; out of ZZZ1. We did a flaps 20 takeoff. We climbed out on a heading of 079 and climbed greater than 600fpm. We performed the wind shear escape maneuver; and resumed our climb. We then advised ATC to report the wind shear out of ZZZ1; and they did. As we got closer; the weather was deteriorating. We briefed this on the ground so we were expecting it. There were storms along the route. As we got closer; we re-ran the landing distance numbers. We saw that with a wet runway; we were going to be too heavy to land on runway XY into ZZZ. We decided to go with runway XX. The crosswind component was 23 kts; which is in legal limits for a wet runway. We got the updated weather which was '1'. We decided to perform a risk assessment and I decided to transfer the controls to the captain. We transferred the autopilot and the transponder to the captain side. Controls were transferred in cruise. The approach was briefed already; so we continued on to the descent and approach as normal; for the RNAV XX. Winds were 160@13G23.  We were stable at 1000ft. I made the appropriate callouts during descent. I then called runway in sight and we continued in for landing. At 10 ft above the ground we were idle and in our flare. We had two wind shear encounters within a few seconds. The left wing ended up touching the ground. We parked at the FBO and did a walk around and discovered the wingtip strike. We reported the winds shear to the tower.

I believe that the other aircraft's lack of situational; or visual awareness was a direct factor; and if not; a blatant disregard for; or perhaps a lack of knowledge of; aviation collision avoidance rules. I confidently say that ADS-B; and particularly ADSB-IN was responsible for the safe and uneventful outcome of the situation. Maintaining visual and situational awareness at all times is extremely important for all aviators as well as knowledge of how to handle close encounters such as these.

column121: This is a description of dangerous and reckless helicopter operation that nearly resulted in substantial damage to my airplane; and could have severely injured me. The incident involved helicopter Aircraft X  at the ZZZ.I had parked my airplane in front of fuel pump #1 at the fuel island; had electrostatically grounded the aircraft; set the ladder in front of the wing in preparation for fueling; and had opened the pilot's door completely. I was at the fuel island terminal activating the pump when I noticed helicopter Aircraft X approaching. The helicopter approached from taxiway 1 and proceeded towards its landing area at the FBO on a northerly track behind my aircraft. The helicopter flew within approximately 70 feet of my aircraft in the non movement area carrying substantial power which created significant rotor wash that started rocking and moving my aircraft.  As I ran to my aircraft to stop its movement; the ladder in front of the wing began to fall forward. I caught the ladder and grabbed the wing strut to stop the aircraft's movement.  The helicopter then pivoted to face east and land behind my aircraft; generating even more rotor wash and blasting my aircraft while I braced against the strut to prevent the aircraft from moving further. I could barely hold it and the aircraft moved about five feet forward and pivoted sideways due to the rotor wash. Had I not caught the ladder; it would have struck my propeller causing substantial damage.Had I been on the ladder; I would have been knocked off; and could be seriously injured. Had I not been able to stabilize and stop the movement of my aircraft; substantial damage could have resulted. It was fortunate that the open door does not appear to have been damaged by the rotor wash (I will have a mechanic inspect it).After the helicopter landed and shut down I approached the pilot to discuss the incident. She stated that she saw my aircraft; and she explicitly said she saw the ladder and the open door; but proceeded anyway. When I pointed out the effect of her flight on my aircraft she said 'what am I supposed to do?'  She maintained that she was perfectly justified in flying the way she did. I informed her that in more than forty years of flying I have never had a helicopter or any other aircraft operate in such a way as to endanger my aircraft with their rotor or prop or jet blast. She kept asking 'what am I supposed to do?'  I asked why she did not avoid my airplane; and she stated that the helicopter is an emergency response vehicle. I asked if she was responding to an emergency; and she stated that she was not. She also said I should take it up with the FBO.I related the incident to an experienced helicopter flight instructor at ZZZ; who was appalled by the incident and stated that the helicopter operation was totally inappropriate and hazardous. He stated that the proper procedure would have been to set the helicopter down far from my aircraft and come in under low power on the skids. I suggest that [helicopter pilot] requires some remedial training on operations in the proximity of other aircraft; and have greater consideration for safe operations.

column123: Autopilot+Autothrottles OFFFD (Flight Director) OnFMC: FMS Bridge visual 28ROn approach as described; ATC said we were following heavy traffic and we called it in sight. A large control wheel deflection was used to maintain wings level and combat the roll moment. In the same breath the Captain moved the throttles forward but we were out of it before the engines spooled up and the throttles were reduced to maintain a safe airspeed once out of the event. Captain elected to fly the approach offset vertically by 200 ft and I agreed with it. 15-20 seconds later we entered another wake; exact same; except to the left and it seemed slightly stronger/longer. column121: When cleared to descend via ZZZZZ arrival to ZZZ; I read back the clearance and the altimeter setting and subsequently entered the altimeter setting in the standby attitude indicator. When we completed the descent checklist we used the altimeter setting set in the standby attitude indicator for each PFD (Primary Flight Display). Just outside of the FAF the FO disconnected the autopilot and the auto throttle as was previously briefed. Inside the final approach fix and somewhere between approximately 500 and 1000 feet the FO asked me if I thought it looked like the automation was bringing us in on a very shallow approach. I agreed and instructed the FO to maintain our altitude and transition to the PAPI. The FO re-intercepted the glideslope and landed without incident.Cause: When we were on the ground we realized that I had input a much higher altimeter setting in the standby attitude indicator which we later used for both PFD altimeter settings thus causing us to fly lower than the automation believed we were at.Suggestions:--In the future I'll write down the altimeter setting from the ATIS or weather request and cross check it with the altimeter setting given on the arrival. If the setting is close then I'll use it for reference in the standby attitude indicator. If it's significantly off then I'll use the predetermined altimeter setting and query the controller.
column123: Pilot monitoring read back the incorrect altimeter setting to ATC during the descent phase of flight.  The altimeter setting was .4 inches of mercury off. We realized this on the ground after landing when hearing the correct altimeter setting on the ground frequency.Suggestions: Cross check the ATC given altimeter setting with the ATIS given altimeter setting to look for discrepancies.

column121: Flight normal until incident. Cruising at FL290 heard loud sound from flight deck door. Checked pressurization and doors page then called FA. FA reported sound coming door; noticed cabin altitude increasing; called ATC and initialized a descent. Advised ATC and diverted to ZZZ. Upon 17000 feet noise ceased and pressurization stabilized. CA transferred controls to me (FO) while he ran through QRH and communication with FA; pax and dispatch. When controls were transferred; unintentionally against Standard Operating Procedure; autopilot and transponder were not switched to FO side. This was due to high workload. Which caused issues later on approach. After reaching 4000 feet with stable cabin pressure we entered a hold to burn gas to get below max landing weight. During which time checklists; communications and procedures were completed. The CA who was initially PF for the flight had me as PM take over due to his recent time off. The autopilot was on the CA side after exchange of controls. During the approach I had the autopilot captured the localizer in white needles due to the crosswind; and at approx 12 mile final switched to green needles and the LOC captured. At the minimum glide slope intersect the GS captured but the autopilot did not descend despite the GS mode being captured which causes the aircraft to be high on approach. As PF I disconnected the autopilot and flew the approach visually which allowed for the aircraft to be back on the glide path and stabilized by 1000 feet for stabilized approach criteria.Cause: High workload and task saturation due to high stress from pressurization loss and diversion. The transfer of controls should have included the autopilot and transponder as required by Standard operating Procedure.Suggestions: In the future despite workload I will make sure to check the autopilot side in my scan.
column123: During cruise at FL290 heard loud sound from behind fight deck. Checked door and pressurization synoptics and all systems were showing normal. Called FA and she reported sound was very loud in cabin and was coming from Cabin service door. Requested and got lower from ATC as a precaution. About 1 minute later; cabin pressure started rising slowly. Used model to assess and plan response. Advised ATC; dispatch; FA; and passengers of intentions. Requested Priority Handling and diverted to unplanned diversion. Passing thru 17000 feet; sound stopped and pressure started working normally again. Held by airport to run checklists and to get below max landing weight.Precautionary landing was normal. No injuries to crew or passengers reported.Once on ground wrote up aircraft and contacted maintenance control. Also phoned dispatcher and Maintenance Control to follow up.Cause: Unexpected threat. Handled with model.Suggestions: I can't think of a way to prevent this event as it was an unexpected threat.

column121: While departing ZZZ on Aircraft X a de-ice truck cut off the airplane; causing injury to both flight attendants. Cause: We pushed back off Gate XX and advised operations that we would need de-ice due to light snow and freezing conditions. The ramp crew pushed us back just past the 'zipper road' and onto the ramp area. The ramp is uncontrolled and the ground crew did not push us back far enough that we were able to make the turn without crossing the zipper road.Once we completed the after start checklist; we advised ground and confirmed taxi instructions to the de-ice are. I looked and cleared right; looked left; then checked to make sure the Radio Tuning Unit (RTU) was on the correct frequency. As I looked back to the right; a de-ice truck was approximately 30-45 degrees off the right side of the airplane. I called 'Deice Truck right side' and started to put my feet on the pedals when the Captain hit the brakes. The deice truck went off the zipper road into the gate area to avoid us; and was traveling approximately 25-30 mph.As the airplane came to an abrupt stop; I heard a grunting noise from the cabin. We immediately advised ground control of the incident and the Captain called the flight attendants to see if they were injured. I could overhear the Captain ask about how the flight attendants hit the ground; and we started the process of deciding to gate return.After confirming with several people from ops; duty pilot; and the flight attendants; the flight went on without further incident. It should be noted that both Flight Attendants were the ones who had and made the final decision to continue the flight. Upon arrival at our destination we asked that paramedics meet us at the gate to ensure there was not any unseen injuries; or any other medical issues that could arise.One Flight Attendant was taken to the hospital and the other was released and continued on with the rest of their flying schedule. Suggestions: Push the airplane back further; retrain the driver of the truck.
column123: We were in front of and nose to the zipper road in ZZZ gate XX. We had just completed after start checklist and cleared both left and right sides and I had just began to make the hard left turn to join the ramp lane  behind us to go de ice. We were single engine. After fo cleared right side visually and verbalized and I looked left and verbally cleared my side I glanced back straight ahead and slightly right to ensure we would clear the ramp equipment in the turn when we were at about a 40 degree angle to the zipper road at this point and we would.it was then out of my right periphery that I saw the de ice truck zoom at about what I estimated 25-30 mph off our Immediate right hand side  at a sharp angle and from slightly behind us to the other size of the zipper road which we were on the immediate other side of. At the same instant the fo saw it as well and verbalized its presence. I had no option and was already applying the brakes. We were moving maybe 2-3 knots as we had only just began to make the turn. The plane decelerated very quickly and I heard a thump noise in back. I immediately set the brake advised ground we would be stopped for a bit and what had happened and then called the FAs in the back to see if there were injuries. Person A advised me they had hit the wall but was ok but that Person B had fallen into the wall and hit her head. She was able to come on the interphone and advised she had fallen into the wall by the emergency exit and hit her head I asked if she needed medical attention and she advised she did but wanted to continue and that she was now seated. I advised them to sit for a few minutes while I figured out a plan on what to do. I called dispatch / duty pilot to build my team and advised them what happened; dispatch  listened to my call with the duty pilot. Duty pilot advised that if they said no to medical in ZZZ and that they wanted to continue we needed to continue. I acknowledged. I talked about it with my FO.I called back to them to get more info on their injuries. I believe I asked if they had worsened or if the were bleeding they said they had/were not and that Person B had an ice pack on her ear. I again reiterated that if they wanted medical attention any way In ZZZ that we could just pull back into the gate and have paramedics check them out. Person B refused said she wanted to go. Person A said that they had also wanted to see medical as well when we arrived at our destination because they had hit their back and shoulder but that they did not want to go back to the gate to ZZZ. I again triple checked with them that they were refusing medical in ZZZ and wanted to continue as we could gate return as I was somewhat uneasy departing ZZZ under the circumstances but i talked about it with the team that i had built and the FAs and went with the consensus and departed. Rest of flight was uneventful and we requested paramedics / customer service meet us at the gate at our destination; which they did. Person A worked their next flight and I believe Person B went to the hospital with the paramedics. I believe the de ice truck cut the corner of the zipper road through the ramp from around the corner of the terminal at a high rate of speed and that why we did not see it. I could not see it at first because it came from an angle behind it off our right. I judged I had no option but to hit the brakes in that split second.Cause: Flight attendants were injured due to rapid declaration when I applied the brakes to avoid a de icing truck that went by us in close proximity and at a higher rate of speed while turning to taxi out of the ramp area. Our failure to see the vehicle approach us.Suggestions: Maybe ensure we as a crew double/ triple check left and right before taxiing.

column121: I was PIC in Aircraft X enroute to SBP cruising at 10;500ft approximately 40NM East of SBP. Flight conditions were clear VFR in stable air. I received an ADSB traffic warning 6 o'clock high. Observing the garmin display; and recorecting the zoom it appeared an aircraft was overtaking my position while descending from above me; with less than 700ft of vertical separation; and a 80knot closing rate. I identified the aircraft from it's ADSB transponder and made a radio call on 121.5 to that tail number; which received no response. I made a 45degree descending left turn down to 10;000ft until making visual contact with the aircraft. Due to the aircraft proximity during the evasive maneuver I did not have high fidelity situational awareness of the other aircraft's location until making visual contact. Aircraft Y had been enroute VFR from ZZZ to SBP on what appears to be a direct course at 12;500ft. Aircraft Y began its decent into SBP; at 174kt. At this time Aircraft X was 1.6NM ahead; 1000ft below and at 130kt. Aircraft Y accelerated to 210kt in the decent; making the closing speed at the incident 80kt.Aircraft X made an evasive descending right turn. There was a less than 200ft of vertical separation; less than 200ft of horizontal separation and Aircraft X was unable to make contact with Aircraft Y on 121.5. The evasive action allowed visual contact to be made; and both aircraft arrived without incident to SBP. In summary: Aircraft Y began an enroute decent; and accelerated during the denent. Uncertain of obstruction or telemetry inside the Aircraft Y aircraft; the pilot was likely unaware of the high speed overtake on the same course and position. Aircraft X was only able to identify the situation through ADSP and Garmin 275 display; and made evasive action avoiding a mid-air collision. It is recommended contact be made to the operator of Aircraft Y to discuss if the onboard ADSB equipment was able to identify the imminent collision; and if so were warning systems functional; to ensure the operator scans the airspace in front of the aircraft when making course/altitude changes; and to remind the operator maintaining auxiliary radios on 121.5 could have allowed air-to-air deconfliction over radio communications.

column121: The aircraft operated was under MEL for a failed B fire detection loop. A loop only selected per the MEL and tested ok on preflight. Shortly before reaching cruise altitude we noticed the fire loop A FAULT light flashing intermittently. A message was sent to dispatch and we were patched through to Maintenance Control. After some confusion in relaying the system failure due to poor radio connectivity we sent an ACARS to Maintenance Control explaining that we had a failed B fire loop and now a fault in the remaining A fire loop.  Maintenance Control advised it was Captain's discretion whether to continue the flight or not. After conferring with the FO we decided it would be better to divert back to ZZZ because we had no working engine fire detection system on either loop. Our thinking is that we had another 4 hours of flying ahead and it would be bad to continue since it would be possible to have an engine fire with no flight deck indication. We coordinated with ATC for a return to ZZZ and ran the appropriate checklists. Flight attendants and passengers were notified. We ran the checklist for overweight landing and opted to land on the longest runway; XXL; with auto brakes 2 to avoid hot brakes. We advised ATC that we wanted fire and rescue to examine the aircraft after landing to verify no smoke or fire on the brakes and no signs of an engine problem. ATC advised that if we wanted the trucks they would have to request priority handling for us. We agreed out of an abundance of caution to have fire and rescue look us over after landing. Subsequent approach and landing were uneventful. Upon exiting the runway post flight inspection showed no signs of engine problems or hot brakes. We taxied uneventfully to the gate. Maintenance entries were made for an overweight landing at 174;000 pounds and the failed fire detection loops.

column121: ZZZ was meant to be a fuel stop on our trip. When we fueled up and departed ZZZ; called for gear up; the gear handle raised but the gear did not retract.  We continued to climb to a safe altitude of 6000 feet and get vectors from the controller while we ran the checklist. The gear handle would not go back down to the 'gear down 'position for some time. Upon reaching the point of the 'gear will not retract' checklist; it called for gear handle down and with some force; the handle finally moved to the down position. The gear indicators throughout the entire time remained 'three green' down and locked. There was never a 'gear unsafe' red light illuminated. There was never a hyd pressure light illuminated to indicate pressure to gear . Never received any other abnormal indications.  Once sufficient fuel had been burnt off to make landing weight; we returned to ZZZ with Airport Rescue and Firefighting positioned   just in case. The landing was uneventful. Two days later we ferried plane for maintenance on a ferry permit. Crew was fine and passengers were sent another aircraft for remainder of their trip.Suggestions: The checklist for 'gear will not retract' addressed some of what we were seeing but not everything. Our concern was that the gear handle being left in the up position might cause a gear collapse on landing if left in that position. Luckily; we were able to move it back to the down and locked position.  With the gear handle down and the gear never having retracted; the checklist was complete.  I believe that ultimately the entire gear handle mechanism got replaced but would like to know for sure what failed in the system to cause this problem.

Departing ZZZ at around 3000 feet loud abnormal noise coming from cabin door area; continued climb to 5000 per ATC instructions monitored noise level. No CAS message displayed; door was locked. Landed at ZZZ XXL without incident. Upon arrival at FBO; Line personnel who had assisted us with the door told us he could see a cable protruding along the side of the main cabin door that wasn't there when we left.We debriefed the flight. We made a good call to return based on the information available to us. Upon closing the aircraft we did note that the metal retraction cable for the door retraction system seemed jammed and was not retracting. We did discuss that as a result of this experience a possible safety suggestion it seems there needs to be a more specific MEL for a main cabin door that is only closing halfway and binding vs. the electric motor burned out so as to identify binding or parts within the retraction system that are not operating according to design.

column121: Around 6;000 feet the auto throttle failed and I called for the Captain to cancel and identify. I asked the Captain to delay running the checklist until we got to 10;000 feet as it was busy. I was in controlling the throttle while monitoring the airspeed and the other instruments. After reaching 10;000 feet; the Captain completed the after take-off checklist and I took the radios and flight controls so he could focus on running the QRH. The Captain ran the QRH for AUTO THROTTLE FAIL" and we waited 10 seconds and attempted to reengage the auto throttles which remained failed. We decided to continue the flight to our destination without the use of the auto throttles. I gave the radios back to the Captain. The Captain notified ATC that we would need to amend our final cruising altitude as we were no longer able to enter RVSM. ATC then asked if we needed any assistance and the Captain replied "No". As we continued to climb and at approximately 14;000 to 15;000 feet the aircraft switched into Flight Path Angle (FPA) mode from FLCH mode. I tried re-engaging FLCH mode; with no success. I changed the FPA to 3 degrees up and started monitoring the VSI and ASI. Next the aircraft went into roll mode. I attempted to engage HDG (Heading) mode; with no success. Then the auto pilot disengaged. As we continued climbing through 16;000 feet; we received a Total Air Temperature (TAT) 2 failure message on the EICAS and we lost the FMS Speeds. We entered IMC and we received an icing conditions EICAS message. We were having multiple cascading failures that were increasing our workload while heading to our destination. We decided to return to the field. I leveled us off at 17;000 feet and the Captain requested a descent to exit icing conditions with vectors back to ZZZ. We were given a descent to 13;000 feet and a heading to return to the field.  The Captain briefed the flight attendants and built; bugged and briefed the RNAV approach to runway XXL into ZZZ. We regained FMS AIRSPEED; while descending through 10;000 feet.I hand flew the aircraft for the remainder of the flight and completed a successful landing without further incidence. The emergency equipment had not been requested; but they rolled the trucks as a precaution."

column121: During climbout from ZZZ; #1 engine vibrations fluctuated wildly; oscillating between 2.0 and 3.5.  High vibrations continued until power was reduced to maintain cruise altitude.  I contacted dispatch through VHF radio and we did a 3 way call between myself; dispatch; and Maintenance Control.  Maintenance informed us during the conference that the #1 engine had a recent history of several writeups for high vibrations and that there was a technical item assigned to that engine to track its performance.  I expressed my concern that this aircraft was assigned to a destination like ZZZ1 (our original destination) given its history.  The three of us agreed that it would be prudent to return to ZZZ given the limited contract maintenance available in ZZZ1 and the high terrain in the area that places a high demand on the engines  in the event of a go-around or takeoff from runway XX.  At the time we were about 6;000 lbs over max landing weight; so we coordinated with ATC to hold until we were under max landing and we returned to ZZZ.  Known history of bad performance on an engine that was also assigned to a destination which has limited contract maintenance.Aircraft with engines that have a recent history of questionable performance should not be assigned.  The lower display in the 737 should be turned on during the after takeoff checklist so that all secondary engine indications are displayed to catch this and other engine situations that slowly creep up on the crew.  The time to be prepared and do something is early before the situation arises; not when the display automatically pops up. This should be standardized across all Boeing fleets.
column123: I was performing PF duties flying Aircraft X from ZZZ Airport to ZZZ1. During climb out it was noticed that the left engine vibration was fluctuating. The CA; performing PM duties; and I each looked and noticed the engine vibration fluctuating in an erratic pattern. I noticed that the initial fluctuation grew from approximately 2.0-2.5 to 1.5-3.5 rapidly and unpredictably; while the right engine remained steady at approximately 0.2. As the PF; I scanned other instruments and all other indications seemed normal; we continued the climb while watching the engine vibrations. The CA opened and referenced the engine vibration checklist in the event we might need it; so that we would be prepared - however we did not perform the checklist as the fluctuations did not go out of limits.We had a brief discussion; which resulted in us not being able to say why the engine was vibrating like that; and that the captain could actually feel the vibration on his side of the cockpit. Shortly after the CA asked if I was comfortable handling the aircraft and radios so that he could try to call dispatch; to which I concurred.Around this time passing through FL280 and leveling at FL290; over Location X I assumed those duties. I noticed that the engine vibration fluctuations lessened but did not resolve at cruise power settings. As the Captain was working through his call to dispatch; I was focused on aviating; navigating; and communicating - having to work route deviations and climbs to avoid weather over Location X. I did note that when we climbed from FL290 to FL330 for weather; the engine vibration fluctuations increased at climb power as they had before - and settled a little lower but did not resolve at cruise power at FL330.I was able to hear a small portion of the conversation the Captain was having; most notably the discussion from the maintenance representative that this aircraft had some form of history of this engine vibration; and that there was a concurrence with dispatch that a return to ZZZ was prudent. The CA informed me after their call that we would return to ZZZ.It was my understanding having discussed with the CA after his call to dispatch that this return to ZZZ was based on there being a known history of fluctuating indications on the left engine for an unknown reason. Our discussions revolved around ZZZ1; the single engine profiles; performance; and potential for the engine to have some form of failure at the wrong moment on those complex departure procedures. After the decision to return to ZZZ the discussion was had weather to land overweight; or to burn down fuel to land under max landing weight. Based on: strong and gusty crosswinds; the potential to damage the aircraft landing heavy; the engine remaining within limits and settling lower at cruise power; I recommended to descend and burn down fuel in holding to below max landing weight; to which the CA agreed. We then returned to ZZZ uneventfully. An engine with a history of engine vibration presentation; which was fluctuating rapidly close to the upper limit. Engines with known issues such as this should not be dispatched. The lower display is turned off per SOP; however passing 10k this screen should be turned on to be monitored during the remainder of the flight.

column121: Just prior to beginning our descent we noticed the green hydraulic quantity was very low just above the amber. Once we started the descent just prior to the fix ZZZZZ on the ZZZZZX arrival; we got an amber HYD G ENG 1 PUMP LO PR ECAM. I continued as PF while my Captain ran through the Ecam procedure. He had me fly the aircraft and run radios while he dealt with this procedure. We elected to level off and enter a hold over ZZZZZ to develop and analyze a plan. The ECAM had us shut down the green ENG 1 PUMP which displayed numerous inop systems; including the possibility of manual gear extension; gear retraction ; nosewheel steering; etc. After advising maintenance; Dispatch; and FA's we determined the best course of action was to request priority handling and divert to ZZZ. I continued flying while my Captain contacted ZZZ ops; reviewed procedure manual pages and briefed FA's of a precautionary landing in ZZZ. We notified ZZZ tower we would be stopping on the runway and would need possible tow off runway as well as Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) to give a quick inspection. Joining final for RWY XXL; we turned on GREEN ENG 1 PUMP as directed by the STATUS page APPR PROCEDURE. We regained back all our inop systems and the aircraft was operating as normal. We landed as normal; came to a stop; and the captain made a PA to the passenger notifying that ARFF would be inspecting the aircraft out of caution. We were able to taxi back to the gate under our own power with no further issues. Event was caused by hydraulic abnormalities. Only mitigation is to continue to be proficient in emergency procedures.
column123: Enroute we received a HYD G SYS LO PR ecam and other subsequent ecams. We performed the ecam methodology as trained. We entered a holding pattern between ZZZ1 and ZZZ. FO remained PF while I spoke with dispatch; ATC; FAs; and passengers. The decision was jointly made to divert to ZZZ; only 45 miles away at that point due to the long runway; acceptable Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) and maintenance personnel. The FO remained PF during the duration of the flight and did a great job. Per the ecam we were able to turn the G pump back on and get the gear and flaps down normally using whatever fluid was left. We stopped on the runway; ARFF performed their inspection; and we we able to taxi to the gate on our own power. We took our time and were deliberate in our actions and decisions. Air Carrier X was a great resource and very helpful during the entire event as was ATC. We are trained very well such that two pilots who have never met or flown together until the day before can be professional and standard and work together in a setting like that.Nothing really from a flight crew perspective. Per the logbook closing actions looks like a faulty hydraulic drain valve and busted o ring. Not sure what we as flight crew could do different for a maintenance item like that

column121: Just after reaching cruise altitude at 36;000FT with the First Officer as PF;  a FA called from the aft galley saying there was a loud wind noise coming from door 2L in the back of the aircraft. I checked the overhead panel and verified no door lights were on; the cabin Altitude was steady at 8000ft with a differential 7.8PSI. I had the FA verify the door 2L handle was secure in the latched position and she verified the door was secure mechanically. The FA said the ambient noise was so loud that they would need ear plugs to continue the flight. I could also hear the loud ambient noise through the intercom as we talked.I told the FAs that the door seal most likely failed or did not engage properly; and that the door was mechanically secure so there was no safety risk of it opening inflight. I told the FAs that I would have a conference call with Maintenance Control and Dispatch to come up with a plan; but most likely we would be returning to ZZZ.I informed the FO/PF who had been listening in what the situation was and had the FO continue to manage the aircraft and ATC coms while I talked to Dispatch and Maintenance Control. After establishing a phone patch with Dispatch and Maintenance Control I relayed the information from the FA and Maintenance Control had me verify the cabin altitude and DIF pressure readings. Ultimately a decision was made to return to ZZZ and that the airplane would be landing about 7500-8000LBS over the max structure landing weight. I had the FO coordinate with ATC new clearance to return to ZZZ and to request lowest altitude possible to burn off as much fuel as possible on the return as well as attempted to lower the Cabin ALT and reduce the ambient noise if possible. An emergency was not declared at the time.I did a Brief with the Purser; then made a cabin PA for the passengers explaining the situation. After referencing the 737 Flight Manual for overweight landing I ultimately decided that due to our landing weight being close to 8;000LBS over the max structure  the need for runway XXR in ZZZ (longest available) as well as the possibility of hot brakes after landing that requesting priority handling and having fire trucks on standby for the brakes was the most conservative plan of action. I informed ATC of the change of status to priority handling and why; then requested runway XXR and to have the fire trucks on standby for a brake check once clear of the runway. ATC passed along all the information and verified our FOB and SOB. I did another briefing revision with the purser due to the change to priority handling status. I then made a PA to the cabin about the reason for the fire tucks meeting the aircraft after landing.After the FMC was set up; Briefings and checklists were complete I took over PF duties of the aircraft. I did this due to the need for a soft landing and the FO was coming back form a leave as we were conducting the FO's requalification training on this trip.A soft landing was made with a VSI of about -210FPM (3.5FPS) at 153;800lbs landing weight. After clearing the runway the fire crew did a circle around the aircraft and reported the brakes looked normal with no glowing or any signs of overheating. A normal taxi to gate XX was made and aircraft parked and passengers deplaned. Maintenance techs met the aircraft and took the details from me after I sent in the Log Book reports for the door and overweight landing. Flight XXXX continued out of gate XX with a different aircraft 90 min later.

column121: Approximately 15 minutes after departing ZZZ and climbing through 28;000 for FL330 over Location X the cabin interphone call chimed.  As pilot monitoring I took the call and was alerted by a very panicked flight attendant that there was a fire in the forward galley.  Details were not very clear but I understood they were getting fire extinguishers and starting to fight the fire.  Without delay I hung up the phone and took control of the aircraft.  The FO immediately informed ATC and we began a turn and descent back towards ZZZ.  Once the aircraft was on the desired path towards ZZZ we were able to speak with the purser and found that the fire was contained to the forward galley oven and had been extinguished using one halon extinguisher.  Control was transferred back to the FO.We communicated with ATC the fire was out but since there was no way to be sure it wouldn't reignite we continued to ZZZ and informed them that it would be an overweight landing.  Dispatch was notified via satcom.A PA was made advising the passengers that we were heading back to ZZZ.The FAs were briefed.A normal approach and landing was made on XXL.We were met by airport vehicles to ensure no issues with brakes or tires.After inspection we taxied to the gate without incident; Crash Fire Rescue (CFR) boarded the aircraft and ensured the fire had been fully extinguished.Passengers were deplaned and a new aircraft took them to ZZZZ.
column123: Fifteen minutes into our climb; at 28;000 feet; the forward galley flight attendants called the flight deck to inform us of a fire. The Captain slid the phone halfway off his cheek; looked at me; and said fire". I asked; "Is it contained?" Given the panic in the galley; we initially believed the fire was not under control. Aircraft controls were transferred to the CA; who initiated a descent and a turn towards ZZZ. I informed ATC of our actions. Shortly after our turn towards ZZZ; the flight attendants called back with additional information. They reported that the fire was located in the forward galley oven and that one fire extinguisher had been used. I repeated this information to the flight attendants to ensure clear communication. The fire had been extinguished. I then relayed this information to the CA. Ultimately; since we could not determine the source of the fire and could not guarantee that it would not reignite; we decided to continue our diversion to ZZZ. We discussed the potential threats associated with an overweight landing and the increased pace of flight deck duties associated with a quick return. We prioritized the important threats appropriately; and trapped them with mitigation strategies. We performed an overweight landing and stopped on the runway until we could assess brake temperatures. The most incredible moment of this flight unfolded when we arrived at the gate. To our astonishment; all of our wheelchair passengers walked off the airplane."

column123: We were at cruise at FL350. Captain and I were finishing up a conversation about misc maintenance codes. I was PF at the time when we got the ECAM. Both the Captain and I identified it immediately and captain assigned duties of me being PF while he ran the Ecam. Completed Ecam procedure; reported it to maintenance. The yellow hydraulic level was completely drained. After a discussion for a plan; the captain and I both agreed to request priority handling due to the loss of systems. We communicated with dispatch; Maintenance Control; and flight attendants as well as passengers. We proceeded to ZZZ and requested the longest runway. We landed on XXR with an uneventful landing. We did have to stop on the runway as there was no nose wheel steering. We were met on the runway by emergency vehicles soon followed by a tug that brought us to gate XX.

column121: Crew was pushing out flight XXX heading to ZZZZ. While our driver was pushing the plane back he was told to reverse to make space for other aircraft. This flight was leaving from gate XX. column121: On Day 0; we had Aircraft X enter RON (Routine Overnight) with pump 2A on MEL and pump 2B requiring removal due to high time. ZZZ says fuel pump 2B canon plug was not connected and pump 2A was missing an O-ring  which caused the leak. The mechanics states that the pump comes with o rings already pre-installed and that they remember connecting the canon plug.  Per the Maintenance Manual the fuel pumps are not RII (Required Inspection Item) since they are internal tank components which internal tank components do not require leak check and no item under ATA 28 requires RII for operational check (system check). The Maintenance Manual states that the preinstall and leak check on fuel tanks panels is RII. I watched one of the techs prep the panels and installed new o rings and lubricants that the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) called for. I did an area check prior to panels being installed to verify no tools or unwanted materials were inside of the tanks. I then stayed nearby to watch the install of the panels and watched the panels be torqued. After; the mechanic finished torquing the panel I verified each bolt by physically going over every bolt with the torque wrench. I then watched the leak check for the panels and after transferring fuel into the center tank there were no leaks noted from the fuel panels.We have one specific mechanic that works here that is a danger to our hanger and he needs to be spoken to because he is constantly messing things up.Suggestions:  Mechanics need to do a better job when it comes to working on the aircraft. They need to make sure they are following the AMM tasks references to ensure this does not happen again.
column123: On Day 0 I was the lead for RON (Routine Overnight) Aircraft X. The aircraft required fuel pump 2A and 2B to be changed for an MEL and suggested for high time respectively. When the aircraft landed in ZZZ; fuel was noted to be leaking from the aircraft on the ground and was brought into maintenance. They found that pump 2A was leaking due to a missing O-ring on the cannon plug that separates the tank from a dry area. These pumps come from stock with an O-ring preinstalled; as pump 2B had. Before leaving the hanger; a leak check had been performed and no fuel was noted to be leaking. I believe the person performing the leak check on the ground may not have noticed the leak because it was not coming from the panels being inspected.Cause: Attempting to meet deadlines and failing to properly double check/inspect work.Suggestions:  Inspect parts from stock for damage or missing components prior to installation. Perform more thorough area checks and double check work prior to installation of panels.

column121: In the interest of safety; I am writing this report to help pilots be more aware of the risks of improper fuel planning. On Day 0; a passenger and I made our way to ZZZ for a joyride. When we arrived at the airport; I immediately began my preflight with Aircraft X. My standard walk-around includes checking all control surfaces; propeller; tires; brakes; oil; and fuel. Fuel is always my last task. On this particular day; I visually verified that both tanks were full. I also strained the fuel to ensure no contaminants were present. Since this was a day VFR joyride; I calculated the distance and time we would be flying; and it was agreed we would just go where we wanted to.The flight was uneventful for the first portion as we made our way from ZZZ to ZZZ1 at 4;500 feet; where we conducted a landing and then flew up to Location X for pictures. We then flew from Location X to ZZZ2; where I flew the RNAV XX approach. At that point; I decided not to stop and check the fuel and performed a low approach; believing I had plenty of fuel to make it back to ZZZ.I knew the aircraft held 38 gallons of usable fuel and estimated a burn rate of 8 GPH. At the time we executed the low approach at ZZZ2; we had only been flying for approximately 3 hours; which I believed was sufficient to return to ZZZ.I then began setting up for a practice RNAV XY approach into ZZZ. After crossing ZZZZZ on approximately an 8-mile final and descending through about 2;500 feet; the engine began to sputter. I checked the total flight time; which was approximately 4 hours and 5 minutes. I immediately looked for the nearest airport on the GPS and initiated a 180-degree turn to attempt to return to ZZZ3; which was approximately 4 miles behind us.The engine continued to sputter and then completely lost power shortly after leveling the turn. At that point; it was clear we did not have the altitude or power to reach an airport. I immediately began running the emergency checklist and pitched for best glide and began looking for a suitable field.Around 100 feet AGL; I noticed the airspeed decreasing and added full flaps. The selected field was clear of crops; and I executed a soft-field landing. There were no injuries and no damage to the aircraft.Upon review of the aircraft; it was determined that both fuel tanks were empty due to higher-than-expected fuel consumption during the flight. Even though we departed with full fuel; I did not adequately calculate the fuel required for the flight we ultimately conducted.Additionally; the mixture was not properly adjusted during portions of the flight; which likely contributed to increased fuel consumption. The decision to continue from ZZZ2 without verifying fuel quantity was also a contributing factor and; in hindsight; could have prevented the situation.As PIC; I take responsibility for the outcome of this flight and the planning decisions that led to this situation. This experience highlighted a lapse in judgment that resulted in a scenario I had not intended.I am proud of how the situation was handled. I remained calm; followed established procedures; and relied on my training to safely land the aircraft without injury or damage.I learned more from this experience than any single flight lesson. It reinforced the importance of thorough planning and disciplined decision-making.In the future I will ensure fuel requirements are properly calculated; including legal reserves; even on shorter or 'joyride' flights. Properly adjust the mixture throughout all phases of flight. Stop and verify fuel status rather than relying on assumptions.This is an experience I will not forget; and it has reinforced the importance of completing all calculations thoroughly and maintaining situational awareness throughout the entire flight.

column121: For the past several years I have flown my employer to view the preparations of grounds for the event. This flight entailed 3-4 circular orbits at 500-600 ft with airspeeds ranging from 60-80 knots before departing south to ZZZ. Approximately 15 minutes later we departed ZZZ; enroute back to the hanger. While in cruise; we overflew Location X from south to north at an altitude of 500 ft and 100 knots airspeed. Within 1.5 hours of landing at the hanger we were approached by (2) Sheriff's deputies who informed us that they were operating drones overhead as part of their security detail. He said we flew at an altitude below one of the drones; which was at 200ft. We vehemently denied the possibility. Before leaving one deputy stated that there was no active TFR; but there is a heightened security risk; due to conflicts abroad. Had we been aware of these facts we would not have conducted the flight. Drones are increasingly being used by law enforcement due to low cost and are less intrusive from the ground (low noise and visibility). Before drones; law enforcement helicopters were deployed for this type of surveillance. They were easily seen by other helicopters in the vicinity and monitored an air-to-air frequency to communicate with other aircraft. Unfortunately; this level of safety does not exist with drones. They are invisible to aircraft and are most often stationary. Corrective actions: Local law enforcement when operating security/surveillance drones at events should be required to depict times and location on aircraft navigation equipment via ADS-B. Drones should be required to have a highly reflective surface in addition to higher intensity anti-collision lights. Due to possible inaccurate altitude indications; drone maximum altitude should be reduced below 400ft to increase vertical separation. TFR's should be required when any level of additional security is needed at an outdoor event when security drones are in operation.

column121: I was PF.  We were holding short of runway 07 waiting for takeoff while a Aircraft Y landed in front of us.  After they landed we were told to line up and wait.  The Aircraft Y appeared to clear the runway at the other end and we were cleared for takeoff.  Just after the FO made the '80kt' callout; tower told us 'Aircraft X cancel takeoff clearance.'  After a 1-2 second hesitation I initiated a rejected takeoff.  Asking tower for details on the problem we were told that the Aircraft Y never cleared the hold-short line at the other end.  We exited the runway and reviewed the rejected takeoff considerations.  Because it was >80kts an maintenance logbook entry was required.  I contacted dispatch and maintenance control who directed us to return to the gate for inspection.  After the inspection was complete and brake cooldown times were observed we departed again.Cause: Lack of taxiway and gate space in LIR leads to planes stacking up on the only 2 exits for runway 07.  The aircraft that landed did not have room to clear the runway.  Every takeoff also requires a back-taxi which is very often 'expedited' for traffic.  It seems like the airport does not have the ramp or taxiway space to support the number of operations.
column123: On Day 0; I was pilot monitoring of Aircraft X as first officer with scheduled service from LIR to ZZZ. The captain and I arrived to the airport well-rested after a 23-hour overnight and the arrival to the airport and airplane was standard. There were no issues with any of the aircraft origination or checklists; and no anomalies with respect to preflight duties or clearance delivery/routing. We were given clearance for push back and start from gate XX; which was accomplished normally and we joined the line for taxi to the departure end of the runway. The airport had been on runway 07 operations for the entire time we were there; so a full-length back taxi was required. Upon reaching the runway; we waited in the turnaround for arriving traffic behind an aircraft. There was an arriving Aircraft X that landed a few minutes after the aircraft departed that; once past us; we were issued a line up and wait clearance; which we accepted. After waiting in position for approximately two minutes; we were given a takeoff clearance by the tower. Initial power up and acceleration was normal. I called 80" and almost immediately after; tower calls "Aircraft X; cancel takeoff clearance." The captain and I were a bit confused as there was nothing hazardous immediately apparent in front of us; but we initiated a rejected takeoff. The deceleration was smooth; and callouts were standard. Once stopped; I started a timer and dropped the flaps to 40° and the captain retracted the spoilers and made an announcement to the cabin to remain seated. Once slowed; we were asked if we could make a 180 on the runway to return to the departure end; which we were able to accommodate. I was instructed to perform an after landing flow; and the captain and I began to discuss the requirements for a rejected takeoff and brake cooling requirements from the table in the AOM. The auto brakes did not fire; so we knew we were below 90kt when the reject was initiated; however with the adjustments for the length of taxi and the headwind; we determined that the most conservative cooling time was 45.9 minutes. We were not in the caution or melt zone; so we set the parking brake when coming to a complete stop.When queried the reason for the rejected takeoff clearance; the tower responded that an airplane had not fully cleared the runway. They tried to issue us a second takeoff clearance while we were calculating cooling times and contacting dispatch and maintenance control; and ultimately we were instructed to return to the gate for a visual inspection. We were caught in a lot of traffic; but made our way back to the gate and maintenance was waiting on us. We elected to not give the opportunity to deplane given the efficiency with which we were parked and accommodated by maintenance. The airplane was determined to be safe to continue on; so we closed the main cabin door; and pushed back for a normal flight arriving to ZZZ about an hour and a half late. No injuries were reported and no further problems with the airplane were experienced. Cause: We were issued a late cancellation of takeoff clearance for a runway incursion that was impossible to see from the departure end of the runway. Flight and cabin crew followed SOPs to mitigate injury or escalation of the event."

column121: Flight proceeded normally during our pre-flight duties. We were slightly delayed pushing waiting for wing walkers. Once pushed; we were cleared to start engine 1. Upon starting engine one I had noticed the EICAS message 'PACK 2 VLV CLSD'. I ran the QRH; which did not resolve the issue. Captain and I decided that we needed to go to a hard stand and call maintenance for further troubleshooting/possible deferral of the pack. During our taxi; (starting from gate XX; to the west hard stand) as a means of troubleshooting and isolating variables; we decided to start engine 2; and see if the message would persist with engine bleed air instead of APU bleed air. After starting engine 2; the message persisted. We informed ramp of our issue; pulled into the handstand and the Captain proceeded to call maintenance.Pack 2 inop is flight crew deferrable item; so we followed maintenance's procedures for the deferral and then worked on the next task. As part of the deferral; we were restricted to FL250 (originally FL360) and since this was an MEL affecting our performance and fuel consumption calculations we needed to call dispatch and see if we have enough fuel; and if so; get a new release. Upon calling dispatch we were able to continue with our current fuel on-board; and obtain a new release. After getting our new release we rejoined the departures and the taxi-take off was completely uneventful. The take off was normal until the climb portion where I had noticed the EICAS message 'ENG 2 BLV VLV CLSD' during my after take off flow. I consulted the Captain on the appropriate QRH procedure and conducted the QRH procedure. Upon completion of the procedure the message had cleared and we continued. As we leveled off at FL240 (our final filed altitude); I smelled a burning smell; simultaneously the Captain had noticed the same thing. As we looked at each other; I noticed smoke coming above the Captain's head. We then dawned our O2 masks; and we informed ATC that we needed to immediately return to ZZZ due to 'smoke in the cockpit'. The flight attendant also contacted us about a burning smell. The Captain flew and coordinated our return while I ran the QRH; during this time I transferred radios to the Captain while I continued the QRH. We then descended and received vectors back to ZZZ; we joined the localizer for XXC. Since I was not fully caught up on setting up approach/speeds; I informed the Captain that I 'needed more time' we informed ATC. We continued on that heading for a brief minute; then the Captain determined that the safest course of action was to continue for XXL instead of delay vectors; as we did not know the source; nor the severity of the possible smoke and fumes. I was able to load in the approach speeds and we joined the localizer XXL. He landed very smoothly; we pulled off the runway and asked crash; fire; rescue to confirm that there was not any visible smoke or fire on the exterior of the aircraft. They confirmed that it was clear on the exterior. We then determined that it was not necessary to evacuate the aircraft as there were no signs of persisting smoke or fumes and the flight attendant also did not have any signs of smoke in the cabin. We elected to taxi to the gate. From our brief ACARS message; I said that we were told to go to gate XY. As we taxied into the ramp; ramp control informed us that it was occupied. We then stressed that we need a gate ASAP ! They then directed us to another gate on the concourse. I cannot remember the exact gate; possibly XZ or XA. We then taxied over to the 'vacant' gate; but there was a fuel truck in the way and no rampers. We immediately called operations and informed them that we needed it moved immediately; we proceeded to wait for another few minutes; despite another call. However; we confirmed that there were still no signs of smoke or fumes from the aircraft during the taxi and waiting period; and had a fire truck follow us. We pulled into the gate; deplaned the passengers in an organize manner; and shut down the aircraft.Maintenance determined Pack 1 exhaust duct had blown; and it was ingesting pack exhaust into the cabin (preliminary)

column121: Holding for runway XX in ZZZ for weather to improve to have a better chance of getting in for landing at waypoint ZZZZZ at 4;000ft. After 20 minutes of holding (estimate) weather improves and approach descends us to 3;000ft to proceed inbound. It was my leg (first officer) and began to configure for the approach that would be near minimums. Once inbound; I recognize that the plane ahead of us (corporate) is relatively close but approach permitted us to continue. I would estimate we were in trail by 4-5 miles. Fully configured prior to GS intercept; as we cross ZZZZZ1; the autopilot disconnects; and I lose guidance from the Flight Directors (FD) but continue raw data. Captain and I recognize he still has guidance; and so we transfer the controls at around 1;400ft with the autopilot off. We are stable at this event. Approach then directs us to break off the approach and turn left 90 degrees (cannot remember the specific heading) and climb to 3;000ft. As PM; I turn off the FD's; spin the heading bug and altitude bug while clicking LVL Change and Heading (HDG) select. I believe I did this with the flight directors off; but due to the subsequent events; I am not so sure. As I am doing this; the Captain is calling for flaps 15 and gear up. It is during this that I realize; the Captain is still descending because of the flight directors giving him an improper guidance. The Captain was following the GS down but had began the turn to the requested heading. After setting the flaps to 15; I tell the Captain to climb" repeatedly. He recognizes what he is doing; and corrects to our assigned heading and altitude. The lowest we got was approximately 1;050ft. We also got an audible callout of which I assume was "sink rate" and approach asking us to check our altitude and notified us of the MVA. I cannot recall those 10 seconds exactly; but I assume those were the events that occurred to my best knowledge. From there we cleaned up the plane; and set up for the approach again. To get proper automation; I flipped the NAV frequencies from the LOC to the VOR; and then clicked HDG and LVL change. Captain asked if I wanted to take the plane back; and I did. After I had controls; we both decided leaving the autopilot on the Captains side would allow for better situational awareness and we proceeded as such; and landed the plane with that configuration. We saw the approach lights at around 400ft. There weren't many things that I felt went right if I were to do the situation again. I believe that handing the plane to the Captain at 1500ft; albeit low; was the right decision at the time. I tried to be preventative and cycle the FD's to get to the proper automation; but that did not work as planned. Only once the NAV frequencies were flipped; a preventative action was taken. I also believe the Captain handing the plane back to me for the second approach was a containment action from him; I do not know if he was shaken up or had gotten disoriented by what had just occurred; but I felt very comfortable with flying the plane from the position we were in and do believe it was safe to do so given what had just happened. Not once do I think that CRM had fallen apart; in fact; I think we both excelled at communicating what was happening once the event had happened. I want to bring up that after we had completed our duties as flight crew-members; the Captain did not waste time asking about what happened; what went wrong; etc. Again; I want to emphasize that I never felt that CRM was an issue and the Captain was very approachable about the event afterwards."

I forgot to mention the aft fa brought up a halon just in case after the purser let the others know what had happened. We all met in the mid galley for the information and had about 10 minutes or less until landing. We were told we didn't need to do an evacuation at that point and if anything changed they'd let us know. After we landed the Captain told us our brakes were okay to continue to the gate so no evacuation needed. Once we got to the gate it was determined that everyone would deplane and the aircraft would be taken out of service. column121: I decided; for the safety of Flight; and perhaps a good discussion; to post a little educational rant about a very close midair my student and I watched happen on Day 0 at XA:20 at ZZZ. We were holding short of RWY XX and watched a prior plane on a somewhat long final make a touch and go. A Cherokee then turned their base behind them appropriately and I pointed out to the traffic to my student. Interestingly; we then noticed a subsequent Cessna turn a very low tight left base. The Cherokee by this time was already on final; and had made their call. They then asked if the Cessna had them in sight. They replied in the affirmative and that they would 'extend their base.' For the record; they were already on their base leg. I watched as both planes continued on a collision course right above the Street X intersection with the Cherokee finally climbing and side stepping and the Cessna staying low and flying due south probably about 50 feet of separation between them; then making a radio call 'that was close!' I spoke to the Cherokee pilot afterwards and fortunately they did have the Cessna traffic in sight throughout the incident; so I suspect while it looked close that it would have had a safe outcome regardless of how it looked from my vantage point. A few thoughts for all of us to ponder. I am convinced that the Cessna never had the Cherokee in sight. I presume; perhaps falsely; that they were looking at an ADSB return rather than out the window. We all need a reminder that ADSB is NOT visual separation. When ATC asks you if you have traffic in sight; they mean with your eye balls. Not on your 'fish finder'. Please; for the love of God; do not call it that. Even more importantly; when another pilot asks if you have them in sight; do not reply in the affirmative if you do not. Instead; take action immediately to increase the separation between you. In formation flying when you lose sight of your wingman; you immediately call blind and increase the separation between the aircraft. This isn't checkers; it's flying. And a simple screw up will kill you; or much worse; someone else. ADSB isn't perfect. It has a lag. Sometimes a fraction of a second and sometimes 20 seconds. Are you using a third party device that then wirelessly connects to your foreflight app to show you? Are you holding a phone in your lap? Or is your system installed in the plane and displayed on a Multi-function Flight Display (MFD)? Even primary radar has a lag. Nothing is perfect. More importantly  not everyone has ADSB. It's not required. I don't have it in my plane. It is for situational awareness. It is not meant to replace your eyeballs. When someone on the frequency calls a position you should look outside the plane first; not at your panel or your phone. I presume we all know 91.113 about right of way. Read it again if you haven't this year. Landing traffic has the right of way. If someone is already on final; turn your left base once they are at your 9'o'clock; not while they are still at 11 o'clock. The C210 on Day 0  turned their base low at least a half mile before the Cherokee. In the left seat; low; with a high wing; they had no chance of seeing that Cherokee. Why then did they say traffic was in sight? And what does extending your base leg even mean when you are already on your base?The question I pose to myself; sitting at the threshold; is should I have been empowered to play ATC and demand a go around? My thought was to not clog the frequency while these two worked it out. However in hindsight; there was no negotiation between them. I would have felt very guilty if I had not said something. Kudos to both pilots afterwards for being kind and professional. Neither of them got nasty on the radio (something that I hear too frequently these days) and neither of them chastised each other. The Cessna exited the area and the Cherokee got back in the pattern. I presume both had honest debriefs when they got home. However; the rest of us can stand to learnsomething from this close call before the flying season gets busy. Every year in our country someone dies due to this situation because of two reasons: 1.) they misinterpret 91.113 or 2.) they are too hard headed to realize that even though they are in the right; they neglect to knock off their approach and create separation because - dang-it - they have the right away!!! I argue that this Cherokee; due to the fact that they could see the Cessna making a mistake; could have aborted their touch and go 30 seconds earlier. They could have sidestepped on an upwind to keep the Cessna in sight and learned a valuable lesson that being courteous; even when you were the one that was wronged; is the right thing; and the safe thing; to do. Don't think this thing happens a lot? How many classic 91.113 see and avoid mishaps come to mind right off the bat?  DCA accident?  Centennial accident between the metro liner and Cirrus. Or maybe all of us need to have a little common sense and remind ourselves to be courteous. This means if you are working with a student on instrument work and the pattern is really full; it's not the time to do your circling maneuver. This means if it's clear and a million and you're on an instrument plan in a single engine piston; you shouldn't fly a 10 mile straight in and you should join the pattern in a VFR manner - even if your bladder is about to explode! It means if a turbine is arriving; that the rest of us make way and let them land. We only have one sand box to play in. We should keep it pleasant for every user…we all have a right to be there.
