column121: I was providing flight instruction near ZZZ Airport  when we experienced a total engine failure at approximately 2;500 feet MSL and about 4 NM from the airport. The engine failure occurred without prior warning. The engine abruptly made an abnormal sound and then lost all power completely. A review of the engine indications confirmed a full loss of power; with the engine instruments showing a significant drop.At the onset of the emergency; the student transferred flight controls to me. I confirmed there was no useful engine power and no meaningful response from the engine. I immediately began evaluating available landing options and determined that ZZZ Airport was the best available landing site.Once the airport was selected; the student and I coordinated duties. The student assisted with navigation and frequency management for ZZZ; while I maintained aircraft control; maneuvered toward the airport; and executed the in-flight engine restart checklist. During the restart attempt; the engine tried to relight but did not successfully restart. Instead; it produced backfire-type sounds without developing usable power.I then transmitted on the ZZZ UNICOM frequency that we were experiencing an engine failure and intended to land on Runway XX. At approximately 500 feet AGL; the engine attempted to produce power again and momentarily developed approximately 1;200 to 1;400 RPM for about 10 seconds; but then lost power completely once more.I continued the forced landing and landed the aircraft safely on Runway XX at ZZZ Airport. There was no injury to either occupant and no damage to the aircraft or other property. After touchdown; using the remaining landing energy; I was able to clear the runway and stop on the taxiway.While on the taxiway; I evaluated whether the engine would produce any usable power. With full throttle applied; the engine produced only approximately 400 to 650 RPM; which was unstable and accompanied by significant vibration. Using that limited power; I was able to taxi the aircraft to the FBO area.Maintenance personnel responded and conducted a full inspection of the aircraft. The discrepancies were addressed; documented in the aircraft maintenance records; and the aircraft was subsequently returned to service later that same day.This event involved a sudden and unexpected total engine failure without meaningful prior warning indications. Positive crew coordination between instructor and student; prompt identification of a suitable landing site; emergency checklist execution; and timely radio communication contributed to a safe outcome.

column121: The area east of Corpus Christi to Victoria is without reliable weather reporting stations. Both TFP and RKP have inoperative weather stations. The nearest station is RAS. RAS is on the beach and has different weather than inland airports. We have about 15 airports within a 50-mile radius of CRP. For 15 airports we have less than 6 that could be considered reliable weather stations. TFP; T69; and RKP are very unreliable. On the east half of the CRP area only RAS is reliable and its location makes it a poor choice for weather inland of the coast. Not having wind data in an area known for 30 knots on almost a daily basis; and no ceilings data for a coastal environment is a major safety concern consideration. Lack of maintenance funds is poor reason for not having these stations in good working condition.

column121: I was flying with 3 passengers on an IFR flight plan from ZZZ to 1V6. When passing approximately 8 miles west of APA (location and time is approximate; I did not mark it on the chart) at 9000ft MSL; we encountered two objects that appeared to be drones flying very near our position.I spotted the first object a few hundred feet ahead of us. It reminded me of encountering a bird in flight. It was clear it was slightly lower and to the right of us; so I left the autopilot engaged and didn't take any evasive action. I pointed it out to a passenger (my wife; who is not a pilot; but is familiar with GA due to several hundred hours as a passenger with me). Our initial reaction was 'what was that?' The object was grey/silver; reflected a fair bit of light; but was much more boxy and angular than a mylar balloon would be. It did not look like a typical quadcopter; but was also far enough away that we couldn't really identify any means of flight (wings; propellers; etc). The object was a 1-2ft across; similar in size to a medium bird; but much more metallic/machine looking.Several seconds later; I spotted a second object ahead of us. It was at approximately the same altitude as the first object; but this time to the left of our flight path. I pointed it out as it went by. The passenger in the back seat behind me saw it go by as well. It appeared similar to the first object.Given our groundspeed of around 150kt; we passed by both objects very quickly. It was as if they were standing still. Given the large difference in our speeds; I could not tell whether the objects were moving; or their direction of flight; except that it was much slower than us.I can't think of anything different that I or ATC should have done. Assuming that the objects were drones; whoever was operating them should not have been flying them there without significant coordination with ATC. Given how busy the airspace around Denver is; the danger this kind of operation poses is obvious.

While quickly descending; I noticed that the TCAS showed the airliner as yellow and that it was approximately 500 feet from my altitude as it continued to the Southeast in my direction.The new FAA policy in order to separate airplanes and helicopters went into effect. At an altitude of 2500 MSL; helicopter are often in the departure corridor as airliners ascent to their initial assigned altitude.In this case; it would have been safer to hold my aircraft south of BWI at a lower altitude until it was safe to cross the field. column121: After a regular departure and climb out from ZZZ to ZZZ1 over approximately ZZZZZ the aircraft leveled off at FL310. Right after level several loud bangs were heard from the left side of the aircraft as well as indications of a surging engine or compressor stall. Flight attendants then made contact as they had heard and felt the bangs and saw sparks from engine 1. Control was established and the duties of flying were then given to the First Officer and the Captain then ran the QRC and QRH checklists. After the autothrottles were disconnected in accordance with the checklist the engine then ran normally. Decision was made to return to ZZZ in the interest of safety and a turn and declaration was made. Checklists were then completed as we returned to ZZZ for a normal landing on runway XXC. Crash and Fire inspected the engine and aircraft found no damage and as it was deemed safe we taxied to the gate and parked. Casual factors include long day; multiple legs and maintenance write ups as well as delays. Mitigation was good CRM and use of any and all information available to us to make the safest decision possible.
column123: The flight was normal until leveling off at cruise.  As we were leveling at FL310 the number one engine N1 begin to roll back.  There was a pronounced yaw and roll.  There was also a loud bang.  I did disconnect the Auto Pilot as I was uncomfortable with the autopilot performance.  Just as quickly as it started the engine recovered and began to operate normally. The First Officer said that acts just like a compressor stall.  During this time of what I believe was a compressor stall we also got a calls from the front and aft Flight Attendant position.  They heard the banging they reported they saw sparks coming from the engine number one and vibration in the cabin floor.  I gave control of the aircraft to the First Officer talked with ATC and got a turn back to ZZZ.  We did request priority handling with ATC and were cleared direct to ZZZ.  We ran the QRC for Engine Limit or Surge or Stall; which lead us to the QRH.  Which we completed.  Since the engine was performing normally now; per the QRH we left it running.  We did complete the non routine landing check list.  We told ZZZ approach we would like XXC and to have ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) standing by.  We would be stopping on the runway and I would like them to check for any visible damage or leaks.  That was approved but latter they came back and asked since we would be stopping on the runway if we could accept XYC.  As a crew we felt we had time to make the change so we approved ATC request and switched to XYC.  Landing was normal.  We stopped on the runway.  I did an after landing announcement that the safety vehicles  would look us over.  Then contacted the ARFF command.  We did start the APU after landing and shut down engine number 1.  ARFF approached looked over engine number 1 they reported everything looked normal.  We called ops got a gate and I asked to be followed to the gate by ARFF (another human factor incident was fore most in my thoughts).  We arrived at the gate with out further incident.  ARFF left us and MTX arrived.  We made our calls and Logbook write up and talked to MTX; FA's and Dispatch.Cause: Casual factors.  MTX did mention this was an older engine that was scheduled for replacement.  I have no idea of how close it was for replacement.   Upon arrival MTX did check the engine oil and said the smelled jet fuel in the oil.  Is there a better way to monitor the engines condition as they get closer to overhaul?  Mitigation of Risk.  I think our training department had us well prepared for this situation.  I am flying with a newer First Officer who is on probation and 271 hours on the airplane at the start of our trip.  We did like we are encouraged to in training (assigning the first officer to be PF.  He has really good stick and rudder skills.  He assistance was invaluable.  Very calm and professional.  He help make busy and stressful situation flow smoothly.Recommendations:  One thing I should of done sooner was start the APU instead of waiting till we go on the ground.  Neither of the check list directed us to start it but should have thought of that sooner.  There are a couple other recommendations that came to mind.  Single frequency with ATC and ARFF.  I asked for that while airborne talking to tower they said we will give that to you after you land.  Did not think much of it till we came to a stop on the runway.  I talked to the people while the First Officer was getting the frequency to talk to ARFF. Looking back this was kind of disjointed. After crossing runway XX on taxiway 1; which was closed and not in use; we were instructed by ZZZZ tower to run numbers for taxiway 2 intersection departure for runway XY. We also asked about our sequence to the runway due to enroute spacing over the departure fixes mentioned to us while getting our clearance at the gate; and was told we were 'behind an aircraft.' After receiving this information; EFB returned good performance numbers for our intersection and the FO went through the departure changes checklist. After several inbound arrivals landed; we were now sequenced in front of said 737 who was holding short of runway XY full length from taxiway 1; while Aircraft X; another 737; was given a line up and wait for runway -full length.As we approached the runway XY/2 hold short line we were instructed to line up and wait. My FO read back the clearance 'Aircraft X; runway XY; line up and wait' and I realized this would put us in front of the Aircraft Y 737 in position; but still give us adequate separation on the runway. He remarked to me 'I guess we're going to cut him off' and I said; 'yeah this is definitely a new one for me.' While we were speaking to each other about the odd nuances of this scenario; ZZZ tower issued; in Spanish - what we can now later assume - a takeoff clearance to Aircraft Y. I continued to very slowly taxi the aircraft towards the hold short line; attempting to visualize how far in front of them we'd be and wondering how much we'd be jet-blasting them when the inevitable takeoff clearance was given to us as the preceding aircraft. While paying close attention to Aircraft Y; I noticed their strobe lights were flashing; which; at least per our procedures; is a normal requirement when on an active runway. Due to our angle; in daylight conditions; and approaching at 90 degrees from their right; I wasn't able to detect whether or not the landing lights were on; which would've been a more obvious clue they were issued a takeoff clearance. After visually confirming the approach path of runway XY was clear; my FO again queried tower to confirm our line up and wait instruction; to which tower replied 'affirm.' About the time the aircraft radome crossed the hold short line; my FO noticed the wheels of the 737 moving. He announced 'Stop. Stop!' I looked over at him and simultaneously pressed the toe brakes and set the parking brake once the aircraft stopped. I said to him 'I didn't hear line up and wait behind; I heard line up and wait.' He acknowledged to me he heard the same thing from ATC. He again asked ZZZZ Tower to clarify the clearance and tower said it was a 'line up and wait **behind**' instruction. My FO informed him that he issued us a 'line up and wait' **only** clearance to which the controller responded; 'ohh oops; my bad.' We were then instructed to line up and wait from taxiway 2 and departed shortly afterwards without further incident.

The aircraft remained stable the entire approach and it was VMC conditions so we continued the approach. After the flight during our debrief looking back on the situation the captain and I both agreed a go around would have been the more prudent decision. By the time I thought to call for a go around the EGPWS alert had stopped; and again we were still stable on the approach. During the last 30 minutes of the flight I could feel the onset of fatigue starting to take place. This may have been a contibuting factor as to why I didn't react more quickly and call for a go around. If I could do it again I would call for the go around immediately after hearing the first obstacle caution; especially considering it was night time.

column121: When coming into land on a 45 degree entry to the traffic pattern; the gear was placed into the down position after making the callout of 'below 140; gear down'. The gear motor light lit up; and then turned off once the gear was cycled down. The gear position indicator did not show green nor orange. **The landing gear malfunction checklist was referenced and executed to the extent possible.** ATC had already given landing clearance at this point so I instructed my fellow pilot to let ATC know we were having gear issues and to ask for a low approach and I was going to troubleshoot while he continued to fly the airplane. He did so and we were given an extended downwind to account for airliner traffic as well as troubleshoot. I cycled the gear four separate times to determine if it was a one off incidence or there was another cause. At this rate; we continued with the low approach and asked ATC to verify that the nose gear was facing the correct direction while doing the low approach. We could see it in the mirror but I determined based on audible of the sounds of the gear that it was not locking into position but simply cycling and the nose was the issue. Due to the fact that the 182 has one indicator for three pieces of gear it could have been any of them but I decided it was the nose because of the audibles of the tradition of the gear based on hundreds of hours in the airplane. After verification from ATC and another aircraft that the nose gear was the correct direction we continued on the upwind. The other pilot and I had a short discussion on weather or not to attempt to put the airplane on this runway or the airport it was based out of and I made the decision to keep it at ZZZ due to the availability of emergency services and long and wide runway. In the downwind leg of the traffic patter; we tried varying airspeeds and bank angles to get the gear down. We were unsuccessful. We considered pulling the emergency gear extender but having knowledge of the system and being aware that if it was a locking issue that the application of this would not help we continued. This is because this would have simply made the gear motor manual and we were not having issues with the motor. After this; I briefed my fellow pilot on if the nose were to collapse that I would pull the mixture; throttle; and bring the fuel selector to off and that he would turn off the mags and master and we would both hit the brakes. Following that I **guarded the controls and assisted my student** on the controls and it was a soft touchdown and roll out. On the roll out approximately 10 seconds after landings the nose collapsed; almost simultaneously I pulled the throttle mixture and hit the fuel selector as well as applying the brakes. While doing this; I reminded him to turn off the starter and master. All were off before reaching a complete stop. We then exited the airplane and waited for emergency services.

column121: During this flight; Person A was the sole manipulator of the controls; and I was acting in an instructional capacity; providing guidance as needed to ensure the safety; legality; and overall proficiency of the flight. Person A is an instrument rated pilot; but has not flown for several years except with me for the past few weeks to get proficient again. Approximately 12 miles south of ZZZ; Person A contacted the tower with the current ATIS information and was instructed to 'join right traffic for Runway XXR; maintain 7;000 feet.'We both found this instruction somewhat ambiguous in terms of the expected pattern entry. Based on our understanding; and in consideration of the previously published Letter to Airmen regarding traffic flow at ZZZ; I advised Person A to proceed toward midfield to facilitate entry into the pattern.After proceeding on this heading for approximately one to two minutes; I observed multiple aircraft in potentially conflicting positions. I was actively scanning for traffic and monitoring the situation while anticipating additional instructions or clarification from the tower. During this time; I observed a Cessna 172; believed to be operated by a flight school on a converging flight path.As we anticipated initiating a turn to enter the downwind; the tower instructed us to 'turn right 20 degrees for sequencing.' Person A complied with this instruction; however; we remained uncertain as to which aircraft we were being sequenced behind; as no immediate clarification was provided.While maintaining visual separation and focusing outside the cockpit on traffic avoidance; our aircraft briefly descended below the assigned altitude of 7;000 feet. This deviation was unintentional; and I did not recognize it at the time; as my attention was directed toward identifying and avoiding nearby traffic.Shortly thereafter; the Cessna 172 passed below us; and the tower advised us to look for that traffic. The assigned right turn for sequencing placed us in close proximity to the airport; after which we were instructed to make a right 270-degree turn over the approach end of Runway XX. This sequence of instructions was unexpected and contributed to our uncertainty regarding the intended traffic flow and sequencing.It appeared that the other aircraft was already established on the downwind; which added to our confusion as to why we were directed to turn right; potentially contrary to the established traffic pattern flow; rather than being instructed to enter the pattern via a standard left turn.Ultimately; we acknowledge that we did not maintain the assigned altitude; with a deviation of approximately 200 feet below 7;000 feet. In retrospect; I recognize that I should have requested clarification from the tower regarding their sequencing intentions and pattern entry instructions. At the time; due to the frequency being busy; I hesitated to add additional radio traffic.

Departing and landing traffic was too compressed behind us.And; significantly; the flippant remark made by the ground controller was inappropriate; distracting; and unprofessional. SFO controllers are packing us together as tightly as ever in a highly chaotic environment with the slimmest margin for error. Verbal attitude on the radio only adds to the chaosand erodes safety. With all of the routine havoc in SFO - being held high on approach by ATC; then slow down and get down; needing to pick out conflicting traffic on approach among many similar targets which blend in to the background; converging aircraft turning on to final; the resulting RA's from flying wingtip to wingtip; departing traffic on crossing runways passing right in front of landing traffic; etc… for many years it has felt like SFO is continuously on the verge of a catastrophe. There is a pattern; or a culture; of controllers venting frustrations on the radio with immature remarks and public beratement that we hear regularly around the country; usually at the busiest and most stressful airports. It always adds an unnecessary distraction to all of us on the frequency and it needs to stop. We all work best and safest when we are civil with each other and this needs to be ingrained in the ATC environment. This is a simple human factors component and one change to our system that can and should be made immediately.

column121: At approximately XA:47 my passenger I were training in the pattern at CCO and I heard a transmission telling us we were within 100 feet of another aircraft. We asked them where that happened and they said landing. We tried to get some more details; but didn't want to hog the radio and proceeded to make the next landing a full stop taxi back to gain clarity. We did not talk further with the aircraft telling us we had a near miss. After training; I reviewed flight aware data and pieced together from their break off point that the following may have occurred: As we were practicing a power off 180 maneuver; we made a turn towards the runway almost immediately after pulling power to idle. In doing so; we cut off a plane and as we were higher than normal for that position in the pattern; we did not see any traffic thus seemed to have almost flown ontop of the other aircraft. We were making calls in the pattern; but did not specifically call out a short approach; just downwind; base; final calls. We did not hear calls from the other traffic. The pooer than normal visibility may have contributed to our inability to see the other traffic as well. After the other aircraft took evasive measures; we did hear them key up the radio to tell us we cut them off and they had to break off of final to avoid us. We got a few calls with them; but did not continue to take up radio time discussing the matter in greater details. My passenger and I made a full stop taxi back on our next pattern lap to discuss and try and decifer what happened. We did one additional lap in the pattern before terminating the flight. In that final lap; the aircraft took the runway without making any audible calls to us; but we were hearing other local traffic and another airport's traffic just fine. We were on a longer final and did not have any spacing issues; but the event added to our evaluation that the other aircraft were difficult/impossible to hear at times and may have had radio issues of their own; decreasing our awareness of their position. Additional situational awareness tools such as foreflight and traffic may have helped us in completing the maneuver safely which I will be more diligent about checking before completing short approaches in the future.

column121: Walking down the jet bridge a mechanic from Company X was waiting for me.  He told me that they were working on a fuel leak on the left engine and that it might take approximately 30 minutes. We carried on with our flight preparation; and I relayed the maintenance information to the Relief Pilot who was about to start the walk around.  I called dispatch to keep them in the loop.  He patched we into Maintenance Control and they started working on it with maintenance.  Maintenance came to the cockpit to explain.  He was saying it was just a small amount but with the language barrier he decided to draw me a picture.  His depiction showed a depression in the pylon area that fills with fuel; and when it reaches the top; it spills over and results in the leak.  He also showed me a picture he took on his phone; of a bolt where the fuel seems to be coming from.  He wasn't sure what was on the other side of that bolt or the source of the fuel; but possibly the main tank. I spoke several times with dispatch and Maintenance Control said to call back because they were still working on it.  The maintenance guy came to the cockpit to inform me that he spoke to Company Y maintenance and that we can accept the aircraft if it is a stain and not a leak.  Company Y maintenance confirmed this.  I told maintenance that I was concerned about our twelve and half hour flight home and that pylon collecting fuel.  He thought it would be 'no more than a cup'.  All four pilots went to look at the area in question.  I could see fuel around the bolt and a grease fitting.  I wiped the fuel away and it immediately re-appeared.  It was at this time that the Relief Pilot informed me that when he did the walk around; he observed a steady drip of fuel; almost a steady stream; traveling towards the rear of the pylon and dripping to the ground aft of the combustion section. It was at this point that I refused the aircraft.Cause: The aircraft came in a couple of hours before our arrival.  Maintenance found the leak on their walk around.  How long had this leak been dripping and how much fuel was actually up there leaking; before my Relief Pilot saw it; to when it became a 'small drip'.  They wrote up a 'leak' and then added a 'stain' so they could find a way for someone to accept this aircraft.  It has been a couple of days; and the write up is still not in the software app.  Is this because they don't want the pilots to know what is happening with the aircraft until they actually get in the cockpit and read the book?  If so; why else would you do this unless you want to apply added pressure to the captain to accept an unsafe aircraft.  I recommended an engine run-up to see if the leak reappears.  To my knowledge; this still has not been done.  In the write up; in the book; it says 'leak is considered stain'.  These two are mutually exclusive.  A leak cannot be a stain.It's sad that we are playing semantics when safety is involved.

column121: Aircraft X upon reaching cruise altitude of FL350 received an ECAM for CAB PR SYS 1 FAULT. Ran ECAM; QRH; Follow ups (none) and ECAM Supplemental. Item was listed as 'Crew Awareness;' as suspected. Wrote up the ECAM as it was listed in the status page as an INOP system. Logbook Deferral Sheet #XXXXXXX. Continued to ZZZ without further incident. Maintenance met the aircraft at the gate in ZZZ. They needed to run resets and computer checks so flight crew exited the cockpit. Item was cleared with a Final Action of OK; Message Cleared. Upon returning to the flight deck; I reviewed the sign off in the log book. The troubleshooting took some time and we were about done boarding. I checked the status and the INOP system; CAB PR 1 in Amber was still in box 4 of the ECAM. I called station maintenance and asked for the mechanics to return. The junior mechanic came back to the aircraft and I showed him the status message. He then saw that the system was indeed; not fixed. He said he needed to run the resets again. First Officer stayed in the cockpit while I vacated the area so the mechanic could use my Multipurpose Control Display Unit (MCDU) and seat. He proceeded to troubleshoot the same issue for about 45 minutes. After some time passed; the more senior mechanic arrived back to the aircraft and joined his partner in the cockpit. The first officer exited the aircraft and joined me on the jetbridge. He was listening to the mechanics talk about the issue and basically realize that the system that they signed off; message cleared was in fact; not cleared. They were essentially attempting to fix the system this time without entering anything else into the maintenance logbook to cover up the fact that they didn't actually clear my write up. Eventually; they gave up and decided to MEL the system. Something that should have been done from the very start so that we could have had an on time departure out of ZZZ as this system was allowed on the MEL. They wrote up a new discrepency of CAB PRESS SYS 1 FAULT Logbook Deferral Sheet #XXXXXXY and applied MEL 21-XXX. They pulled and collared circuit breaker D9 and X23. We waited for the sign off to clear the logbook and reviewed an procedure that needed to be accomplished during pre flight to satisfy the MEL. Upon review of the procedure; I saw that we needed to open circuit breaker X23 that controls the Residual Pressure Control Unit (RPCU) on step 1. Step 6 states to close circuit breaker X23. This circuit breaker had been pulled and collared by ZZZ station maintenance. At this time I had lost all faith in these two mechanics. They were rushing to complete a task. I called Air Carrier X Maintenance Control and conferred with them about what to do. I asked if I had permission to remove the  circuit breaker collar since the pre flight pilot procedure was to manipulate the circuit breaker and that it needed to be in the closed/in position for flight. After looking up the MEL and procedure; Maintenance Control agreed with me that the circuit breaker collar needed to be removed and left off to remain in compliance with the MEL. Maintenance Control  mentioned that they station maintenance might have been using an old revision of their repair manuals. At this point; neither the FO or I trusted that station maintenance complied with the maintenance procedures listed in the MEL so I had Maintenance Control go over them with me and he confirmed that by having circuit breaker D9 pulled; the Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) procedures were in compliance. At this same time; the station maintenance called up to the flight deck using the ramp head set and told us to remove the circuit breaker collar at X23 and that they were using the wrong AMM repair manual. He apologized. After reconfiguring the aircraft to the state that was in compliance with the MEL and performing the pre flight tasks associated with it; we deemed the flight safe to continue and left for our destination without further incident. I take this event to be a serious safety infraction as an expired manual was used in the application of an MEL that required circuit breakers to be pulled for flight. Station maintenance's attempt to cover up the fact that they had cleared the write up instead of issuing the MEL was unacceptable. Cause: Use of expired repair; AMM; and MEL manuals by ZZZ station maintenance. Rushing to complete the task by ZZZ station maintenance. Signing off a write up that shouldn't have been signed off. Applying the wrong MEL procedure by ZZZ station maintenance. Air Carrier X's pressure of middle managers to push mechanics; pilots; and other staff to rush; overlooking a safe operation such that they achieve their quarterly bonuses is an egregious causal factor. It should never have come to the pilots needing to check the work of mechanics and fixing these mistakes as the last barrier to safety. These mistakes should never have been made and it shakes the foundation of safety culture and our trust in our peers' ability to perform their jobs safely and correctly. I do not appreciate being pushed to the limits of safety in the name of on time performance. I have a life outside of flying as a father and husband and I take those jobs extremely seriously and they are more important than any job flying airplanes. I intend on making it home to them every time I leave for work. This airline needs a serious look at other work group safety; I'm so tired of the onus being laid upon us time after time; risking our licenses and lives; for what? Bonuses and stock prices. NASA; the FAA; and whomever else has a stake in safety needs to have a look at practices here at Air Carrier X and really push safety first. We say it every day; it's time everyone actually lives it.

column121: During the climb; around 20;000; the PIC and I heard and felt a 'bang'. I looked back and noticed that the aft seated passenger appeared to have just shut the lav door and I thought he slammed the door shut; thus causing the 'bang.' I glanced at the cabin pressure differential gauge and noted there was a split in the differential pressure and that it appeared normal.Just after leveling off at 38;000 the Crew Alerting System (CAS) message 'CABIN ALTITUDE' appeared. We donned our masks; requested priority handling; and started to descend. I pulled out and began to run the checklist. The PIC took the radios and requested a lower altitude and a clearance direct back to our home base. After running the checklist; I took note that the cabin pressure differential gauge still showed a split in differential pressure; and that cabin altitude showed 10;000. The PIC advised the passengers of what happened and one passenger requested the oxygen masks; which the PIC then manually deployed.Once we descended below 8;000 the CAS message 'CABIN ALTITUDE' shut off. We canceled priority handling request and landed uneventfully back at our homebase.What I believe really caused the problem is that the outflow valve or some of the pressurization piping malfunctioned or blew a seal during climbout. To better respond to this issue in the future we could have requested priority handling soon after hearing the 'bang'. I now plan to monitor the cabin pressure differential gauge more closely during the climb and more frequently during level off and cruise.
column123: On our climbout; somewhere around FL200; we heard a bang and felt a pressure wave in the cabin. My first reaction was to look at the cabin pressure differential gauge to see if we had lost pressure. Upon looking at the cabin pressure differential gauge; everything looked to be normal. We had a cabin pressure differential; and our cabin altitude appeared to be at the correct altitude. I also looked for any lights near the cabin pressure differential gauge to indicate a failure of the automated system; and I observed none. I then looked for any Crew Alerting System (CAS) messages on my Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) and did not see any. I then looked back at the passengers to see if I could see anything wrong with the aircraft in the cabin. I noticed that one of the passengers closed the lavatory doors and thought that he might have just slammed it shut. With no issues found; I elected to continue our climb to FL380.Shortly after arriving at our cruise altitude (FL380); we received a CABIN ALTITUDE Master Warning. Both pilots quickly put on their oxygen masks and established communication. I was the flying pilot; took control of the radios; and the pilot monitoring started running the QRH procedure for CABIN ALTITUDE. I requested priority handling and requested an immediate descent. ATC cleared us to FL300 and asked for the number of souls on board and remaining fuel. I responded to those questions; requested a lower altitude; and stated we wanted to return to ZZZ. We were cleared directly to ZZZ and to 10;000 ft. We deployed the passengers' oxygen masks and asked for 8;000 ft. At this point; the pilot monitoring completed the QRH procedure. Upon reaching 8;000 ft.; our master caution cleared; and the QRH procedure was complete; so we advised that we were no longer needed priority handling. We decided to return to our departure airport; ZZZ; and landed safely without further issues.Upon landing; we looked at the aircraft and found no obvious problems. Currently; maintenance is looking at the aircraft to determine the issue. I assume that it is something to do with our outflow valve. We did not have a rapid decompression; and the aircraft was still maintaining a little bit of cabin differential pressure; but not enough to keep the cabin altitude where it should have been. That is why it is my assumption that it has something to do with the outflow valve.  Lessons learned and things we could have done better. After landing safely and discussing the event with my copilot; I found some things that I could have done better.-Upon hearing the bang and feeling the pressure wave; my copilot and I should have been paying closer attention to the cabin pressure differential gauge. We could have potentially caught the issue sooner and descended before we needed to request priority handling.-Secondly; it was hard to hear ATC with the oxygen mask on; and I had to ask them to repeat some things. I could have turned my vox off to eliminate the breathing noise; and I could have turned the volume up more so I could hear better. -Lastly; I could have deployed the oxygen masks sooner for the passengers. I should have deployed them when both me and the copilot donned our oxygen masks.

column121: I was flying with my friend in his airplane during a VFR sightseeing tour through the Grand Canyon Special Flight Rules Area (SFRA). We were northbound in the corridor when we observed traffic at our altitude on an eastbound heading from our left on the ADSB; resulting in a converging situation. The other aircraft subsequently turned southbound while remaining at the same altitude. Per the applicable section of 14 CFR pertaining to this SFRA; direction of flight within the Grand Canyon SFRA corresponds to specific altitude assignments.As the traffic continued to close; We attempted multiple times to establish radio contact with the other aircraft on the CTAF to determine if they had us in sight. No response was received. The applicable section of 14 CFR requires all pilots operating within the SFRA to monitor the designated CTAF frequency.As the closure rate increased and radio contact was not established; I disconnected the autopilot and began maneuvering a descent and right turn to create separation. At that moment; the right seat pilot called 'my controls.' To avoid a dual-input situation during an already time-critical event; I relinquished. The right seat pilot executed a left descend turn. The other aircraft passed at very close range. To my knowledge; I was the only crew member with a visual on the traffic throughout the encounter.Following the incident; I recommended discontinuing the tour and landing. I also attempted to conduct an informal debrief with the other crew members on board; the conversation did not take place at that time.The next day; I identified the pilots from the other aircraft and approached them to discuss the incident and review the applicable SFRA regulations. One pilot engaged in the conversation and indicated they had been receiving flight following services and had been attempting to descend at the time of the encounter. The remaining pilots from that aircraft did not engage in the discussion.Contributing factors were the converging traffic at the same altitude within the SFRA; no radio communication established on CTAF prior to close proximity; cockpit workload and crew coordination dynamics during the avoidance maneuver.Continued pilot education on the Grand Canyon SFRA requirements is recommended; particularly altitude assignments under the applicable section of 14 CFR and CTAF monitoring requirements. Review of CRM protocols for dual-pilot operations during traffic conflict situations; including clear pre-flight agreements on control transfer procedures.

column121: I was acting as Pilot-in-Command (PIC)/MEI for an instructional flight at ZZZ1. During our seventh lap of the traffic pattern; the student reported that the right engine manifold pressure (MAP) failed to decrease when the throttle lever was retarded. I verified that while the throttle lever could increase power; it would not respond to downward input.Upon identifying the malfunction; the student relinquished the controls. I contacted ZZZ1 [Tower]; requested an immediate departure from the pattern; and diverted to ZZZ. ZZZ1 [Tower] cleared us for a northwest departure and coordinated VFR flight following with ZZZ [TRACON].Upon transitioning to ZZZ [Tower]; I advised them of the stuck throttle. ZZZ [Tower] vectored traffic to accommodate our entry; allowing for a right downwind for XXR. I requested an extended downwind to ensure a lengthy stabilized final approach.During the descent; I briefed the student on our options. I determined that shutting down and feathering the right engine would severely diminish aircraft performance and negate our ability to perform a go-around. Instead; I elected to conduct an approach using the stuck left engine at approximately 20' MAP; while managing the right engine's power via the throttle control as necessary. To ensure a safe; predictable landing; I planned to pull both mixtures to idle cut-off in the flare; thereby eliminating the risk of asymmetric thrust during the rollout.As we neared the landing phase; ZZZ [Tower] moved a departing aircraft from XXR to XXL; clearing us to land. Recognizing the presence of traffic behind us; I notified ZZZ [Tower] of the mechanical issue and my intention to secure both engines via the mixtures upon landing; noting that we would likely be unable to clear the runway under our own power. When ZZZ [Tower] inquired if I wished to request priority handling; I confirmed in the affirmative and requested that a tug be dispatched to our location.The landing was executed as planned. After the flare I pulled both mixtures to idle cut-off. The landing was uneventful and the aircraft retained sufficient momentum to turn onto taxiway 1 and clear the runway. Once off the active surface; I secured the fuel and electrical systems and exited the aircraft. The aircraft was met by ground personnel and towed to the school's hangar. I performed a thorough post-flight debrief with the student regarding the incident and our Aeronautical Decision Making process.

column121: At approximately XA:00 local at ZZZ; my student and I were departing for a fly-in event at ZZZ1. The student had approximately 10 hours of private pilot training at the time.Preflight and taxi to Runway XX were uneventful. After receiving takeoff clearance; the student began the takeoff roll and applied power. During the roll; the aircraft began drifting to the right--either due to excessive right rudder input or a crosswind from the east causing a weathervaning effect.In an attempt to avoid departing the runway into the grass; the student rotated early and aggressively; placing the aircraft in approximately a 15-30 degree nose-high attitude.I verbalized; 'I have the controls;' and attempted to lower the nose to reduce the angle of attack for a standard climbout. The student was unresponsive; his fight-or-flight response appeared fully active; and he was fighting me on the controls with both hands.I had to physically remove his arms and hands from the controls in order to regain control. I was then able to lower the nose enough for the stall warning to cease.The remainder of the flight was uneventful.Contributing factors may have included slight complacency during the takeoff phase. In hindsight; more active rudder coaching--such as prompting or assisting with left rudder during the takeoff roll--may have helped prevent the initial deviation.After the flight; we conducted a debrief. The student understood what occurred and recognized that he had placed the aircraft in a potential power-on stall situation.After further discussion with other instructors; an alternative technique was suggested: temporarily blocking the student's visual reference (e.g.; covering their eyes) to interrupt the startle/freeze response and regain control of the aircraft. I plan to evaluate this technique and incorporate it into future training as appropriate.The purpose of this report is to recommend that flight instructors incorporate a mandatory simulated takeoff upset prevention scenario; including techniques to ensure the student releases the controls when necessary. I believe this should be a required task in the CFI ACS (Airman Certification Standards).Lighter or less physically strong instructors may be at a disadvantage when a student resists. A DPE could simulate early rotation and/or poor directional control during the takeoff roll; transitioning into a high but still safe climb. The instructor should emphasize a clear positive exchange of flight controls; and be prepared to take immediate; decisive action such as covering their eyes to regain control of the aircraft if the student does not comply.

It appeared Aircraft Y was trying to join the 45 from the north; and made a tight turn to enter the pattern. Aircraft Y appeared to be attempting a 45 degree entry very close to the airport from the N; which put us on a course where Aircraft Y was in our blind spot below.After reviewing AC 90-66C; we determined the best course of action for the future when crossing midfield for a teardrop entry on the 45; is to cross; fly outbound at least 2 miles; and descend prior to turning inbound on the 45. We also determined to be more clear when stating intentions to enter the pattern on the 45; so as to provide more situational awareness for fellow aviators. column121: I was entering a straight-in approach to runway XX at ZZZ; intending to practice crosswind landing. I believe winds were 300 @15kt; and knowing it was a strong crosswind I wanted to test this specific airplane in those winds. This was the first contributing factor; not having done crosswind landing in some time; and not in this airplane. I was not strongly considering my minimums.I had significant right-rudder input; as well as moderate left aileron; lined up with the runway and doing fine until I hit a strong downdraft over the highway. I had expected this downdraft having flown this approach before; but the downdraft felt much stronger than what I'd prepared for and I elected to go-around. Not having a solid plan for the go-around and aerodynamic effects of full power from the crosswind landing configuration into a climb was my second contributing factor. I knew I may go-around; but I hadn't visualized it and prepared for it sufficiently. As power was added; I failed to maintain left aileron and the plane began to yaw to the right. I failed remove rudder and maintain runway heading; and panic started to set in. I failed to notice my right leg was still mashing the right rudder for several seconds.At this point I was doing everything I could to maintain airspeed well above stall; instinctually pushing the nose down and for some reason I let the airplane turn to the right as I struggled to maintain level flight and airspeed. I realized my foot was heavily or possibly full right rudder once I had significantly deviated from runway heading and neutralized the rudder after at this point. I stabilized the climb and headed south; maintaining separation from the tree line south of the airport. At this time I was close to heading 140; roughly 2000ft to the West side of the XY approach; low; headed downwind. I elected to head straight back to my departure airport ZZZ1 and end the flight.My performance in this flight was definitely inadequate. I did not take appropriate action to train on this specific flight condition in my aircraft with a CFI; or refresh with a CFI in recent months on higher crosswinds; and my skillset has obviously diminished; or I overestimated my minimums for this aircraft; a C150D with a horton STOL kit. My judgement to take a leisurely scenic flight and 'throw in some crosswind practice' on my way North created risks due to insufficient planning and contingency planning for 'whatifs' and I was not prepared to react properly in my go-around. I hope my experience will help others to not make the same mistake. Practicing crosswind landings is crucial; briefing phases of flight; and their resultant phases of flight; whether it be landing or going around; is crucial. I made a decision to challenge myself; without preparing myself. I had to work VERY hard to recover from what should have been an ordinary crosswind practice approach and landing; and this is largely due to the startle effect and subsequent panic when my right leg became frozen subconsciously. I'm happy nobody was hurt.In the future I will practice in a simulator and with a CFI; and refresh my personal minimums to better judge what I can do safely. I will review proper crosswind technique; and go-arounds in crosswinds. I will also research what I can do to avoid freezing any particular control in urgent situations. I think making sure I am in the best condition to fly is also imperative; as being dehydrated; tired; or less than optimal overall can have dire effects when stressors are added.

column121: On Day 0; while working a very busy sector XX; I was placed in an operational situation that I believed was unsafe due to traffic saturation; excessive workload; and the lack of safe alternatives. I was advised by the Controller in Charge that sector XY was going to shut me off and that; if not; I would need to hold and/or vector aircraft because of the traffic volume. I immediately stated that; given the complexity of the operation; the safest course of action was to ground stop departures rather than continue feeding traffic into an overloaded sector or require tactical vectoring in already saturated airspace.I was then advised that; at managements request; I was expected to spin aircraft. I stated that I would not do so because; in my judgment; vectoring aircraft in close proximity at the same altitudes during a high-workload saturated operation was unsafe and created unacceptable risk. I advised that I would instead descend aircraft and call them to the sector that owned FL240 through FL340; which I believed was the safer alternative under the circumstances.The aircraft I specifically recall being involved were Aircraft X and Aircraft Y at FL310 and FL330. Aircraft Z may also have been involved in the overall situation; although I do not specifically recall shipping that aircraft without a handoff.As Aircraft X and Aircraft Y approached the sector boundary; my Radar Associate initiated a handoff to sector XZ. The receiving controller advised that he was unable and would not take the handoff. I then got on the line myself as the Radar Position and explained that we were extremely busy; that sector XY was shutting us off; and that we needed assistance. The receiving controller again refused to accept the aircraft. At that point; I believed I had been left without a safe operational alternative. In my judgment; additional vectoring or spinning of aircraft in that environment would have created a greater and more immediate hazard. I therefore advised that I was going to ship the aircraft without handoffs because no safe alternative was being made available to me.In my judgment; the more dangerous action would have been to vector and spin aircraft at the same altitude during a saturated; high-workload operation; as I had been directed to do. There was an expectation of compliance even where safety concerns had been raised.I am concerned that this event reflects a broader pattern in which unsafe operational situations are allowed to develop and persist without sufficient corrective action. When controllers raise legitimate safety concerns and are met with pressure rather than support and mitigation; operational risk is normalized instead of corrected. If these conditions are allowed to continue unchecked; unfortunate consequences may result.I am submitting this report because I believe I was placed in an unsafe operational situation; was directed to take action that I believed increased risk; and refused to compromise safety. A stronger stand for safety must be taken by management to ensure controllers are supported in making safe operational decisions and to protect and preserve human life.Establish clear procedures for sector saturation events so departures are stopped; sectors are shut off; or other traffic management initiatives are implemented before controllers are forced into unsafe tactical situations.Controllers should not be directed to use tactics they identify in real time as unsafe. When a controller raises a safety objection; management should be required to assess and mitigate the hazard rather than pressure compliance.Require immediate supervisory escalation when a receiving sector refuses handoffs during a saturation event so the controller is not left without a safe operational outlet.Provide additional training for management and supervisory personnel on safety culture; operational risk management; and response to controller-raised safety concerns; with emphasis on supporting safe decisions.Conduct a review of staffing; traffic flow practices; workload management; and recurring saturation events to determine whether unsafe conditions are being allowed to develop without timely corrective action.Reinforce through policy and practice that protecting human life and operational safety takes priority over production pressure or unquestioned compliance with management direction.I respectfully recommend that this event be reviewed not as an isolated occurrence; but as a warning of broader workload; coordination; and safety-culture issues that require corrective action before a more serious incident occurs.

column121: While at cruise at FL330; upon turning off the center fuel tank pumps; an imbalance of between 500-600 lbs low was observed in the right tank. We ran the crossfeed checklist to balance the tanks. We referenced the flight progress tool and noted we were about 1000 lbs lighter than our planned fuel should have been. We ran the suspected fuel leak checklist. Once balanced we started a timer. Per the checklist if in 30 minutes a difference of 500 lbs is observed a fuel leak is verified. We reached the 500 lbs difference in in 9 minutes. Our fuel projected at landing was continuing to decrease.We coordinated with dispatch; our flight attendants; made announcements to the passengers; requested priority handling with ATC; started a decent; and diverted directly for ZZZ. Per the checklist we shut down the engine number 2 on the side with the confirmed fuel leak. We observed a stop in the loss of fuel post engine 2 shutdown. We also ran the overweight landing checklist as we landed about 2;000 lbs overweight. Upon landing on Runway XXR at ZZZ; we cleared the runway and had Airport Rescue and Firefighting inspect the aircraft. After no abnormalities were observed we single engine taxied to the gate. Proper logbook entries for the fuel leak and overweight landing were made post shutdown at the gate.
column123: At FL330 when we turned the pumps off; we noticed a fuel imbalance of 500 lbs; so we executed the IMBALANCE checklist on 2.120.20.  After the tanks were balanced; we noticed that our prog page showed 1000 lbs less at the destination than the flight progress tool.  Given this; we decided to rerun the checklist again; but followed it to the NG Fuel Leak on 2.120.7.  In Step five we recorded the left tank as having 7440 lbs and the right tank as having 7370 pounds.  We started the clock to time for 30 min.  During this time I noted total fuel flow of approximately 6600 pounds per hour and our destination predicted fuel continuing to decrease to 1300 lbs less than previously predicted.  Within 9 minutes; the fuel split had exceeded 500 lbs and continued to over 600 lbs.  In accordance with Step 6 of the checklist; a fuel leak is confirmed.  In accordance with Step 7; we proceeded to step 11 and began the process of shutting down the engine.  We began our descent from FL330 and diverted to ZZZ.  Priority handling was requested and we shut down the number 2 engine in level flight at 12000 ft.  We completed the NG Fuel Leak checklist and landed at ZZZ with the number 2 engine shut down.  Upon landing; crash and rescue did not notice any issues and we taxied back to the gate.

column121: While at approximately 15;000 feet and a little over 300 KIAS while in the climb to ZZZ1 we heard a very loud noise and felt a thud along with some vibrations. In the second the passed we determined that it was likely the nose gear doors deploying. I then disengaged the autopilot; put thrust to idle; deployed speed breaks; and leveled our attitude to bleed speed quickly to get below 250 KIAS to reduce aerodynamic load on the doors. During this maneuver the captain and I verified via the EICAS that the nose gear had not deployed. Upon reaching a reasonable speed for our new configuration we referred to the QRH 'NOSE LANDING GEAR UP DOOR OPEN'. The captain decided that it was best to request priority handling and commence a return to ZZZ out of precaution. I flew and worked comms while the captain worked through notifying ATC; Dispatch; the FA (to include the special procedures); and the pax. We then reconvened and completed the necessary cruise; descent; and approach checks and briefings. I had two major threats I included in the brief. My concerns were structural damage to the door that may impede the operation and deployment of the nose gear door and thus secondly a chance that the nose gear would deploy properly. For these reasons I decided that I would deploy the gear prior to commencing the approach to verify a three green; down and locked condition. If we did not get that; we had a plan to hold and execute the procedures for that condition. Due to our concerns of structural damage to the doors we felt it appropriate and precautions to have ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) respond.Following an uneventful landing; we were escorted to our gate by operations and ARFF. The post flight inspection revealed no noticeable deformities to the nose gear doors.
column123: During the climb through approximately 16;000 feet at 300 KIAS; we heard a loud noise consistent with landing gear deployment. The landing gear handle was in the UP position; and the door indication page showed all doors green.Despite these normal indications; we suspected an uncommanded opening of the nose landing gear door. We ran the QRH for the non-annunciated Nose Landing Gear Up Door Open checklist. We reduced airspeed below 250 KIAS; notified ATC; and I exercised my authority as Pilot in Command to requested priority handling with ZZZ Center. Approximately 10 miles from the runway; we lowered the landing gear and confirmed it functioned normally.The aircraft landed uneventfully and taxied to the gate under its own power. There were no injuries to passengers or crew. After shutdown; I contacted Dispatch; the Chief Pilot; and Maintenance Control.

The first half of the trip involved duty periods extending close to midnight; which may have contributed to cumulative fatigue and influenced our decision-making.Suggestions: Overall; I feel like we handled this situation appropriately and in the interest of passenger safety. Had we had been at a high speed; an aborted takeoff might not have been appropriate however we were at minimal speed.

column121: While conducting a flight for the purpose of completing a Certificated Flight Instructor (CFI) Practical Test; the incident aircraft (PA28R-200) experienced retractable gear malfunction/collapse and erroneous indications. While approaching the right downwind for RWY XXR and after contacting ZZZ Tower; both the Designated Pilot Examiner (DPE) and CFI candidate on board the incident aircraft witnessed the two main gear lights illuminated and the nose-wheel indicator light OFF after setting the gear selector switch in the 'DOWN' position. Both pilots onboard immediately established appropriate CRM and began troubleshooting efforts. These efforts included: Several pass-by's for a controller/tower visual inspection of the landing gear; multiple usage of the 'emergency landing gear extension' checklist and yawing maneuvers; and one final tower confirmation that the gear was down prior to landing. Throughout the 'troubleshooting' phase of the flight; the 'gear in transit' light would remain illuminated and a whining noise (suspected by the pilots to be a hydraulic pump) was audibly heard. After the incident aircraft made the several low passes; the ZZZ Tower Controller stated that the gear appeared to be down and that he was unsure the gear was locked. Ultimately; the decision was made between both pilots on-board to make a landing on Runway XXL (longer and wider runway). Understanding that the nose wheel indicator light remained OFF; the landing was briefed in the flight-deck by the pilots. It would be a smooth landing (using similar techniques as required for a soft-field landing) and the aircraft would be allowed to 'roll' with no braking as necessary in order to prevent the nose gear from collapsing in the event it was not locked and uncontrollably-lowered by itself. Priority handling was [given] by the tower and fire-emergency services were requested by the pilots prior to landing. Approximately 20-30 minutes after first responders were contacted; emergency vehicles and airport personnel were ready. It was decided that the DPE would land the aircraft on Runway XXL and the CFI Candidate would operate the only exit door located at the right side of the aircraft. Upon landing; the aircraft's main landing gears touched down smoothly and within seconds of landing the right main gear slowly collapsed by itself. Upon feeling this unexpected condition; the DPE corrected by deflecting the control wheel to the left in an effort to prevent the hard impact of the right (lowering) wingtip with the runway. Eventually; the right wing/wingtip would impact the runway causing the right wing to drift aft and the aircraft to veer off the runway and into the dirt just off the right side of Runway XXL. As the aircraft came to a stop; the engine was immediately isolated/starved of fuel and the aircraft's right door was opened. An immediate evacuation was initiated and no injuries or fire occurred. Emergency services and airport personnel responded in a quick manner and were ready to assist pilots as necessary. In retrospect; this incident showed me how critical Crew Resource Management (CRM) is in the event of an emergency. despite having large differences in experience between the DPE and CFI Candidate; both pilots communicated; split tasks; and assessed the situation continuously. Aside from the CRM found in the flight-deck; it is my opinion that the assistance/communication that ZZZ Tower Provided was concise and necessary to the outcome of the best case scenario of this incident. With this in mind; it was emphasized/learned that communication and clear actions both inside and outside the flight-deck are necessary in the event of an emergency.

column121: Everything was normal until very short final below 50 feet. Winds were a little gusty but the FO was handling the plane well and we were stable. The first concern I got was coming through 30 feet and the FO had not begun a sufficient flare rotation; so I said something to the effect of 'round it out.' This began a period of just 3-4 seconds where everything happened; starting with a very firm touchdown mains first. The plane either bounced or fully extended the gear shocks; but movement was definitely upward and I called for a go-around. As the aircraft settled back down onto the runway I looked down at the thrust levers and in that instant it appeared that the FO had started the reverse process part of the landing sequence; and then went up to TOGA mode after my Go Around call. Since I thought I had seen Thrust Reversers activated; I said something like 'forget it. I have the aircraft'; and control was immediately relinquished to me. I went into full reverse with approximately 7000ft of runway remaining and the aircraft was fully settled and under control. Again; this sequence of events happened very quickly; just a couple of seconds; during which I was working off of outside visual cues and a brief glance at the thrust levers. I did not see the VSI or Primary Flight Display (PFD) and cannot say what they were reading at touchdown; but got some info after parking from the jumpseater who helped us debrief and break down what went wrong. Rollout and taxi-in were normal; and after the parking checklist; the FO and I debriefed the landing and requested input from the jumpseater; who was performing a FAA Line Operations Safety Assessment (LOSA). Knowing that LOSA observers don't normally debrief; I felt like this event was important enough to request his input just as a fellow air carrier Captain. He pointed out two things that in the moment I did not even realize had occurred: our touchdown pitch had approached 10 degrees; and we got the 'pitch pitch pitch' aural. In those few seconds where everything was coming at us fast; I must have had a tunnel vision effect that did not allow that cue into my thought process. Had he not told us; I would not have know that occurred. After the debrief; the FO and I went outside to check for any indications of a tail strike and found none.
column123: I was PF for a visual approach (backed up by ILS) to XXR at ZZZ.  We had a FAA Line Operations Safety Assessment (LOSA) safety observer on the flight deck. Approach was normal; uneventful with normal Flight Manual (FM) speeds for configuration.  Aircraft was stabilized; fully configured; and checklist complete approximately 1 NM prior to ZZZZZ (GS intercept/FAF) with clearance to land on XXR.  Winds were reported with gusty conditions on XXR. I flew the glide slope on instrumentation down on glide slope backed up with PAPIs for 3 degree GS. Ride conditions down the GS were bumpy.Aimpoint for landing on XXR was the approach end 1000' mark. Crossed the runway threshold approximately 55' and started a very slow power pull while maintaining same aim point.  Started full power pull at 30' and kept same aim point with bumpy conditions while flying down to touchdown approximately 1200-1300'.  I made a late transition to runway end for visual flare cues giving and had an incomplete flare and higher deck angle.  Upon main gear touchdown and flying the nose to ground; I began to 'crack' reverse thrust on thrust levers while the CA simultaneously called a Go Around. This lead to some confusion; and CA called disregard as he saw that I was beginning the thrust reverser sequence and determined it was a safe and manageable situation. CA took control of the aircraft for the remainder of the landing roll and exit off of XXR. During this multi-event sequence the LOSA observer indicated (after flight) that the aircraft verbalized a 'pitch; pitch' call in the flare round out most likely due to the windy conditions on final and flare.  CA and FO visually inspected aircraft. No issues or defects to aircraft.

We set up and briefed the approach; reviewed the landing gear gravity extension procedure; as well as the towing procedure. With the failure of the G HYD system; we had to stop on the runway (XXR) due to no Nose Wheel Steering. Airport Rescue and Firefighting was standing by and cleared the aircraft of any imminent threat. The tow was hooked up on the runway after completing the towing procedure checklist and we were towed back to gate XX."

column121: Midway through the flight to ZZZZ; hydraulic pressure system 4 failed. Our first indication was multiple brake source alerts; both as an EICAS advisory and aural caution alert. Checking the hydraulic schematic; the pilot flying and pilot monitoring noticed a loss of hydraulic fluid quantity in hydraulic reservoir 4. We called the Captain to the flight deck. After four brake source alerts; HYD PRESS SYS 4 checklist appeared on the EICAS. The PM ran the electronic checklist to completion. We then started an ACARS conversation with Dispatch; notifying them we lost hydraulic system 4. Concerns at this time: low weather minimums into ZZZZ and loss of ability to legally perform Cat2/Cat3 auto-land; fuel in the event of a missed approach or go around (with hyd sys 4 off; landing gear would not retract once down) rendering a higher than planned fuel burn to our alternate airport; possibility of diverting in an area surrounded by hostile airspace and with few viable available options for diversion airports; planning a longer than normal landing configuration set up while keeping compliance with ATC; manual brake landing as well as manual speed brake deployment and reverse thrust only on 2 and 3 as recommended by the checklist notes; and finally only having one runway available in ZZZZ (the longer runway is under construction and closed).The Captain patched in a SatCom call to dispatch and discussed the condition of our flight. The weather at ZZZZ improved to Cat 1 forecasted so the decision was made to continue to and land at ZZZZ; RWY XX.The landing was completed by the Captain; following all alternate procedures in accordance with the QRH and associated notes. The manual brake landing caused for higher than planned brake temperatures; several brakes in the 7's Brake Temperature Monitoring System and one brake pad peaking briefly at 8. No damage; no melted fuse plugs; and no observable problems resulted. After shut down; ground crew and maintenance was advised of the hydraulic system 4 failure and the hot brake condition.Suspected failure of Engine Driven hydraulic pump for hydraulic system 4. Possible associated hydraulic fluid leak resulted in a gradual total loss of reservoir fluid.Consider improving the quality of headsets provided on the aircraft. Normally; I have my own. However; my baggage was lost day one of my pattern and I am traveling these two weeks without. I have had to resort to using the headsets provided on the aircraft. Unfortunately; they are of such low quality that communication with ATC and my other crew members was a major challenge and inconvenience which added only another (but fixable) layer of complexity to an already busy; and complex non-normal situation.

column121: Full duration of flight was normal with no 'noted' issues - Departure; enroute; arrival; approach; and landing were are normal with no abnormalities noted - normal turn off at intersection of Runway XX and Taxiway 1; right turn; with another right turn onto taxiway 2 for gate XX as instructed by ATC - as passing across the hold short lines; I called for 'Flaps up' and requested the APU to be started as the taxi was short to Gate XX - after completing the turn onto Taxiway 2; the aircraft was doing approx 2 to 3 kts across the ground with the nosewheel on the yellow taxiway centerline as the post flight check was completed by the FO - as the APU reached 75% of N1 the aircraft AC power completely shut down - both IDG's (Integrated Drive Generators) from both running engines were deactivated - the aircraft lost nose wheel steering as well as all displays reverted to battery operation - I immediately stopped the aircraft on the taxiway and set the parking brake - FO called the FA's to check their status while I evaluated what was going on - the APU reached 100% and became the source of AC power - asked the FO to make announcement to the passengers to remain seated as the FA's indicated people were getting up to grab bags (although the aircraft was not at the gate but all signage was turned off) - while I notified ATC that we needed to sit in place without the need for assistance while we determined the best course of action - as the aircraft was technically 'rebooting' itself; we awaited for all EICAS messages to clear - after approx 90 seconds; the aircraft was fully powered up (note; both engines were still running) - 2 EICAS messages were left on - IDG 1 (and 2) FAIL Caution messages - I called for the QRH for both - after following the procedure - the IDG's were cleared and reset and back online - we checked other EICAS status pages (including HYD and Power) to ensure we were both reassured the aircraft was safe to move under its own power with the note 'if it happens again we will call for Ops to tow us to the gate' - we notified ATC we could continue and was cleared to continue our taxi - parked at XX without any further issues - we noted prior to departure the APU had previous write ups' but did not seem to be related to what we experienced. Both the FO and myself agreed to call Maintenance Control to discuss what happened and to see what they wanted - after that conversation with Maintenance Control they agreed we did what was necessary and asked for write up in the logbook. I completed the Info to Maintenance as instructed. Post flight walk-around inspection was normal. The station was not going to relocate the aircraft to a RON spot; so a normal shutdown and power off was completed with no issues. Post brief with the FO resulted in all CRM decisions were approprate and did not pose any risk to the safety of passengers; crew; or aircraft. The cause of the power failure is unknown by myself at this time.Suggestions: all aspects of the issue were handled without issue. Maintenance will need to continue to investigate what might have caused this post landing during the taxi.
column123: Flight was conducted normally from departure to landing. No issues or abnormalities during this time. Upon landing XXL we had a normal landing; rollout; and turn off. Once we acquired our taxi clearance from tower we were cleared to taxi from intersection 1 down 2 to our gate XX. Once we were clear of the runway and were heading down 2; CA called for Flaps Up" triggering after landing checklist. Once that was completed I offered to start the APU for the short taxi; CA agreed. Upon starting the APU as N1 reached approximately 75% the aircraft AC power shutdown. The flight deck went dark and the EICAS populated numerous messages. CA brought it to a stop and set the parking brake. I advised ground we need to stop for a moment before checking in with the FAs to make sure they were alright while the aircraft finished running through the EICAS messages. The FAs advised passengers had started getting up so I made a PA to remain in their seats. CA had communicated with ATC to advise that we did not need assistance at that time. After approximately 90 seconds the EICAS finished its reboot and had two remaining messages IDG (Integrated Drive Generator) 1 (and 2) FAIL Caution message. CA called for QRH checklist which I pulled up then we completed the procedure outlined. Both IDG FAIL messages disappeared. We checked the status page for both HYD and ELC. We were able to regain nose wheel steering and obtained a clearance from ATC to continue our taxi to gate XX. We left both engines running until parked to not make anymore system changes. Crew noted "if this happens again we will call Ops to tow us to the gate" We were able to park at the gate with no further issues. Crew had discussed previous write-ups regarding the APU but did not seem to be related to what we experienced. Upon arriving at the gate the crew agreed to call Maintenance Control and make a "info to Maintenance" write-up at Maintenance Control discretion. Post flight walk around was normal. Shutdown and power off completed with no issues. Post brief with CA determined all CRM decisions were appropriate and did not pose risk to the safety of the passengers; crew; or aircraft.Cause: Failure of power transfer during APU start"
