column121: Began taxi before receiving All Clear salute; with tug and marshallers below field of vision. Preconception that a salute was received.  No damage or injuries.  Stopped airplane.  Completed salute. Remainder of flight completed without issue.Cause: Received 'clear to start engines' immediately after Clear to Push instructions given.  This caused both engine starts to be completed relatively early.  As occurs regularly in ZZZ; when I don't immediately see the salute; marshallers sometimes return to the gate - usually before engine starts are complete.  Ran the After Start tasks and checklist.  FO and I did not see the marshaller or Lektro cart (my seat is in the highest position while in ramp areas.  This operation was run with one Lektro cart driver and one Marshaller.  FO sent taxi request command.  Waited some time and did not hear from ramp; so FO radioed for taxi and we received a taxi clearance.  We cleared left and right sides; turned on taxi light; and began to move the airplane in a right turn.  The Lektro cart driver ran out from under the airplane giving the stop signal; and I stopped the airplane - realizing we had not actually received an all clear salute.  The marshaller also moved to a visible position with the headset bag.  I opened the window to confirm that we had not hit the tug or a marshaller; which was confirmed that we did not.  Lektro cart driver moved the cart to a visible position and we received the all clear salute.  Notified ramp that we needed 5 minutes in position; and received the ok.  We called for and received a new taxi clearance and proceeded to the runway.  Remainder of flight completed with no issue.  Suggestions: One Marshaller to remain visible between 10 and 2 o'clock positions.  Lektro cart driver retrieve the headset if there are only two marshallers. Preferably use three marshallers.  Use a pole or lighted antenna on low/small Lektro carts; to remain visible from flight desk.  Confirm via call-out with FO that both of us have seen the salute.  Avoid distractions until the all clear salute is received.  If unsure; stop or open the window to see below.
column123: I was first officer acting as pilot monitoring during pushback; engine start; and taxi out.  Captain coordinated successful nose wheel capture with ramp crew via headset.  I sent ACARS silent push request; received push clearance from Ramp tower; and captain relayed clearance to ground crew.  Two ground crew members began moving aircraft and almost immediately cleared us for engine start; captain directed me to start engines one and two.  I started both engines over the course of approximately 1.5-2 minutes during push back and release from tug; ground crew movement was not visible to me during this process and me responsibility was to monitor the engine start rather than push back progress.  I stated 'normal start' after completing the second engine start and captain called for the next flow; we completed this and he called for the after start checklist; which we ran and completed.  At this point I had not seen or heard ground crew in some time and believed they had disconnected and given the all clear salute while I was heads down during engine start; as the after start checklist is called for following the salute in normal ops.  At this point we would normally be ready to taxi; so I sent ACARS silent taxi request.  Ramp tower did not respond via VHF after .5-1.5 minutes; so I called for taxi via VHF. During that period there was still no sight or sound from the two ground crew; which the captain and I both believed had disconnected and cleared the aircraft.  We received a taxi clearance from Ramp tower after the second request; the Captain visually cleared left and I visually cleared right for the tight 180 turn we would be making; neither saw any issues; I turned on the taxi light; and the captain began a tight right 180.  After moving the nose about 20 degrees the captain abruptly stopped the aircraft and was looking down out his left window. He then opened the window and began talking to ground crew who were apparently disconnected from the aircraft but not yet clear of the area.  The captain confirmed there were no injuries; no damage to the aircraft; and that the two ground crew would immediately clear the area. Seeing no issues and having coordinated with everyone we thought was relevant we departed and completed the flight.Cause: The ground crew and tug were not physically visible from my seated position after initial capture with the tug.  There were two rather than the usual three ground crew members; so no one on the ground was standing in a visible position to coordinate ground crew movements with the cockpit after headset disconnect.  There were no raised flags or wands from the tug to make its presence known to anyone in the cockpit.  I do not recall the voice interaction between captain and ground crew during push back and disconnect; only that everything was being coordinated normally while I was heads down starting the engines; but in our Standard Operating Procedures the FO's indication that ground crew is all clear is that the Captain calls for the after start checklist.  Had there been any visual; voice; or checklist/flow confirmation or even slight suspicion on my part that the ground crew was not clear; I would have delayed the taxi request; told the captain the aircraft was not clear for a turn; etc; I simply was not aware the ground crew was under the aircraft even after a delayed clearance to taxi.Suggestions: Tugs should have a raised wand; flag; light bar; etc. so that from the cockpit there is an indication that the tug is below or directly in front of the aircraft.  Three ground crew should be utilized with one between the 10 and 2 o'clock positions so that signals can be relayed between the ground crew members directly below the aircraft and the cockpit; when headsets have been disconnected.  The Standard Operating Procedres should include confirmation that the FO has seen the ground crew salute or some other verification step that they acknowledge the ground crew is clear; rather than the captain being the sole crew member confirming this.

column121: Upon arrival at the aircraft; I was advised the aircraft had experienced a significant maintenance event involving the hydraulic system. While reviewing the aircraft status in the Logbook; no MEL had yet been issued; and I was awaiting clarification on which MEL; if any; would be applied in order to properly evaluate its applicability and associated safety margin.After discussing the discrepancy with the previous Captain who made the original write-up; as well as dispatch / Maintenance Control; I developed concern that an incorrect MEL could be applied to the discrepancy; potentially masking the actual system involved. Specifically; Maintenance Control referenced the yellow hydraulic electric pump; while the original discrepancy involved the yellow engine-driven pump; indicating a possible misalignment between the reported condition and the anticipated MEL application.Given the potential for an incorrect MEL application to inappropriately authorize dispatch of an aircraft with an unresolved or non-deferrable condition; I determined it was necessary to delay boarding until the discrepancy and maintenance action could be fully verified.I proceeded to the gate area and instructed the gate agent; Person A; to hold boarding until I could verify the maintenance status with local maintenance; Dispatch; and Maintenance Control.The agent responded that boarding would continue; stating; 'No; the tower instructed us to board.' I reiterated my instruction to stop boarding; emphasizing the need to confirm the aircraft's airworthiness. The agent again refused and stated that I was 'not in charge of boarding.'I issued a third and final instruction to not board the aircraft; then returned to the flight deck and contacted Station Operations via radio to request a supervisor.A supervisor subsequently arrived at the flight deck and acknowledged concerns regarding the gate agent's conduct. I requested a reassignment of the gate agent; which was completed.Following coordination with Maintenance Control; it was confirmed that an incorrect MEL had been applied to the discrepancy; and the actual system affected was not eligible for MEL deferral. As a result; the aircraft was removed from service and a replacement aircraft was assigned. The flight was completed successfully. As of the time of this Report submission; aircraft X remains out of service for the hydraulic system discrepancy; now exceeding approximately 34 hours; further reinforcing the significance of the original maintenance issue and the importance of delaying boarding pending proper evaluation.This event highlights multiple breakdowns in communication; coordination; and adherence to established authority during an active maintenance situation:The gate agent's immediate refusal to comply with direction to hold boarding introduced undue time pressure to accept a maintenance action without proper evaluation. This type of operational pressure can lead to rushed decision-making by flight crews. Given that this was a known recurring issue from the prior leg; which manifested shortly after takeoff; there was a credible risk that proceeding under these conditions could have resulted in an in-flight abnormal or escalation.The gate agent's behavior became a distraction from a higher-priority safety issue; specifically the need to correctly diagnose and resolve the hydraulic discrepancy. This diverted attention and resources away from critical troubleshooting.The agent's unwillingness to follow direct instructions from the Captain raised concern regarding reliability in time-critical situations; including the ability to execute essential duties during an emergency (e.g.; evacuation or emergency deplaning).Local ZZZ maintenance demonstrated a misunderstanding of the original discrepancy and appeared to pursue a path focused on expediency rather than full verification of the write-up in the Logbook. This created risk of applying an incorrect MEL to an unrelated system.There was a lack of direct communication from local maintenance to the flight crew. I spent approximately 15-20 minutes attempting to gather information independently; as no maintenance personnel initially made contact at the aircraft to discuss the discrepancy.Initial coordination with Maintenance Control was also ineffective. Maintenance Control declined to engage in discussion regarding MEL applicability; citing local maintenance authority. This was inconsistent with standard practice; as Maintenance Control is typically involved in MEL evaluation and troubleshooting coordination. After further effort; I was able to establish direct communication with the responsible A320 Maintenance Control team member; at which point it was confirmed that the incorrect procedure was being considered.Overall; these combined factors--external pressure to board; lack of coordinated communication; recurrence of the discrepancy; and misapplication risk of maintenance procedures--significantly increased operational complexity and reduced safety margins during a critical phase of aircraft evaluation.Cause: 	•	Breakdown in adherence to Captain's authority: Gate agent refusal to comply with explicit instruction to hold boarding during an active safety evaluation.	•	Operational time pressure ('get-there-itis' at the gate): Immediate push to board created pressure to accept a maintenance action without adequate verification.	•	Maintenance misdiagnosis risk: Local maintenance did not fully verify the original discrepancy in the Logbook and appeared to pursue an expedient corrective path; increasing the likelihood of incorrect MEL application.	•	Ineffective communication and coordination: Lack of timely; direct communication between flight crew; local maintenance; and Maintenance Control; initial reluctance from Maintenance Control to engage in MEL discussion further delayed accurate assessment.	•	Distraction from critical task: Gate agent interaction diverted attention from troubleshooting and evaluating a known recurring hydraulic issue from the prior leg.	•	Lack of standardized escalation: No clear or immediate pathway to pause operations (boarding) while resolving conflicting maintenance information.	•	Reinforce Captain's authority: Ensure all gate/customer service personnel understand that boarding must stop when directed by the Captain for safety-related reasons.	•	Establish a formal 'boarding hold' protocol: Create a standardized procedure that clearly pauses boarding when an aircraft is under active maintenance review or airworthiness uncertainty.	•	Improve maintenance verification procedures: Require local maintenance to validate discrepancies against the original write-up prior to MEL application; especially for system-specific issues.	•	Strengthen Maintenance Control involvement: Reinforce expectation that Maintenance Control actively participates in MEL determination and troubleshooting coordination; regardless of station-level activity.	•	Enhance communication standards: Require direct; timely communication between maintenance and flight crew during active discrepancies before operational decisions (e.g.; boarding) proceed.	•	Training on operational risk awareness: Educate gate and maintenance personnel on the risks associated with time pressure and recurring discrepancies; emphasizing safety over schedule.	•	Standardize escalation pathways: Ensure flight crews have a clear; rapid method to involve station leadership when operational conflicts arise that impact safety decisions.

There were no illuminated lights when we checked the annunciator lights and the amperage was at a normal range. During the run up we leaned the mixture out for best power. Both magnetos had a normal drop of less than 175 RPMs and the difference between the two drops did not exceed 50 RPMs. On takeoff; we received normal RPM output and our temperature and pressures all remained in the green; normal range. On climb out we maintained a normal climb out rate with normal airspeed; we maintained 80 knots and climbed out at 500 FPM. We turned crosswind for our departure at 2;700' and continued our climb over the cement plant to exit the airport environment to the north. We continued to climb on a northern heading until we reached 5;500'. At 5;500' we leveled the plane out and brought our RPMs back to 2300. Shortly after bringing the RPMs back to 2300 we heard a loud noise from the engine. The noise sounded like a boom. We immediately lost all RPMs and both the vacuum and oil light illuminated. I increased the throttle to see if we could maintain altitude or climb but we could not. I then turned us to the south to circle to keep us close to the small airpark west of us. while I attempted to restart the engine by ensuring that the fuel pump was on; putting the mixture full; and switching the fuel tanks. I then cranked the starter but there was no indication that the engine would turn over and restart. At this point I knew that we would not make it back to the airport; we were 7 miles north and we did not have adequate altitude to return back to our original point of departure. I knew that we were going to have to land at ZZZ Airpark so we turned northwest to head directly to the airpark. I did not have adequate time to advise ATC. We started a slow descent at our gliding speed of 76 kts. I added in the first notch of flaps (10°) when we were a mile away from the airport. I added another notch of flaps (25°) when we were short final. We didn't have excess altitude so we had to come in low. On our approach; our right wing grazed through shrubs but it did not cause us to falter off of our path. We touched down on the runway and the plane veered to the right slightly because of the gravel but we maintained control and brought the plane to a stop in the center of the runway. We then shut down the engine and performed the engine securing checklist.

column123: On Day 0; I was receiving dual instruction in a PA 28R-180 with my instructor while completing the required flight time needed in a complex aircraft for my commercial requirements.We were returning to ZZZ Airport following a cross-country flight from ZZZ1. Approximately 4-5 nautical miles from the airport; we began our before-landing checklist and initiated the GUMPS flow. At that time; our airspeed was at or slightly above the maximum allowable speed for landing gear extension; so we made the decision to delay extending the landing gear until the aircraft slowed and continued with the rest of our checklist.As we continued toward the airport; our workload increased due to pattern entry; radio communications; and configuring for landing. During this time; although the checklist had been initiated earlier; we did not complete a final verification that the landing gear had been extended.On final approach; both my instructor and I were focused on maintaining a stable approach and landing. We did not visually or physically confirm gear extension prior to touchdown. Another pilot attempted to alert us via radio; however; we misunderstood the transmission and did not recognize it as a warning regarding the landing gear.The aircraft touched down with the landing gear retracted. After landing; we secured the aircraft and exited safely. There were no injuries.Upon reflection; I recognize several contributing factors; including initiating the before-landing checklist too early; delaying gear extension without establishing a clear follow-up trigger; increased workload in the pattern; and a breakdown in final verification procedures. This resulted in a loss of situational awareness regarding the landing gear status.This experience has reinforced the importance of strict adherence to checklist discipline and redundant verification of critical configuration items. Moving forward; I will ensure that landing gear extension is verified multiple times during the approach; including on downwind; base; and final; with a positive confirmation of 'gear down; three green' prior to landing. I will also incorporate physical verification of the gear position and avoid performing critical checklist items prematurely.I take this event seriously and am committed to applying the lessons learned to ensure it does not happen again.

Based on this assessment and normal indications at that time; a second takeoff attempt was initiated.During the second takeoff roll; the right (No. 2) engine again did not produce expected torque with CAWI activated. The crew rejected the takeoff a second time. The aircraft was brought to a safe stop; exited the runway; and returned to the ramp for further evaluation. No injuries occurred.This event highlights the challenges associated with diagnosing abnormal engine indications during high-workload phases of flight such as takeoff. The fluctuating torque indication on the first attempt created ambiguity regarding whether the issue was mechanical or related to configuration.The decision to attempt a second takeoff was influenced by a perceived; correctable configuration issue and the absence of persistent abnormal indications while stopped. However; recurrence of insufficient torque on the second attempt suggests the possibility of an underlying mechanical or system-related issue.This event also underscores the importance of conservative decision-making when abnormal engine indications are observed during takeoff; even if a potential explanation is identified.

column121: Due to circumstances beyond my control; this is the first chance I have had to finish this report and review it before submission.While flying the arrival to LAX and programing the FMS for the assigned runway; my finger accidental touched the Vectors to Final button on the Garmin GTC (Garmin Touch Screen) which immediately caused lost of FMS sequencing. ATC was notified immediately that a wrong button had been pressed and a heading and altitude to descend to was needed. SOCAL assisted in the request. I managed to get the arrival reloaded and told ATC that we could resume the arrival again. Unfortunately; my copilot did not press the NAV button on the mode control panel and while was busy trying to reloaded the correct approach procedure for RWY24R; I hadn't noticed the course deviation. I saw what was happening and brought the error to my coworkers attention and immediately confirmed the error with the SOCAL controller when he said that we appeared to be off course. We corrected and got the FMS capture for lateral navigation.We were told we were following Aircraft Y that was turning right base. We saw Aircraft Y and advised the traffic in sight. It wasn't more than a few seconds later that Aircraft X began to receive light turbulence when all of sudden; the airplane was rolled to the left uncontrollably. I can only estimate the roll to the left felt like 45-50 degrees of bank.  Our aircraft was not subjected to any unusual of out tolerance G forces; just a significant roll due to strong vortices.  The aircraft upset was eventual corrected but we were both shaken up.  We just didn't know if it was over.  I communicated the event to the SOCAL controller.  He asked if we wanted to change to the south complex and fly to 25L behind a jet. Both of us agreed to flying to 25L instead.Unfortunately; I programmed the FMS for 24L; not 25L. So when the vector heading of 220 degrees to join caused the aircraft to intercept the 24L LOC; we inadvertently flew in the flight track of another flight. Realizing the error; I was able to program 25L correctly and we were able to get onto the correct flight path eventually. Suggestions: 1. Obviously; the Garmin screen is very touchy. It's critical to go slow when programming.2. An aircraft upset event requires notification followed by possible delay vectors to regain mental clarity and composure ; especially behind a commercial airliner. You have to slow down cockpit tasks.3. Even during a traumatic event; standard SOP and mode confirmation along dual verification must happen so that future errors can be trapped.

column121: I (FO) was pilot flying with AP (Autopilot) and AT (Autothrottles) engaged during the climb to cruise altitude of FL370. Climbing through FL355; through clear and smooth air; we experienced sudden windshear causing airspeed to increase 20-30 kts and VSI increasing to around 4500fpm. As I saw the airspeed approaching redline I reduced thrust and as the clacker sounded the CA took the controls; disengaged AP and AT; continued to reduce speed below red line and began to level off. CA returned flight controls to me just before we got to the back side of the windshear and quickly lost 20-30kt and approached minimum maneuver speed. I told the CA I will be descending to FL 360 in order to reduce pitch and regain airspeed at that altitude and he made the request to ATC. ATC continued our descent to FL350 where we leveled off on airspeed and reengaged AP and AT. CA made an Airplane Maintenance Logbook entry for the over speed. Flight continued to ZZZ with no issues. Cause: The event's main causal factor was meteorological. Unknown windshear at altitude. I would say another causal factor could be my monitoring of speed as I could have noticed the speed increase slightly sooner; however the dramatic performance increase and decrease would have occurred regardless of reaction time. Proper training and execution of that training were essential in regaining airspeed control. Performance demonstrations at high altitude in the simulator were helpful during this event. Because of those demonstrations and knowledge it was clear that after the loss of performance on the back side of the windshear; a decrease in altitude was necessary for proper and timely airspeed recovery. More of these demonstrations and relating this meteorological/performance possibility to other factors that we talk about; such as microbursts; will help in mitigating risk by helping pilots with timely recognition and recovery.
column123: FO was PF.  At XA:30 climbing through FL360 in the vicinity of ZZZZZ intersection we experienced an immediate vertical wind sheer of +22 to +30 knots.  CA took controls; disengaged AP (Autopilot) and pitched up and reduced thrust. We experienced what we believe was high speed buffet; which felt like cobblestone" or "washboard" turbulence; but felt more like shaking which we felt in the simulator. Airspeed then immediately dropped to min maneuvering speed +5 knots.  Pitch limit indicators were in view. We transferred controls back to the FO and exercised emergency authority and descended immediately to FL360. The flight attendants were up in the cabin at the time. No injuries were reported. We notified dispatch. We completed an Airplane Maintenance Logbook entry.Cause: When the airspeed dropped dramatically on the other side of the windshear; we knew to pitch down and descend to quickly regain flying speed. Just like the simulator. Both pilots were on the same page about what was needed. I recommend that during recurrent training; a high speed buffet is demonstrated in the simulator. As a former check pilot; I've experienced this; but it is not in the curriculum as far as I am aware. In the simulator; we'd have to fly to red line +40 or +50 to see this effect.  This flight showed high speed buffet around redline +20 knots.In hindsight I would not have reduced thrust as much as I did knowing that this was a transient condition; with an imminent reversal in trend.  Much like an increasing headwind / decreasing tailwind condition like we see in microbursts."

column121: Flight experienced GPS interference consistent with jamming/spoofing while operating in the Turkey region. During this phase; one or both GPS receivers were intermittently lost or unreliable. Standard degradation of navigation capability was observed and managed.Continuing for the remainder of the flight; or nearly the remainder of the flight; after exiting the interference region; anomalous system behavior continued while one GPS remained offline. The aircraft clock began oscillating between correct time and an offset of approximately five minutes. This was not a steady offset but a repeating switching between time sources.This time instability resulted in multiple downstream effects:• CPDLC instability; including repeated logoff/logon requests from ATC (LPPO); likely due to message timing/sequence issues.• ADS-C / ADS-B discrepancies. (On a prior flight) ATC reported position inconsistency on approach to DEL; with the aircraft depicted approximately 0.5-1.0 NM north of actual position while established on the ILS. Approach and Tower control seemed to think we were not on the localizer; and maybe believed we were lining up for the wrong runway. They seemed very concerned. Other crew members on the flight related being directed to go around on a prior flight to DEL for the same reason.• NAT ADS Position reporting becoming unusable due to reporting over a fix at a time in the future. We reverted to HF Voice position reports for the entire crossing.• Nuisance EGPWS alert (WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP") at cruise altitude (FL360). (Prior flight)The aircraft flagged the GPWS TERR POS; however; nuisance alerts continued to be generated. In the absence of company guidance addressing this condition; I selected TERR Override to suppress repeated false warnings and reduce distraction during flight. Various conditions persisted well beyond the geographic area of known interference; and one GPS position never recovered. Mitigation actions included increased cross-checking of navigation sources; use of procedural separation techniques (including HF position reporting when appropriate); and cautious use of datalink functions. However; no flight deck intervention was available to isolate or reset the affected time source.Cause: This condition presents more than a nuisance. Incorrect time and position outputs can lead to:• Misleading ATC surveillance displays• CPDLC communication failures or delays• False terrain warnings; including at cruise altitude• Increased crew workload and distraction during critical and non-critical phases of flight.Consider system-level mitigation to prevent corrupted GPS-derived time and position from being intermittently accepted after initial rejection. A more robust isolation of unreliable inputs; or a crew-selectable means to inhibit GPS-derived time and/or terrain alerting when flagged unreliable; may improve resilience.A means for resetting an individual GPS receiver inflight. With the incidence of jamming/spoofing likely to increase; there needs to be an emphasis on making our aircraft more resilient. Another aircraft type flew through the jamming/spoofing areas with considerably less bother."

column121: My student who is training to become a private pilot was planning to solo today. They had completed the initial solo; but this flight was supposed to be a pattern solo. It had been some time since they had flown solo; we had flown a pattern lesson the previous week with ten landings to smooth out their landing flare technique (tended to not flare enough leading to hard landings); and towards the end of the lesson the landings were pretty good. So today just to make sure everything was good I decided to run a few laps in the pattern with them before they went solo today. We did three laps in the pattern and had no concerns with their takeoffs and landings. After the third lap in the pattern; I had my student drop me off at the FBO and I was going to observe the rest of the lesson from the ground. The student then proceeded to complete seven laps in the traffic pattern using runway XX at ZZZ with no issues. The weather was 10SM Visibility; sky CLR; with winds 220 at 7KTS. After the seventh landing the student then proceeded to take off. I was told by the student that after they increased the power; they were rolling down the runway and glanced over to the right side of the cockpit to make sure the oil temperature and oil pressure was in the green. At that time the right wing started to roll moving the plane to the left on the runway. The student then proceeded to pull power and tried to maintain control and drove the plane into the grass on the left side of the runway. I then ran over to make sure the student was okay and that the plane was okay. After assessing the situation and seeing my student was okay and the plane seemed to be fine; I taxied the plane out of the grass and back to the main ramp. Plane had no damage and the taxiway; lights; and signs on the side of the runway by [taxiway] 1 had not been damaged. Upon review from what I saw on the ground and from what I was told by my student the contributing factor to this accident was an incorrect input of the flight controls and not correcting for the crosswind on takeoff. As the flight instructor I need to be more vigilant on teaching cross wind corrections and make sure my students know the importance of them. Also to keep their eyes down the runway during the takeoff roll to see the trends and movement of the aircraft so the correct crosswind corrections can be made.

I was informed that the company owned a drone; so I waited until there was an opportunity to use it. I have never flown a drone before and I have never been trained to. Today; I operated the drone at a residential site from about XA:25 - XA:55. The goal was to capture photos or videos of a completed backyard that has been designed and built by the landscaping firm. I did not have any issues with operating the drone and I did not fly above 300 feet; and that was only for a brief moment to begin descent of the property. Most of the flying was close to the ground. While I was operating the drone within 10-20 feet in the air; I did hear and notice a helicopter overhead. By reflex; I soon landed the drone. When the helicopter returned (or it may have been another); I had already ceased operating the drone. I did not believe that I was doing anything improper at the time. Still; it prompted me to conduct an online search about laws regarding drone usage. I then learned that I am required to be licensed to operate the drone; and also that I cannot fly within 5 miles of an airport. I performed a Google search and realized that this address was within 5 miles of ZZZ Airport. This news brought me anxiety; for I did not intend to violate any FAA laws and I had no idea that the airport was so close to the job site. I do not know if my inadvertent action was discovered or reported to or by the FAA; as it could have just been routine helicopter operation; but I did later learn that my drone has a digital ID that can appear and be noticed. I informed my employers right away about this; in case they are contacted. The drone belongs to the business owners and I was using their drone on site; operating alone with no training or awareness of the laws. I regret operating the drone today and I wish I had been aware of the requirements. I do not plan on operating the drone again until I am licensed and have obtained approval to fly in any airspace requiring it.

column121: Unintentional UAS Operation in Class D Airspace (First Flight Experience)During my first-ever recreational drone flight; which occurred at approximately XA:00; I unintentionally operated within Class D airspace without prior authorization.The flight took place in an area that I later learned corresponds to a 100-foot LAANC grid within Class D airspace. column121: Runway 16R was the active. I (training on Local Control) had control of Runway 16R. Ground Control (GC) had control of runways 16L; 10; and 4. GC had a vehicle that needed to mow the area immediately surrounding the intersection of runways 16R and 10. Ground would request permission from me to have the vehicle enter the intersection. When I needed Runway 16R clear; I would inform ground; and they would have the vehicle exit Runway 16R and remain on Runway 10 for quick re-entry. Each time I give GC permission to enter the runway; I put my memory aid up on the Runway Incursion Device (RID); as required by our SOP. I had a VFR helicopter maneuvering about 300 feet above ground level (AGL) several miles south of the field inspecting a power line. I had Aircraft X ready for takeoff at Runway 16R at Taxiway Papa. Another aircraft was taxiing northbound on Papa and would be ready to depart shortly. Because the helicopter was in the way of the departing aircraft; I coordinated with the departure controller and received a left turn heading 100 or heading 110; which would get the departure well east of the helicopter. I wrote the coordinated heading on the flight strip as a not-required memory aid to give the aircraft the turn when clearing it for takeoff. At that time; the vehicle was in the intersection of runways 16R and 10; and my memory aid was where it should have been. After seeing the helicopter out the window to the south and turning to look at Aircraft X to the north ready to depart; I cleared Aircraft X for takeoff. I issued the left turn and gave the aircraft the wind and the position of the helicopter. Aircraft X then entered the runway and began powering their engines up; all the while the pickup truck is parked on the runway. The ground controller noticed Aircraft X moving and mentioned it to me; then exclaimed that the vehicle was still where I had coordinated that it could be: halfway down the runway directly ahead of the departing Aircraft X. I told Aircraft X to cancel takeoff clearance and turn right at Taxiway Mike. The pilot promptly read back my instructions; slowed the aircraft; and exited the runway at Mike. The pilot then asked me why their takeoff clearance was cancelled. I informed them that there was a vehicle on the runway. The ground controller had the vehicle exit Runway 16R. The other departing aircraft was ahead of Aircraft X at this point and departed first. Aircraft X next; but this time runway heading because the helicopter was not a factor. Aircraft X never got closer than 3;250 feet to the vehicle.If I had had direct communication with the vehicle; rather than the vehicle being on GC's frequency; I would likely have been more aware and would have talked to the vehicle before talking to the aircraft. I need to ensure my normal scan (including the RID and runways) does not get compromised when I have additional things to include in my scan (in this case; the helicopter in a specific place out the window and the heading in a small box on the flight strip). If I had looked at the RID and seen the memory aid or looked at the runway and seen the truck; I would not have cleared the Aircraft X for takeoff.
column123: I was training a developmental on the Local Control (LC) position. Traffic had been average; and the session up to that point was uninteresting. The Controller in Charge (CIC) position was de-combined; and the CIC and Ground Control (GC) controller were having a conversation. A vehicle had been proceeding onto the intersection of the active Runway 16R and Runway 10 periodically. The developmental cleared Aircraft X for takeoff from Runway 16R; which is approximately 5000 feet from the intersection. It appeared to me that the vehicle was near the edge of the safety area; so I was unclear if he had exited. I was about to ask the developmental; when the GC controller jumped up and said that the vehicle was still in the intersection. The developmental cancelled Aircraft X's takeoff clearance and taxied them back around to the departure end. When exiting the runway; Aircraft X asked the reason for the cancellation.The memory aid for the runway being occupied was used.The primary failure here was in the scan; the developmental failed to scan the runway for the vehicle; and failed to acknowledge the memory aid they had displayed. As the trainer; I failed to acknowledge with certainty that the vehicle had not yet exited the runway. I gave the developmental; who is close to certification; too much leeway and benefit of the doubt that my memory was lacking and not his actions.I also feel that this developmental sees extra scrutiny and harassment from other controllers due to his personality. This may cause me to give him extra space to work traffic to prove them wrong; which may have contributed to this scenario.

column121: While operating Aircraft X from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2; at approximately XA:15 UTC and in cruise at FL360; we heard a bang from the left side of the aircraft and felt a slight disturbance. Prior to that event; the flight had been normal; with me acting as PF and the Captain acting as PM.Immediately after the noise; we observed an ENG 1 OUT message on EICAS and verified that we had a No. 1 engine failure. The flight attendant contacted the flight deck and reported that passengers had heard the noise and that some appeared concerned. We advised the flight attendant to stand by while we focused on aircraft control and the immediate abnormal procedures.I remained PF and continued flying the aircraft. The Captain requested priority handling with ATC and requested descent to FL230. The Captain set began the applicable engine-out QRH; and turned the APU on. During the procedure; I monitored aircraft control; guarded and confirmed the required actions as appropriate; and continued the descent.After the No. 1 engine was safely secured; the Captain coordinated with Dispatch and we elected to divert to ZZZ. ATC then cleared us direct ZZZ and issued descend and maintain 11;000 feet. During the descent; the Captain made a PA advising the passengers that we had experienced an engine failure and were diverting to ZZZ for a safe landing; while I set up the FMS and prepared for the approach.During the descent; we also observed a PACK 1 OVHT (Overheat) message. The Captain selected PACK 1 OFF. Later; we observed a Rudder Hardover Protection Fail message. After ensuring the aircraft remained stable in the engine-out condition; I transferred control of the aircraft to the Captain; and the related QRH was completed while continuing the diversion.The flight attendant continued her procedures and kept the cabin under control. The approach and single-engine landing at ZZZ were completed without further difficulty by the Captain. After clearing the runway; Engine 2 was shut down and fire/rescue personnel performed an external inspection of Engine 1. We were advised that there was no visible external fire or smoke. Afterward; Engine 2 was restarted and the aircraft taxied to Gate XX.At no point did I perceive a loss of aircraft controllability. Workload was elevated but manageable; and CRM among the Captain; myself; the flight attendant; ATC; and Dispatch was effective throughout the event.Suggestions: The company's engine-out training was very helpful during this event. Continued emphasis on maintaining proficiency and currency in engine-out scenarios would be beneficial.
column123: While operating Aircraft X from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2; at approximately XA:15Z and in cruise at FL360; we heard a loud bang from the left side of the aircraft and felt a slight disturbance. Please read that back and report to me once the cabin is ready."She acknowledged and began cabin preparation.After securing the engine; I coordinated with Dispatch regarding a suitable alternate for single engine operations. Dispatch recommended ZZZ. We advised ATC of our intent to divert and were cleared direct ZZZ; with a subsequent descent clearance to 11;000 feet.During the descent; I made a PA to the passengers:"Folks; this is your captain speaking. We've experienced a loss of our number one engine and will be diverting to ZZZ. There is no need for concern; we will have you safely on the ground in approximately 15 minutes."The announcement was delivered in a calm and controlled manner.First Officer configured the FMS and prepared for the approach while I continued coordinating with ATC; Dispatch; and the cabin. The flight attendant later confirmed that the cabin was prepared.During the descent; we observed a PACK 1 OVHT (Overheat) message; which was addressed by selecting PACK 1 OFF in accordance with QRH procedures. We also received a Rudder Hard Over Protection Fail message. After confirming the aircraft remained stable; the associated QRH was completed and no additional action was required.We verified that the aircraft was below maximum landing weight and completed performance calculations using QRH; along with obtaining current weather for ZZZ from ATC.Once all QRH and abnormal procedures were completed; with the exception of the landing checklist; I briefed First Officer that I would assume control of the aircraft for the approach and landing. A positive transfer of controls was completed at that time.I then hand-flew the aircraft from base to final to better assess handling characteristics; trim; and aircraft response in the single-engine configuration. First Officer continued in a monitoring role and handled the landing checklist at the appropriate time.We maintained a methodical and disciplined approach throughout the event; verbally confirming actions and ensuring all procedures were completed.The approach and single engine landing at ZZZ were completed without further issue. We landed using Flaps 22 on Runway XXL and exited the runway at taxiway 1.After clearing the runway; we stopped at Taxiway 1 and shut down Engine 2 to allow emergency personnel to approach the aircraft. Fire andrescue crews performed an external inspection of Engine 1 using thermal imaging equipment and reported no signs of fire or abnormal heat.Following the inspection; Engine 2 was restarted; and we taxied to Gate XX; where the terminating checklist was completed.Post-flight; we coordinated with Company; Maintenance; and Union representatives to complete all required reports and write ups.At the gate; I addressed the passengers; informing them of the next steps; including that a replacement aircraft would be provided for transportation to ZZZ3. I also thanked them for their patience and cooperation. The message was well received.Suggestions: CRM was a key factor in the successful management of this event. I could not have asked for a stronger First Officer or Flight Attendant. We worked cohesively as a team; maintaining clear communication while continuously supporting and cross-checking one another. Although the situation involved a high workload; it remained manageable due to this coordination; discipline; and adherence to SOPs."

column121: After departing ZZZ for ZZZ1 we received a call from the number one flight attendant climbing through approximately 10;000ft. The number one stated that there was an extreme amount of noise coming from the forward entry door. As he was speaking to me on the inter phone I could audibly hear the loud rushing air noise and the flight attendant was having to yell to communicate with me. The pressurization was on schedule and there was nothing on the gauges to alert us of any kind of issue with the system. We discussed with the number one that we were going to climb a little higher to see if the door will get a seal on it. Some aircraft need a little more pressure to create a good seal. As we climbed we contacted the number one and he stated that there was no change it was still loud. I then called dispatch and Maintenance Control and went over the issue with them. They all agreed this was not normal. As I was talking to them the cabin crew was calling to let us know the passengers were uncomfortable. It was at this point we decided to take the plane back to ZZZ instead of continuing over the ocean to ZZZ1. We discussed that the plane would be slightly overweight for landing and given the unknown situation with the door we advised ATC and started coordinating with ATC for a return to ZZZ. On our way in to ZZZ we ran the overweight landing QRH procedure and the non routine landing checklist. The rest of the flight was unremarkable and we made our way to the gate for a normal deplaning via jet bridge. At the gate I made the entries in the logbook for the pressurization issue and the over weight landing. Cause: Casual factors in this event are mechanical failures as well as communication and crew coordination. This is the type of event that could really only be discovered during flight as the AC is not pressurized enough on the ground to know. I did follow up with the actions of the mechanics and it seems there was a tear in the door pressurization seal. Mitigation may have to occur on overnight maintenance checks of door pressurization seals.

column121: The flight crew arrived at ZZZZ to operate Aircraft X to ZZZ1 on-time on Day 0.  While completing our receiving checklist; the CA noticed that the CA's oxygen mask (interphone) would not test properly; and that there was not a proper 'switch over;' to the mask-microphone function.  After confirming that the First Officer's mask was working properly; and attempting to resolve the issue multiple times; dispatch was informed and maintenance was called to the aicraft.  Maintenance confirmed that the CA's mask was not working properly; and upon further investgiation; damage was found to the cables connecting the mask to the aicraft in the flight deck.  Maintenance informed us that they would 'swap;' the mask assembly box with the second observer's mask to resolve the issue.  This process took several hours as it proved to be a difficult task to accomplish due to the ergonomics of the assemblies. After the procedure was complete; the maintenance technicians proceeded to begin the 'sign off;' process; and took the logbook to 'close out;' the open write-up.  While this was happening; the aircraft unexpectedly rolled forward completely uncommanded into the chocks.  The Captain first noticed this; and it was confirmed by the remaining maintenance crew still onboard the aicraft.  We verified that the parking brake was still engaged by first looking at the E/WD; and then looked at the 'triple indicator;' to see that both the accumulator and both brake pressure indicators were showing zero pressure.  After coordinating with maintenance; the yellow pump was turned on which immediately pressurized the yellow system.  Hydraulic cavitations were felt and heard; and the 'triple indicator;' immediatley showed tha the system was pressurized. At this point; we realized that there may be an issue with the accumulator.  At no point did we suspect that the indicator was incorrectly reporting the pressure; as it was confirmed on two separate 'known states;' that the pressure was first 'lost;' and then 'recharged.'  During the next 35-40 minutes of troubleshooting and invesgitation; we noticed that the presure in the accumulator was dropping rapidly; and the brake pressure indicators were also showing a loss of pressure. The manual states that 'EFFECTIVE ON A/C ALL - Accumulators maintain the parking pressure for at least 12 hours.  Yellow accumulators can be pressurized by pressuring the yellow electric pump switch. Brake and accumulator pressure are indiciated on the triple indicator.'  The total time elapsed from first parking brake application (aircraft block-in from ZZZ1) to the aircraft moving into the chocks was approxmately 3 hours -- clearly outside of the normal expectation for the system. At this point; we were notified that the airport authority had instructed us to move the aicraft off of the gate because it was needed for another aircraft.  We proceeded to 'deplane;' the customers; and maintenance moved the aicraft to another suitable gate.  This process took several hours; and during this time; on-site maintenance worked to test the aicraft and seek a resolution.  Ultimately; the flight was cancelled due to the extended delay as the inflight crew had worked the incoming flight from ZZZ1; and we were rapidly approaching our MOT (Minimum Off Time). We were notified that we would be operating an extra section for the route; Aircraft Y on Day 1.The next morning; after waking up in ZZZZ; I noticed that the schedule stated that the flight would be operated with the same tail number; Aircraft X and there was an MEL applied -- MEL 32-XX-XXX.  In my opinion; after reviewing the MEL details; this was an incorrect MEL for the situation; instead referencing the indicator not being correct.  At this time; I felt that maintenance control was attempting to apply the MEL that would allow us to depart while the aicraft was still in an unsafe condition to fly.  Ultimately; the issue was resolved via a 'tail swap;' to another aicraft; and AircraftX was grounded.

column121: I was assigned from reserve to operate Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1.During preflight; the First Officer and I reviewed the aircraft logbook and MELs. Multiple MELs were noted; including two related to the air conditioning system. Neither MEL contained Operations Procedures or notes indicating degraded cabin temperature performance. During cockpit preparation; I observed the PACK FLOW selector in the HIGH position. As this was not required by any MEL or procedure; it was returned to NORM.Pushback was slightly delayed due to ramp congestion. Taxi and takeoff were uneventful. During climb; passing approximately 10;000 feet; the flight attendants reported increasing cabin temperatures in the aft cabin. In response; I selected all temperature zones to full cold and set PACK FLOW to HIGH. A subsequent report from the cabin indicated that conditions were worsening; with very hot air from the vents.The COND page was reviewed and indicated increasing cabin temperatures and elevated trim air temperature (approximately 150°C). I made a PA to inform passengers that we were working to address the situation. At that point; I transferred aircraft control to the First Officer and requested a level-off from ATC to allow time for system evaluation and troubleshooting.No ECAM messages were present; and no applicable non-annunciated procedures were identified in the QRH. Based on system indications; we selected the HOT AIR pushbutton OFF; no improvement was observed.I established communication with Maintenance Control via SATCOM and provided a summary of system indications and cabin reports. In coordination with Maintenance Control; we selected the HOT AIR push button OFF and performed a pack reset. These actions did not result in any sustained improvement. Cabin temperatures continued to increase; reaching approximately 105°F forward and 100°F aft. Concurrently; the cabin crew continued to report worsening conditions and increasing passenger discomfort.Given the lack of response to corrective actions; continued adverse temperature indications; and ongoing cabin reports; the First Officer and I assessed the situation as a safety concern and elected to discontinue the flight and return to ZZZ.The First Officer coordinated the return with ATC while I remained in communication with Maintenance Control. During the return; trim air temperature briefly decreased; however; cabin temperatures remained elevated and subsequently increased again. Based on this trend; the decision to return was reaffirmed.I advised the cabin crew and passengers of the return. Due to workload during the approach phase; I contacted ZZZ operations via VHF to advise of the return and request notification to dispatch.The approach and landing were uneventful. After arrival at the gate; a logbook entry was made and the aircraft was subsequently removed from service.

column121: Shortly after departure from ZZZ Airport; while climbing through approximately 1;500 feet AGL; the crew received an amber ECAM message: DOOR R AFT EMERGENCY EXIT.The message appeared after the Takeoff Inhibit phase; at which point we leveled at 5;000 feet and requested vectors to troubleshoot. ECAM and QRH procedures were initiated.Per QRH guidance; continuation of flight may be considered if pressurization is confirmed normal. However; during coordination with the cabin crew; a physical inspection of the door revealed that the handle had become detached and the door appeared unsecured (unlocked"/not properly seated).This created a discrepancy between: System indications and QRH conditional guidance; and Direct physical observation from the cabin crew indicating a potential door integrity issue.Additionally; due to the early phase of flight in which the ECAM message occurred (approximately 1;500 feet AGL); there was limited opportunity to reliably assess cabin pressurization performance prior to reaching higher altitudes where any degradation could become operationally significant.Given: The uncertainty regarding the mechanical status of the emergency exit; The abnormal condition of a detached handle; The limited ability to confirm stable pressurization early in the climb; The planned routing over the ZZZZZ/oceanic segment; where diversion options are more limited; I assessed that continuing the flight would introduce unnecessary risk; particularly in the event of a pressurization or structural issue. Given these factors; delaying the decision until further climb would have reduced available margins and increased exposure to risk in a less favorable operational environment. After completing the QRH; I coordinated with Dispatch via SATCOM; briefed the passengers; and elected to return to ZZZ for a precautionary landing. The aircraft landed without further incident."

column121: Shortly after liftoff; we raised the landing gear; noticed the Nose Pitch Trim was not corresponding correctly to the flying pilots (Captain) input. As the aircraft accelerated through 800' feet; both pilots recognized the excessive pressure it took for me to keep the nose at the proper pitch angle for climb. column121: I was arriving at ZZZ in gusty southerly wind conditions. The reported winds were approximately 170° at 11 knots; gusting to 18 knots. Visual observation of the windsock indicated variable and gusty conditions.On the first approach; I experienced instability on short final related to gusty conditions and airspeed management. Recognizing the unstable condition; I executed a go-around.On the second approach; I increased my approach speed and initially maintained runway alignment. However; during the landing phase near touchdown; I encountered a gust while applying significant control input to maintain directional control in the crosswind. The aircraft deviated left of centerline and exited the runway into the grass; where it came to a stop in soft ground.There were no injuries; and there was no apparent damage to the aircraft. The aircraft is being inspected prior to return to service.This event highlighted the importance of maintaining adequate control margin in gusty crosswind conditions. While the reported winds were within expected limits; the variability and gusts resulted in higher control input requirements than anticipated on short final.In reviewing the event; I recognize that increasing control demand earlier on final approach was an indicator of reduced margin. Continuing the approach into the flare under those conditions reduced my ability to respond effectively to a gust at touchdown.Going forward; I will use earlier decision points based on control input and stability; and will discontinue the approach if increasing control demand indicates diminishing margin. I will also ensure appropriate energy margin is maintained in gusty conditions.

We suspended trying to transfer fuel and began to run the Fuel Leak Engine QRH procedure. We stopped it short of shutting down the engine because we were not concerned with suspected leak enough to justify shutting down an engine; making things more complicated than they had to be. We deemed it safe and appropriate to request priority handling and divert to ZZZ1 giving us a reasonable amount of time to safely execute the diversion while monitoring our fuel situation. As we continued the right side continued to decrease fuel more than the left with no other outlying indications. Upon landing we had Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) check out the aircraft to make a visual inspection; they reported nothing noticeable and so we continued to the gate and had ARFF follow us until we were shut down at the gate and cancelled the priority handling.Cause: Suspected Mechanical issue; we ran appropriate QRH procedure.

column121: Our flight was from ZZZ.  We boarded Aircraft X and found the flight deck and forward galley in a bit of disarray; with gear pins; papers; and rags on the cockpit floor and a mechanic's headset and pitot tube covers in the galley.  The aircraft had been sitting in ZZZ for what I recall was a few days from the logbook.  We requested that a mechanic come to retrieve any items that didn't belong on the airplane and ensure that everything that was required to be onboard was accounted for; which they did.  My FO verified that no gear-pins; collars; reverser locking pins; etc. were in place on the exterior of the aircraft.We departed on time and taxied to runway XXL for takeoff.  The takeoff was normal and we received a vector of 230 and clearance to 10;000 feet from ZZZ departure.  Passing through approximately 6;000 feet; an ECAM message appeared; ENG 2 EGT OVER-TEMP" with engine parameters in agreement.  I was the pilot monitoring and began the non-normal plan strategy; which led us to reducing thrust to see if the EGT would come below the high-limit.  It did; but after a brief discussion of our situation and about how such a reduction in thrust didn't make flying all the way to  our destination seem very practical or wise; we decided that returning to ZZZ would be prudent.  This discussion was cut short by a second ECAM; "ENG2 EPR MODE FAIL"; so the plan strategy began once again.  The ECAM action led us to a reversion to N1 mode of thrust control and subsequent loss of auto-thrust; and that went smoothly.  My FO; whose capacity to fly the aircraft extraordinarily well and handle high task-loading with apparent ease (while I was quite busy with QRH followups; STATUS page updates; the ECAM Supplemental manual; diversion notification; etc.); was able to observe that increasing the thrust on the affected engine close to climb would cause another over temperature condition while decreasing the thrust to idle also caused a sharp increase in temperature up to the limit.  Unusual.  I notified the flight attendants and passengers of the need to return to ZZZ for a mechanical discrepancy.  We notified ATC for a more immediate return to the airport; although the situation was quite under control; the strange behavior of the EGT on the affected engine gave us enough reason to think being on the ground sooner than later would be a good idea.  We performed an overweight landing checklist for what would be a landing at approximately 4;000 pounds over maximum landing weight.  During landing the #2 engine thrust reverser didn't deploy; and displayed amber when selected to reverse.  After clearing the runway we noticed that the #2 engine; when at idle; was approximately 150 degrees hotter than the #1 engine at idle; but within limits.  After shutdown; we also noted an "ENG2 FADEC" Class 2 status message.  Before I had the chance to pick up my iPad to begin making all of the necessary logbook entries; we were greeted on the flight deck by two mechanics who noted that they weren't very surprised by our return because the airplane had "quite a history".  They mentioned that the work done on the airplane over the last day or two involved replacing pieces of a wiring harness; but the reality was that the airplane simply needed an engine change.  I can't speak to the veracity of that statement; but it was said to me.  I spoke with our dispatcher; Chief Pilot.  We swapped to another A-320 at the neighboring gate and departed about 2 hours late for a successful flight.Cause: The specific causal factors; at least in so far as what caused the EGT to over-temp in such a way with the follow-on failures (Engine Pressure Ratio mode failure; thrust reverser failure; Full Authority Digital Engine Control fault) aren't available to me at this point; so I could only speculate.  My decades of experience flying turbine engines would lead me to believe that the engine's turbine tolerances had become excessive and the engine was simply out of time.  That would agree with the statement the mechanics made to me; but I can't verify that.  As I sit writing this; it's not immediately apparent to me why an EGT exceedance (at least one that's not severe) would cause the other issues; too.  Concerning this; I don't have any recommendations for this situation to be prevented; but I can speak to the effectiveness of the planned strategy and of course recommend the reinforcement of its teaching.  An EGT over-temp on a high-time engine for a brief period during takeoff isn't exactly unheard of; and in fact is even allowed in some cases with a maintenance discrepancy item; but this event unfolded in a rather unexpected way after the over-temp occurred; and the planned strategy is indispensable in such a situation."

He was flying and working with atc to get us to ZZZ2; We agreed to get priority handling to the airport; (with engine issues that could be unknown we wanted to get on the ground as quick as possible ) and proceeded to ZZZ2. I used the iPad and contacted our dispatcher informed of the issue and our intention to go to ZZZ2. I then went to the qrh and non routine landing page went through that. I talked to the FA's and made a pa to the pax. At this point the FO had us descending toward ZZZ2 and had the plane ready for approach. column121: On departure out of ZZZ we received an engine exceedance Crew Alerting System (CAS) message briefly. PM observed the message and called for the low speed abort. We cleared the runway and taxied back to ramp to contact maintenance and company.Cause: Tail wind component was within limits and winds were variable in direction. We determined we were within safe and legal tailwind component limit of ten knots. We believe the tailwind component may have shifted which generated the momentary CAS.Suggestions: Crew will be even more conservative below the published tail wind component maximum to help ensure the possibility a shifting tail wind component does not necessitate another low speed abort.
column123: We were attempting to fly from ZZZ after landing on runway XX. We deplaned our passenger; fueled; and prepared to takeoff on XY. We had collectively decided that runway XY was the more favorable runway due to the local ceilings as well as the fact this was the only runway where a Departure Procedure existed. We had shifting and gusty winds for our landing and departure; but had made a determination that we had not exceeded the 10kts tailwind limit for the CE-700. We also determined that the performance assessment and associated limitations were met for this strategy. We lined up on the runway; ran up the engines for static takeoff; checked the engine instruments; and began our takeoff roll. My role was PM at the time; and as we proceeded in the low speed section of the takeoff roll. we received an amber Crew Alerting System (CAS) message stating that one of the engine limits was being exceeded. I believe the CAS message was 'ENG EXCEEDANCE'; which engine I cannot recall. I immediately called for an aborted takeoff; and the PF complied. We exited the runway; called clearance to cancel our release; ran our checklist and called maintenance to proceed with whatever they needed. We waited for maintenance to get back to us; and they determined that we were released to attempt another takeoff. We never did; as there was no legal way to depart the other runway; so we taxied back to the ramp.Cause: I believe that this was likely caused by the winds at the time of the event. While we had determined that the aircraft's tailwind component limitation was respected; the wind was highly variable as it gusted through the mountains near ZZZ. I believe that what happened was that during our takeoff roll; there was a change in wind that either caused a momentarily exceedance of the tailwind component or a change in crosswind loading on the engines. Either way; the change in engine intake airflow likely caused the engine to momentarily near an exceedance. The checklist for this CAS message explains that it appears when the engine N2 is in the transient region and close to exceeding an operating limit.Suggestions: While I believe that we were within the limitations of the aircraft; I also think that this instance is a great example that the limitations we fly with are legally defined sharp lines; with a good side and a bad side. In reality; the equipment's ability to perform is not as sharp as the limitations that try to define the ability to perform. While we were legal to attempt takeoff; it is clear that between the gusty and shifting winds and the existing tailwind component; we had managed to find an area where the machine was unable to perform despite what the book says. Perhaps the wind momentarily gusted past 10 kts of tailwind; but we will never know. What we both seem to be taking away from this instance is that we need to consider the totality of the situation a bit more in-depth before simply relying on exactly which side of a limitation we are on. We should have taken into account all of the wind shifting and gust factor as well as the tailwind component and simply declined the takeoff. I will be more cautious of these types of situations in the future; and will be ready to discuss with flight support why we were unable to take off even if we seem to be in limitations on paper.

column121: Day 23Statement on Aircraft X LH outboard flap maintenance.     On Day 0/1 Aircraft X was input at ZZZ for R3. My crew accomplished the base checklist in which we discovered; and I created found faults for.1)	LH wing OTBD (Outboard) upper split flap panel OTBD edge rubbing on bottom of aileron panel (Day 1)2)	LH wing OTBD flap at INBD (Inboard) actuator fairing has excessive play in fairing. (Day 1)     At the end of the shift; I gave a turnover about the damaged flap; and the actuator play at the fairing; to management during the shift turnover meeting and to the oncoming lead tech at the aircraft (as per SOP). As I recall now; I had even shown one of the on-coming managers the damaged flap and the play in the actuator at the inboard fairing.     On the evening of Day 7; our first night back I was informed at the lead turnover meeting; that the flap needed to be removed for evaluation since the ETIC (Estimated Time in Commission) was Day 10. My crew consisted of 5 technicians; 3 of which I assigned leading edge/fuel tank inspection tasks and the remaining 2 the task of removing the LH outboard flap for evaluation.     I provided the 2 technicians with the fault task card; maintenance manual procedure; and the illustrated parts manual for removal of the flaps. At which point my focus was then on the wing leading edges of which were found numerous cracks in the inner skins; and the inspection of the fuel tanks.     The flap was removed and I was told that there appeared to be damage to the actual hinge assembly; and that numerous spacers appeared to have been damaged by the play; and possibly some were missing. Me and the QC (Quality Control) tech looked over the flap and agreed with the techs that this did appear to be what was occurring. I then created a found fault (LH OTBD flap removed FOM (Maintenance Facility) Day 7) linking it to the actuator play fault. I was going to order the parts that appeared to be needed but had seen that the day shift lead tech had ordered everything but two bolts and two nuts on Day 6. At this time I ordered the bolts and the nuts. Again; at the end of my shift; I gave a turnover to management during the shift turnover meeting and to the oncoming lead tech at the aircraft (as per SOP). Also; at the end of my shifts for the remaining two days; I gave a turnover at the shift meeting stating all the parts that were on back order which were the shims and bolts.This was the last time that me and my crew had any interaction with Aircraft X until our meeting to discuss why the flap was removed the way that it was.Suggestions:  Management not wait 7 days to have technicians investigate a discrepancy if the due out time is in 10 days to where they are putting any shift/technician in a hurry up and get it done framework. Also when turnovers are given in meetings instead of the normal management shaking their heads and doing nothing; that they actually listen assigning someone in management to these large discrepancies to coordinate the way that these are worked from investigating the fault; through ordering of the parts; then verifying and expediting the acquisition of said parts instead of waiting to the last minute. Lead techs can only do so much with the resources that we have; and sometimes there are things that the resources available to management allow them to achieve at a more adequate/positive outcome.
column123: On Day 0; damage to an aircraft flap was identified; and the task was formally assigned on Day 6. With the aircraft scheduled for departure on Day 9; the timeline for assessment and corrective action was limited.Person A urgently requested assistance from myself and Person B to troubleshoot the unknown cause of the flap damage. Upon initial inspection; we identified noticeable play in the mount bolts connecting the flap surface to the outboard flap assembly.After careful evaluation; both technicians determined that a more detailed inspection of the mount bolt holes and associated bushings was required. This necessitated removal of the flap surface to allow for a thorough assessment. Following removal; excessive wear and elongation were discovered in the bolt holes; which had contributed to damage of the upper flap airfoil. Based on these findings; the flap surface hardware and bolt holes were found unserviceable.All hardware and shims were retained and temporarily reinstalled in their original positions following removal to preserve configuration integrity. A comprehensive turnover was conducted by Person C; both during shift handoff and at the morning meeting; ensuring the incoming team was fully informed of the worn flap surface attaching hardware and the status of the discrepancy.Suggestions:  A follow-up review found that the current maintenance documentation does not clearly address flap removal from the location used; and no cautions were identified regarding removal via the four attachment bolts in configurations that include factory-installed shims.To help prevent this from happening again; maintenance personnel will be reminded to ensure the task being performed is clearly supported by approved data and to seek additional guidance whenever procedures are unclear or not specifically addressed. This event will be forwarded for review; with consideration given to updating the maintenance manual to better define approved removal methods; highlight configuration considerations such as shimming; and include a note or reference outlining proper removal and reinstallation procedures when accessing the flap from this location. This event will also be shared with maintenance teams to reinforce the importance of confirming procedures prior to disassembly; especially when working under time constraints.

column121: Requested priority handling on a the approach segment to runway XX into ZZZ. The aircraft was on its second flight after maintenance. Leg one was a no passenger test flight / reposition all systems checked and functioned well. Second flight everything worked great until 1.5 miles from the FAF a dot above; I put the gear down. Gear symbols went to transition but took longer than normal. Finally the nose wheel turned green; however; the mains turned a red box. I got the following Crew Alerting System (CAS) messages: landing gear disagree; hyd low pressure; break fail. I was already talking to ZZZ [Tower]; I was already visual. I advised them of the issue that I'd like to level over fly the airport and climb to 12;000 for safe maneuvering to run checklists and return to the field. I advised that we would be requesting priority handling because the hydraulic failure meant we would have to shut down on the runway and be towed in. As we flew over the field the main landing gear due to the airflow over it locked in place and received three green indicators and the landing gear disagree message disappeared. I requested the trucks as a precautionary; hydraulic fluid is highly flammable. ZZZ [Tower] transferred me back to ZZZ [ARTCC] who gave me a heading and an altitude. We coordinated further details for the priority handling. I ran both my break fail check list and the hydraulic low pressure checklist. Upon completion I got the final vector to the IAF ZZZZZ and started the approach there. Though we were in visual conditions I requested the ILS due to the nature of the situation. Once established ZZZ [ARTCC] passed me back to ZZZ [Tower] and provided them with further details and information of the nature of the situation. I landed runway XX; stopped the airplane with the parking brake. Set the brake I advised ZZZ [Tower] we would be unable to exit the runway due to loss of hydraulics and limited pressure in the accumulator. He advised it be okay to shut down. We shut down the engines; priority handling vehicles; Maintenance and tow crew came out and made sure all were okay. We inserted the gear pins to prevent a potential gear collapse during towing; disconnected the nose torque link and were towed off the runway. NO aircraft damage; no passenger or crew injuries; and no airport damage.

column121: I departed in Mooney with a destination of ZZZ. The weather was exceptionally favorable--clear and sunny; with some ground fog in the region. I climbed to an altitude of 13;000 feet; enjoying a smooth IFR flight.As I began my descent towards ZZZ; everything seemed normal. I arrived and made my approach for landing. During the landing phase; I touched down at the typical speed of 55 to 60 knots. Upon landing; the steering did not feel normal; and the aircraft began to veer left of centerline. My first thought was that I might have a flat nose wheel tire. I provided control input to correct the course; and while the aircraft initially responded; it soon began to veer to the right. It wasn't long before the nose gear collapsed; causing the nose to drop and the propeller to strike the pavement at an approximate ground speed of 30 to 35 knots; resulting in the engine shutting down.After communicating with the tower about the collapse of the nose gear and informing them that I was evacuating the aircraft on the runway; I pulled the mixture knob; switched the fuel selector to the off position; turned the master switch off; switched the ignition to the off position; removed the keys; and placed them on the dashboard. I then grabbed my handheld radio to remain in contact with the control tower before evacuating the airplane.Once outside; I conducted a visual inspection of the aircraft and noticed no damage other than the collapsed nose gear and bent propeller. Additionally; there were no fuel leaks or indications of leaking oil. The nose landing gear doors remained unscathed; as they did not contact the pavement due to the collapsed nose gear's ability to keep the aircraft elevated. I also noted that the nose tire was fully inflated.Soon after; personnel arrived to assist me. A forklift was utilized to lift the nose of the aircraft using cargo straps attached to the propeller and to pull it to the ramp.

column121: While conducting a commercial mission for Company X; I utilized a 100 ft LAANC approval for an area adjacent to a 0 ft Class D grid. My operational plan was to remain within the 100 ft zone and utilize the aircraft's zoom capabilities to capture the target property.Throughout the flight; the remote controller interface froze on multiple occasions; significantly hindering my ability to monitor real-time telemetry and positioning. Additionally; the flight app's visual map depicted the Class D boundary incorrectly. These technical issues; combined with sustained strong wind conditions (documented by multiple controller warnings); resulted in the aircraft operating within the 0 ft Class D boundary for the majority of the 9-minute and 28-second flight.Based on the delayed and inconsistent data provided by the frozen interface and the inaccurate map; I believed the aircraft remained within the approved 100 ft ceiling during the operation. This deviation was confirmed during a routine post-flight review of the recorded flight path on Day 0; which revealed that the actual coordinates of the aircraft had overlapped the restricted boundary despite the real-time map interface showing it as clear.At approximately XA:17 into the flight; the controller issued a 'Manned Aircraft Warning.' Upon receiving this alert and recognizing a potential conflict; I immediately initiated a manual override to exit the unauthorized airspace and performed an expedited landing; touching down at XB:28. I am filing this report to document how a combination of interface failures; mapping inconsistencies; and environmental factors led to this unintentional deviation; and to record the immediate corrective action taken upon discovery

column121: During cruise at FL370 on flight to ZZZ; approximately 100 NM prior to the ZZZZZ fix; both FMS units failed nearly simultaneously; resulting in FMS1 and FMS2 failure advisories and an associated Autothrottle FAIL caution. The aircraft reverted to basic modes; maintaining altitude and roll.
