In accordance with QRH guidance; the crew transitioned to alternate navigation methods and promptly notified ATC of the dual FMS failure; requesting assistance and exit from RVSM airspace. ATC issued step-down descents from FL370 to FL350 and then FL270 and provided radar vectors for navigation.The crew attempted to navigate using raw data via the ZZZ [VOR] by selecting V/L (green needles) and tuning NAV radios; however; no reliable lateral guidance was received. ATC continued to provide vectors. Dispatch and flight attendants were informed; and the crew used additional resources such as Jeppesen charts and flight tracking website to maintain situational awareness. Fuel status was manually calculated and monitored; confirming sufficient fuel to continue to destination. An emergency was not declared.Approximately 200 NM from ZZZ; the crew manually computed top of descent and landing performance data. Weather at ZZZ was VFR. As the aircraft approached the terminal area; VOR navigation became available; and the crew conducted an ILS approach to Runway XXR using raw data. column121: Aircraft X was placed on a maintenance hold prior to boarding when maintenance discovered a hydraulic leak on the left wing. Maintenance cleared the issue; and we proceeded with an approximately 45-minute delay. The crew briefed the issue as a potential threat that would be mitigated by monitoring the hydraulic system prior to entering ETOPS airspace.Shortly before level off; the First Officer initiated a log to monitor the hydraulic system quantity and pressure. Very quickly; the HYD synoptic showed a steady decrease in hydraulic quantity on the left side at a loss of .01 every 8-9 minutes.If that rate were to remain steady; we calculated that the left hydraulic quantity would read 55% by the time we reach ZZZZ1. Complicating the matter was that the Flight Plan Release included a ZZZZ1 Field Report that indicated a wet runway; with a 500/500/500. As a restricted Captain; I am not authorized for a CAT III approach. If those conditions had persisted; we would have been eligible for a CAT II approach using the exemption. However; during our previous threat briefing; it was discussed that fog at ZZZZ1 tends to be the most intense at dawn rather than around midnight; which was the time of the Field Report.As we typically do not monitor the HYD synoptic page in flight; we initially reviewed the Aircraft Systems Manual (ASM); Quick Reference Handbook (QRH); and Aircraft Operating Manual (AOM) to determine if a continued decrease in hydraulic quantity on the left side is normal in flight. We could not find any information in the manuals that indicated it was normal. At this time; we were near ZZZ airspace and initiated a SATCOM call to dispatch to confer with the Maintenance Control. At the conclusion of the initial call with Maintenance Control; we determined the best course of action to be to continue monitoring the hydraulic quantity to see if the trend persisted and to call back on SATCOM prior to the ETOPS Entry Point if the trend continued.Upon entering ZZZZ [ARTCC] airspace; the trend of decreasing HYD quantity on the left system continued at the same rate. We subsequently contacted dispatch and requested a second conference call with Maintenance Control. During the second call with Maintenance Control; we inquired about the normalcy of the decreasing loss of indicated HYD quantity on the left side. Maintenance Control informed us that this situation was not normal. At this juncture; as a crew; we determined the most suitable course of action to be to divert prior to the ETOPS entry point. ZZZ1 was the closest option; but considering redundancy in the HYD system; maintenance facility; and the ease of rebooking passengers; we concluded that ZZZ was a more appropriate diversion field. FO began the QRC proceeding with Quick Action Item for ENG FIRE (on the ground). I moved to start APU and establish contact with cabin. It was at this time; that I realized that due differences in button location between Basic and Enhanced aircraft and multiple versions of both; that I may not have actually broadcast initial remain seated" pa using the proper function on Audio Control Panel. After placing #1 FA into loop and asking for them to look from windows to see if we were missing anything; I used handset to make addition pa to passengers to explain our situation; that they were to remain seated and that equipment was approaching aircraft. Dispatch was notified of our situation. FO finished checklist; initiated contact with Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF); maintained contact with ATC and then did the most important thing; added a pause to our procedure to make sure we were still working towards the completion together. ARFF contacted; stated no further fire or flames noticed and that the temperature; that had been upwards of 1000C; was in fact reducing. They also inspected left landing gear. column121: On Day 0; on our flight to ISP I; the FO; was the PF and the CA was the PM.After dealing with an inflight issue; we prepared for the approach and started our descent into our destination. Both the CA and I had never been to ISP; and after a careful review of the airport company pages; we briefed what to expect. We prepared; per the ATIS and the airport company pages; for the ILS for runway 24; expecting vectors to the IF CORAM. In addition; as the airport company pages informed us of increased GA traffic in the area; we exercised extra caution scanning for aircrafts.Once on frequency with the final approach controller and at 3000 feet; we were given a final vector for the approach between the FAF UKEGE (1400 feet) and IF CORAM (2000 feet); while being instructed to descend to 2000 feet. We were asked to call for the airport in sight. As soon as we made visual contact with the field; we communicated it to ATC; which cleared us for the visual approach to runway 24 and handed us over to tower; at around 2500 feet; on a relatively short base leg.The aircraft was now on a shorter than expected base leg; too high for appropriate glide slope intercept between the FAF (at 1400 feet) and the IF (at 2000 feet); additionally requiring to slow down for an appropriate descent and approach intercept. At 210 knots; with flaps 1 configuration; I elected to pre-select 180 knots; asked the CA to lower the gear and to accomplish a descent to 1500 feet. Being cleared to fly the visual approach I requested the CA to select DIRECT to the FAF; with the intention of intercepting vertical and lateral guidance to runway 24 at the FAF; at 1500 feet.We descended from 2500 feet to 1500 feet; while slowing from 210 knots down to 180 knots. Just prior to level off I noticed a momentary descent rate of -2100 FPM. During the level off; ATC advised us of a Low Altitude Alert; most likely caused by the momentary descent rate of -2100FPM; to which the CA replied Roger; we are leveling out". As we were approaching the FAF at 1500 feet; I asked the CA for flaps 2;  continued to slow down and asked for flaps 3. The low altitude alert was also followed by a traffic advisory from ATC; which paired with workload saturation; contributed to distracting us from realizing the aircraft did not capture the glideslope.Upon recognition of the unsuccessful GS intercept; I promptly disconnected the autopilot and attempted; while maintaining an appropriate rate of descent and speed; to re-intercept the GS or go back on a 2 red 2 white PAPI configuration. The aircraft was on a FLAPS FULL landing configuration at this point. While safely getting close to re-intercept; at 500 feet AGL we initiated a Go Around for unstable approach; and advised ATC; which vectored us back on final. We landed safely following the second approach.The first approach which ended with a Go around; was the result of multiple factors. Firstly; the FAF altitude was 1400 feet; and preselecting 1500 feet while going direct to the FAF resulted in reaching the FAF 100 feet above GS intercept. In addition; higher workload resulted from expecting an ILS and vectors outside the IF; to then being unexpectedly vectored between the FAF and the IF; on a shorter base and a visual approach. Lastly; the increased presence of GA traffic contributed to ATC calling us for GA traffic on our right as we were passing the FAF. At the same time; traffic appeared on our display to our left. These events greatly contributed as the distractions that ultimately resulted in not realizing that the aircraft did not intercept the GS."

column121: On Day 0 starting at approximately XA:50 local; two near-collision events occurred within a short amount of time at Sequim Valley Airport (W28); involving myself (Aircraft X); an Aircraft Y; and Aircraft Z.Incident 1 -- Runway Incursion by Aircraft Y Causing Me to Abort Takeoff.(The conflict data entered above on this form refers to this specific incident. The 2nd incident described below; concerns a 3rd plane; has even smaller margins for their near-miss.)I was operating Aircraft X and had completed all pre-departure checks. I made radio calls on CTAF 122.7 announcing my intention to taxi onto and depart Runway 09. After lining up at the Runway 09 threshold; I observed Aircraft Y move from the parking area to the runway edge at midfield (2100' ahead from me); then taxi onto the runway and proceed toward Runway 27 -- the opposite end from where I was positioned. No radio calls were made by the aircraft at any point during this time. I made multiple calls to the aircraft and multiple radio checks; no response was received. I elected to abort my intended takeoff and vacate the runway rather than risk departure with an aircraft of unknown intent on the runway.After I vacated; the Aircraft Y pilot then disclosed he had been on the wrong frequency the entire time. Despite this; his first action upon returning to the correct frequency was to announce his departure without first assessing the traffic situation or acknowledging the conflict he had caused.Incident 2 -- Near Midair Collision between Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z:At approximately XB:04 local; while Aircraft Y was positioned at the Runway 27 threshold preparing to depart; Aircraft Z executed what appeared to be a go-around or touch-and-go on Runway 09 and climbed out directly over Aircraft Y at an estimated vertical separation of no more than 100 feet. Aircraft Y appeared unaware that Aircraft Z had passed overhead. Aircraft Z subsequently called on CTAF to apologize; disclosing they had also been on the wrong frequency throughout their approach and pattern.Contributing Factors:Two of three aircraft at the airport were simultaneously tuned to the wrong CTAF frequency; rendering the standard self-announce separation system ineffective.W28's runway configuration requires prolonged runway occupancy to reach thresholds; increasing exposure time and collision risk.The Aircraft Y pilot; after discovering his frequency error; did not pause to assess the traffic situation before proceeding with departure.The narrow runway (40 ft) with no parallel taxiway significantly reduces margins for error.What Prevented a Worse Outcome:I visually detected Aircraft Y before initiating my takeoff roll and held position.I elected to vacate the runway rather than assume the other pilot's intentions.Aircraft Z's go-around (likely triggered by sighting Aircraft Y on the runway) provided vertical separation.Recommended Preventive Measures:Encourage pilots who discover a frequency error to pause; listen; and build situational awareness of the existing traffic situation before taking any further action.At narrow runways like W28 where no parallel taxiway exists; hold-short lines should be positioned to provide greater lateral clearance from the runway edge; and pilots should be explicitly encouraged -- through signage or Chart Supplement notes -- to perform a thorough visual check for aircraft already on the runway before entering.

column121: Chain of events and discovery: During an introduction flight I followed checklist usage; however after the run-up I demonstrated to the student that it is important to lean out the mixture while waiting to take off to prevent the spark plugs from fouling. I aggressively leaned the mixture as prescribed; but forgot to re-apply the appropriate mixture for takeoff (full in this case with a density altitude in the negatives). As the aircraft began to accelerate with the student's full application of power; the engine stuttered and stopped on the takeoff roll. I scanned the cockpit and noted the problem. I immediately felt a sinking feeling in my stomach; but was simultaneously struck with fear for how dangerous that situation could have been if we were off the ground. I notified other airplanes on the CTAF that we were stopped on the runway; re-started the engine and taxied off the runway. This event shook me up. As a new instructor; it was a wake up call that it is harder to diagnose issues without my hands on the controls. It was also a shock for how fast everything occurred. I have replayed the event many times in my mind and considered what I should have done differently. I am so thankful that we both walked away safely; and for the instructors that demonstrated aggressive lean procedures to me. This technique caused the engine to stop on the ground rather than in flight.Contributing factors: As a new instructor I was undoubtedly focused on the new students performance during the takeoff. The previous mental space that I would have devoted to re-applying mixture was now distracted with my student. This inadvertently and unnecessarily lowered my situation awareness. Another causing factor was lack of a final flow or adequate takeoff checklist before applying full power.Correcting actions: A learning lesson for me from this was to always use the demonstrate / performance method. An external factor at play was me trying to make the introduction flight as fun as possible by letting the student takeoff. In retrospect; I should have simply let the student put his hands on the controls to feel the correct application. If I would have focused on the demonstrating the correct configuration; the next time the student would also have knowledge of the correct mixture configuration. Additionally; my attention would be less on the students control inputs and more on an overall scan for improved safety. Another learning lesson is two fold: 1) Updating the takeoff checklist in the airplane to include mixture configuration (3rd party checklist and manufacturer's didn't include this). 2) performing a final takeoff flow in all airplanes to cover the most important items; especially ones like mixture that might have changed. For example; once on centerline; I will callout as I confirm: mixture set; props forward (if applicable); throttle forward. Closing notes: This was a very humbling event for me. I feel thankful that nothing serious happened; and I hope to do the most learning I can do from this to prevent another occurrence like this from happening. I also hope that others can learn from my mistake. I apologized for/debriefed my mistake hope that it does not negatively influence his training.

Finally; on one call the dispatcher answered; but I only got a few words in before the call dropped.  After the failed SATCOM attempts; I went to the CALL ME" button on ACARS. I then resorted to just using ACARS messages; and the dispatcher and I successfully coordinated over ACARS from that point onwards. When trying to contact dispatch via Company X on VHF2; I used the FO's radio tuning panel to change the VHF2 frequency.  However; I didn't notice the Offside Tuning Light was on nor that the FO's Radio Tuning Switch was selected to VHF1.  As a result; I made the Company X VHF frequency ACTIVE in VHF 1; but was listening to both VHF1 and VHF2; and transmitting on VHF 2.  I was therefore unable to communicate with dispatch via Company X and abandoned that idea after a few minutes.  Then I noticed on my own Radio Tuning Panel that VHF1 was on Company X; and switched it back to ZZZZ [ARTCC]  We completed the diversion to ZZZZ1; using VHF1 normally.  After arriving at the gate; I called the dispatcher by cellphone and learned that he couldn't hear any of my transmissions on the Company X frequency (but I could hear him). column121: I was conducting touch-and-go practice at CCR in Aircraft X; VFR in VMC. I was in contact with Concord Tower on 119.7.Tower cleared me for the option on Runway 19L. They instructed me to turn left and join the left traffic pattern for Runway 32L and cleared me for the option on 32L. I acknowledged 'cleared for the option 32L.'While on the base-to-final turn for 32L; I heard Tower clear another aircraft for takeoff on Runway 19L. The other pilot acknowledged the clearance. On short final for 32L; I observed the departing aircraft beginning its takeoff roll on the intersecting Runway 19L. (XA:30) To avoid a potential collision at the intersection; I immediately initiated a go-around.Tower then instructed me to 'continue downwind for 32L' and said they would call my base. I replied 'negative; I am on short final 32L; going around.' Tower responded with 'sorry' and stated they 'did not see where I was.'After the go-around; I re-entered the left pattern for 32L and completed two uneventful touch-and-goes.Later; while on the upwind from Runway 32L; I heard a jet request landing on Runway 1L and receive clearance to land on 1L. I offered to Tower that I could switch my next touch-and-go to Runway 1R to avoid being on an intersecting runway with the arriving jet. Tower replied that it would not be necessary and instructed me to enter a right pattern for Runway 32R.On downwind for 32R; abeam the numbers; Tower instructed a short approach to 32R; then immediately said 'negative; that is not going to work' and directed me to make a left 360 for spacing. It appeared Tower had not accounted for the proximity of the jet on final to 1L (intersecting runways). (XA:38)After completing the 360; I was cleared for the option on Runway 1R as the jet landed on 1L. I completed the touch-and-go on 1R followed by a full-stop on 32R without further incident.Contributing factors I observed: Multiple rapid runway configuration changes; intersecting active runways (19/32 and 1/32); controller apparently losing situational awareness of my position twice; and instructions that created potential conflicts with departing and arriving traffic on intersecting runways. column121: During departure from GNV; I was cleared for takeoff from Runway 7 and instructed to maintain runway heading to 3;000 feet. Tower also provided wind direction and velocity information. The takeoff was normal. At approximately 700-900 feet; I was instructed to contact Jacksonville Approach. I complied and continued the climb to 3;000 feet as assigned; applying wind correction while operating in IMC conditions.At approximately 2;000 feet; I encountered a significant wind shear event which caused an abrupt lift of the left wing; resulting in a strong right bank. The combination of the bank angle and climb angle of attack brought the aircraft close to a stall condition due to increased stall speed at higher angles of attack.I immediately prioritized aircraft control (Aviate); leveling the wings with left control input and reducing angle of attack to regain airspeed and prevent a stall. After regaining full control of the aircraft; I transitioned to navigation (Navigate); where I verified heading; altitude; and vertical speed; and observed a deviation from the assigned runway heading. I initiated corrective action to return to the assigned heading.While correcting; Jacksonville Approach contacted me and inquired about the heading . I advised that the deviation was caused by wind shear. After a few minutes Approach then issued new heading and altitude instructions; which I followed; and I continued the climb to the assigned altitude.

column121: I was operating Cessna 150. Prior to the flight; my scheduled flights were canceled because the owner/operator stated that the aircraft needed a 100-hour inspection. Based on that explanation; I understood that the aircraft would be unavailable until the required inspection was completed and the aircraft was confirmed airworthy.However; during the same weekend when I was told the aircraft would be down for the 100-hour inspection; the aircraft was operated for approximately 40 additional hours. This made me question whether the 100-hour inspection was actually performed at that time; whether it was properly completed before the aircraft was returned to service; or whether the aircraft was being operated beyond its inspection status. No clear maintenance log entry or inspection signoff was provided to me before I flew the aircraft.During the flight; the aircraft experienced an engine failure or serious engine malfunction involving a cylinder failure. I monitored the available engine instruments. Oil pressure and oil temperature indications appeared normal; including after the event when troubleshooting was performed; and the engine was restarted; but only limited to 2100 RPM under full throttle. However; the aircraft's cylinder head temperature indication was not available to the pilot because the CHT system had reportedly been disconnected. There was no clear cockpit indication available to me that would have warned of the developing cylinder problem.After the incident; I was informed that a mechanic had previously heard the aircraft backfire on the ground and attempted to stop it; but the aircraft was not stopped before the flight. This information was not communicated to me; the pilot; before departure. If I had been told that the aircraft had backfired or showed signs of abnormal engine operation; I would not have accepted or continued the flight without further maintenance inspection and written confirmation that the aircraft was airworthy.My safety concern is that the aircraft may have been released for flight even though the stated 100-hour inspection was not performed; not properly completed; or not properly communicated to the pilots. If the inspection had been performed correctly; the cylinder condition; compression; ignition system; spark plugs; and related engine components should have been checked before the aircraft was returned to service. The later cylinder failure and the report of prior backfiring raise concern that an existing mechanical issue may have been missed or not addressed.Another safety concern is cockpit instrumentation and placarding. If an engine monitoring system; such as CHT; is installed but disconnected; the pilot should have clear information on its status; including proper INOP placarding if required. In this event; the normal oil pressure and oil temperature indications did not provide warning of the cylinder-related failure; and the unavailable CHT indication reduced my ability as pilot to detect abnormal engine conditions before the failure became serious.In addition; the aircraft was operated under a dry lease structure; where operational control should rest with the renter. However; scheduling and maintenance availability were controlled by the owner/operator. My flights were canceled for the stated purpose of maintenance; but the aircraft was reportedly still operated by others during the same general period. This created confusion about who had operational control; whether the aircraft was actually down for inspection; and whether the aircraft had been properly inspected before being released.The main lesson from this event is that a pilot should not rely solely on verbal statements about maintenance status. Any required inspection; especially a 100-hour inspection; should be clearly documented and communicated before the aircraft is returned to service. Any reported engine abnormality; including backfire; rough running; abnormal sound; or suspected cylinder/ignition issue; should be immediately communicated to the pilot; documented as a discrepancy; inspected by qualified maintenance personnel; and resolved before further flight.In the future; I will personally request confirmation of the maintenance log after any major inspection or maintenance-related cancellation; verify the status of any inoperative instruments before accepting the aircraft; and decline the aircraft if there is any report of abnormal engine operation that has not been clearly inspected; documented; and resolved.To prevent recurrence; aircraft owners; lease operators; and maintenance personnel should establish a clear process that requires written confirmation when a required inspection is completed. Aircraft should not be released for flight based only on verbal statements. Any abnormal engine operation observed on the ground should be immediately communicated to the pilot and entered as a maintenance discrepancy. The aircraft should remain grounded until the discrepancy is inspected; corrected; and signed off by qualified maintenance personnel.
